Short review: http://images.akamai.steamusercontent.com/ugc/431571327798766106/93745073670DC86C31A3BED192BD073E62DD89D8/ I just did a 1191 hit combo with a skinny French boxer. What other game allows you to do that? --------------------------------- Long review: This game plays very, very nice. The graphics may look like doodoo, but when the gameplay is so excellent, it really doesn't matter. It's kind of charming in its own way. Mechanics: Your characters have a lot of attacks and you can do all sorts of crazy juggle combos; just watch the trailer to see the kind of extreme techniques that you have at your disposal. You'll never feel limited and you'll keep wanting to discover more and more combos. Controls: Sharp, on point. This is very important in a beat em up. Button layout is easy to comprehend. Music: Very catchy music! It resembles 90s techno, which is the perfect tribute to a classic beat em up. Extras: Co-op is couch 4 player and players can jump in. There are two campaigns and while they share similar areas, you recruit CPU allies in the second one to help out. There is also Challenge, Survival and Versus. The game can be very challenging on Normal, don't be ashamed to play on Easy or ask a friend to join you. Conclusion: Just buy the game, it's way too much fun! A wonderful tribute to old beat em ups and lots of nods to 2D fighting games. There's even Jesse from Breaking Bad as a playable character! At 10 bucks, it's a steal. You'll get plenty of your money's worth.

I'll be the first to admit, I'm not a traditional fighting game lover. I play Smash Bros (not even Melee, I play Wii U). I was born long after the age of traditional arcade fighters as well, so I have no nostalgia-driven connection to these kinds of games. On top of it all, I don't have an Xbox 360 controller to play this with; I'm typing this review with the same keyboard I use to play this game. Nevertheless, this game is so fun and charming. The controls are completely customizable and therefore very easy to pick up and start playing. While the game isn't super balanced, namely Bob Lennon destroys everyone, it is still fun and the wide array of characters prevents this moderate lack of balance from destroying the game. The game has two campaigns with several difficulties for each, so completing the game is a task for the dedicated. That being said, the game feels oddly shallow in content for some reason. But with a friend to play with, this is mostly negated. I bought this game at half-price for $4.99, and at that price the game is an 8.3/10. At full $9.99 price, the game receives a 7.9/10. Not a must-buy at either price, but definitely a fun and charming addition to any game library of any type of gamer.

Redemption: Eternal Quest is an adventuerer management sim less about the adventures and more about the characters your send on those adventures. The game starts you out with a varaiaty of adventurers each randomly generated. You can have 6 in your guild at any time. Each character has his own stats and special trait that givem them an edge on adventures. The stats also affect things like how long a character will contract themselves to you and how much gold they want for doing so. For example, a character with high loyalty might be very willing to resign your pact for a few more years but one with low loyalty might rip you off for only a one year pact at a time. There are classes you can send characters on, three generated randomly at a time that last for what I think is a random number of seasons before changing to another class. Some classes take longer to train in than others. The adventures themselves are slightly interactive. You some times get choices like choosing to go left or right, what spot to explore in the dungeons (It should be noted that dungeons are all lyed out exactly the same with 3 3 branching choices with hidden outcomes placed randomly the layout of the dungeon has no real outcome on this) or wether or not to explore ruins. I found the flavor text of the adventures and the day to day guild life of the game to be varied enough to be interesting. I love this game, it's not a tripple A must have block buster, but for the price it is fun enough to waste a few hours on. You can play with various different game lengths and game modes to make the game easier or more difficult. My favorite so far is a short 25 year campaign with perminent death. It's a great game to play while on the phone with a friend or listening to music.
Very interesting game. If you like management games, I would definitely recommend this. The dungeon crawl and minion mechanics are very unique. Good stuff!

Redemption: Eternal Quest is a text based game with a team of warriors that fight and adventure on behalf of the player in a fantasy management game, the player can have up to six warriors at a time on the roster and send up to four of them on each adventure to find hidden treasure, ancient places of power, monsters to fight and many more interesting random events which can be both good or bad. Each warrior will have a pact in place much like a mercenary contract stating how much pay they require to work for you and how for how many years that service will be,the fees can vary from one time payments to yearly salary or even a percentage of the money made from treasure that's found along the journey but when a pact ends they might demand a better deal so this part of the game is a lot about balancing the books and deciding whether to have warriors fired or hire more which can be found at the hireling pool, at the end of the day this game is about staying a float with gold so tough decisions might have to be made. Each warrior also as different stats, traits, strengths and weakness that can help or hinder you through out your adventures, two in particular are combat and dexteritywhich form a score towards the battle card games that use many monster and magic based picture cards with a random score to determin a total battle score, you can use between one to three cards per battle if you have them and the total score must be higher than the enemies score to beat them, up to eight battle cardscan be held at any one time and you can earn them through battles, opening chests and buying them every season. If you are looking for a management game that isn't about Soccer then give this a try because it's a nice adventure game that uses the power of your imagination.

First review here! Great game, really immersive narration which lets you discover the world of Philip K Di c k (thanks for the Steam censorship for a surname). I didn't know about this author before, but my curiosity is peaked now as a big fan of SciFi. It's an interesting first person exploration game, where you get to uncover multiple parallel realities. You do not get everything handed to you, and it's up to you to figure out the mechanics behind the discovery of every clue. Really creative piece of art, definitely recommended!

I really enjoyed this. It maybe helps if you are a fan of the sci-fi writer Philip K. D-i-c-k (thanks swear-word filter!), whose life and works inspired the game (and are alluded to within it). For example, PKD had all sorts of 'interesting' ideas about parallel worlds, alternate realities, artificial intelligence, robots, and mind-alterting drugs/technologies. The game mechanics are simple (find the Sigils and click on them -- that's basically it!), but the overall tone and theme are very engaging. There are clues to the location of the Sigils if you pay close attention to lighting and audio cues, or to apparent visual 'glitches' (not all of which are bugs!). The art and music are excellent, and the 'other world' portal effect is very nice too. Caveats: there *are* a few genuine bugs (dodgy collision etc.), and the only save-points are automatic ones at the start of each chapter.. so give yourself time to play a whole section in one sitting (each of the 3 main chapters takes about an hour to get through).

tldr version - a tentative yes to recommending the game, given the low price and that it is innovative and quirky. I would have caveats on that recommendation, and those are in the LBRIA (long but read it anyway) version below - I am a big fan of PKD. Some works inspired by him (take the novel 'Philip K ♥♥♥♥ is Dead, Alas' for example) can be excellent and expand upon the PKD universe in interesting ways, almost existing as part of it. I didn't feel this game really did that though, to me it felt more like re-used ideas from his books and writings without any real expansion on them, which was a shame. - It also seemed to miss some of the charm and humour that fills a PKD novel. - Personally, I was a bit uncomfortable with the audio used in the end chapter, but to save on any sort of spoiler I won't discuss what that was. Those who know PKD's life will know what the audio represents. - I fell through a wall to ground level from the first floor, leaving the elevator I used to get there still up top. I could then enter a big open space behind where the elevator should have been - doing so triggered the elevator to come down, which promptly pushed me through the wall, trapping me between the wall, a desk and a door. The kind of reality breakdown the game had not intended to include! I was disappointed that this relatively short, small, and fairly constrained game had bugs like that in it. - No saves. If you start a chapter, finish it, else you'll be back at the start when you come in again. This is particularly vexing if you get squeezed into a stuck situation by a glitched elevator, for example. - No explanation at the beginning! For those stuck, type the faded letters representing the ongoing story on the typewriter. For the rest of the game, I like that the mechanics weren't explained and it was a voyage of small discoveries, but it will leave people thinking it's crashed if you throw them in to a static screen with none of the expected keys doing anything right at the outset. - Very short, so keep that in mind if considering it. Doesn't seem to be much that would reward repeat playthroughs (based on having repeated some chapters due to the lack of saves ahem.) - The mixing of realities sure was neat though, as were the stories of each chapter. Just wish it had been developed further, personally. - The areas to explore are fairly limited, and the mechanics of the puzzles are too. Since it's short, that doesn't get old, but did leave me feeling like this could have been so much more! - If you like The Stanley Parable, you might like this too; though Stanley is more rewarding of repeat playthroughs, and manages to have more of the wry humour and wit that would have fitted in well here!

This game is short in gameplay, content, replayability, and commentary on Philip K. ♥♥♥♥. What is there is a perfectly functional Stanley Parable experience, and one that looks visually interesting. The hidden object gameplay is functional, but lacking. There is no real interactivity in this game, and playing it unfolds like an Linklater-esque indie movie where hunting for glowing sigils unfolds the plot. Also, the latter half of the game is weak and unoriginal, and my enthusiasm plummeted when the predictable revealed itself. Just when the game's central theme is beginning to get interesting, it grinds to a halt. I finished this game in two hours. Even at sale, I would consider this overpriced, and I've contemplated getting a refund on the strength of the experience being such a short one. Buying this game is more like renting a movie than adding another game to your library. Did I enjoy the experience? Yes, somewhat. Would I recommend it to others? No. For this price you can also get one of PKD's novels, or a collection of short stories. If you've read it all, and you're so starved for ♥♥♥♥ that anything will do, maybe you'll find satisfaction in one of Californium's back alleys. Or maybe the experience will leave you feeling dirty and used.
Paranoia? Mental Illness? Broken Home? You too can experience the downward spiral into alcohol and drugs that made Philip K. ♥♥♥♥ the writer he is!

Respectable effort, aesthetically this is probably more true to PKD than most of the movie adaptations out there (A Scanner Darkly coming closest). It is quite minimal in its gameplay and narrative, but in many ways it is a knowing and loving homage. It won't be everyone's cup of tea, but for a hardcore PKD-head it is an essential experience in how it recreates the ontologically suspect, shifting realities of PKD worlds within the simple framework of a 'hidden object' game. The themes are semaphored rather than fully developed, and I wouldn't say no to a more adventure-game treatment with a bit more depth, but I found the final chapter strangely moving and effective nonetheless, the music was a very nice touch. Thanks to the devs for this brief trip into the mind of my favourite author ever.

I've been eagerly anticipating this game, and it did not disappoint. It can get pretty frustrating at some points but I felt that it was well balanced and provides just the right amount of difficulty. There will always be a point when you realize what you were doing wrong or you figure out another way to tackle the mission that's faster and more efficient than what you were doing before, and it feels incredibly satisfying when you successfully pull a plan off. I feel like 3 chapters isn't enough, but considering the level editor, achievements, and amount of time I've poured into this game (I have just finished chapter 2) I definitely got my money's worth. Buy it now if you can, don't wait 5000 years for it to go on sale, the devs deserve the money. Some notes: -The weapons all feel different; all of the guns have varying degrees of accuracy, power, and bullet count. I kind of wish there were more melee weapons though. -The pixellated art style is quite lovely, and I feel like it's a step up from Risk of Rain in many aspects (though I loved Risk of Rain's art as well). -Chris Christodoulou's music is amazing as always, and sometimes I found myself pausing the game just to listen. -Really loved the different environments in the game (especially the clubs), and I like that stuff slowly gets added to your apartment. -One gripe I have about the game is that the requirements for getting 5 stars aren't very clear, though I guess it's mostly based on accuracy of headshots. -Headhunter+hammer master race.

Frustratingly tedious. That's really the main reason I have for not recommending this game. It's just frustratingly tedious. When I heard that there was a Gunpoint/Hotline Miami mashup, I thought that it would be perfect for me straight away. Turns out I was wrong. Deadbolt is exactly like I said above, essentially a side-scrolling Hotline Miami. It's a lot like Gunpoint too. 2D, side scrolling levels filled with all kinds of enemies that you can take out in different, creative ways. Sounds great. The gun fights are viscerally satisfying, as the game handles blood and dismemberment extremely well. I grabbed a high powered revolver near the beginning of the game and stuck with it throughout the game, blowing heads off and smearing blood all over walls in intense gunfights. The shooting mechanics are tight and responsive. The game itself is short. I can imagine one would blitz through the entire thing if the later levels weren't tedious grinds. The levels themselves aren't very consistent. Some are really well designed, but then others end up just being a flat layout of a few rooms in a grid formation. As for the actual story, it was interesting enough. You play as a reaper called Deadbolt as you investigate a gang called the 'Zombie Kingz', and you find yourself wrapped in a city-wide operation between a load of other gangs. Now, onto the bad part. The frustrating tediousness of Deadbolt is entirely due to its lack of checkpoints. You see, in Hotline Miami, the system was perfect. Each level was split into multiple parts filled with enemies, and once you finished one part, you'd hit a checkpoint and you'd be done with that part of the level, which meant you wouldn't spend too long on the same level. In Deadbolt, however, you get the entire level all at once, with no checkpoints. You die in one shot and have to take on everyone else in the level without taking any damage at all. The tediousness comes from having to restart the level. In a game like this, you're meant to die many times and keep restarting and working out a routine. The routine is a small plan you form on how to take out each enemy in the most efficient way. You start the level thinking 'Knock on this door, shoot this guy at this time, then grab his gun and shoot this other guy, then close this door to avoid being shot and hide behind this cover at this exact moment to avoid another shot.' The routine works, so you keep doing it every time as you begin to learn each enemy's mindset and they become predictable. The problem is that Deadbolt will force you to keep killing the same enemies, again, and again, and again. Even if you've nailed it down the science, EVERY time you die, you'll have to kill them all again. Sure, it sounds simple enough, you just keep using the same routine and move onto the next group of enemies, but then you attack the next group of enemies, and they kill you instantly, and then suddenly you're back to the beginning again, killing the first group again. Eventually, killing the same group of enemies in the same way again and again gets boring, after which you start to lose interest, and just wish they'd be dead already so you could move onto the fresh content and stop playing through the same part you've already played. The earlier levels of Deadbolt are alright, as they aren't so densely populated, but as you go on, you can spend a half hour killing the same group of enemies over and over, just to finish ONE level. This tediousness pretty much killed the game for me, and left me wishing it would just end. I haven't even unlocked all the weapons, and I couldn't be bothered, because the last 4 hours I spent in this game were just mindnumbingly repetitive and boring. Also, I should add that controls are little bit inconsistent. To swap weapons, you've gotta scroll up for your primary, but down for your secondary. But then when you're using a staircase, you press W to go up and W to go down. Just confused me a little bit at first. For the smaller, earlier levels, this game really shines. Later on, it's just a pain in the ♥♥♥. As much as I'd like to love Deadbolt, and as much as I'd love to put it in the same category as Superhot, Hotline Miami, Gunpoint and Mark of the Ninja, it just isn't fun to play. Oh, I should also add that the soundtrack is really ♥♥♥♥in' good. Like, really good. Whoever made that soundtrack deserves a raise.

However, the Story Mode is still pretty fun and you can squeeze a good 6-8 hours from it. Now to what the game TRULY excels at... The fighting mechanics. This is quite honestly some of the best fighting I've ever had the chance to play with. Period. I personally enjoy the heavy style of the Mortal Kombat series (and Injustice) to the more brisk, choppy style of Street Fighter. If that's your thing, then pick this up. The combat is fluid, extremely in-depth, even better than MK9's, and allows you perform some pretty crazy combos. Also, the character roster is pretty large and includes every character you'd want in a DC fighting game. An intense technical fighter, in the same vein as Mortal Kombat, made by the same team (NetherRealm Studios). Using the DC license to it's fullest, Injustice: Gods Among Us focuses on what appears to be an all new story, that actually works quite well. There's an alternate universe where Superman has lost his way, killed Lois Lane and destroying Metropolis (not really shown) due to the Joker's tricks. Superman ends up killing the joker. Characters from the normal comic's continuity (Earth 2?) cross over, and it tells a story over a number of battles and cutscenes where famous characters come into conflict. All that's to say there's viable and solid reasons why Batman and Superman fight, as well as all sorts of other match ups. Of course that's JUST the story mode. The game has a standard progression mode, a mission mode (Earn stars by completing different challenges), online multiplayer and the rest that someone expects from a fighting game. And the Ultimate Edition version also includes all the DC characters as well to add more longevity into the game. That being said it's a fighting game, so the combat is what is' important. And the fighting in Injustice is Solid, if a touch uninspired. Most of the characters's moves fit into a street fighter move list. Quarter circle forwards, or back, back and forward or similar move sets. There's nothing as complicated as Zangiefs moves, but at the same time, the faster move sets allow the user to pop them at will. The game also moves quite fast, so while most moves are blockable it takes a little skill to properly block (or use a move that counters it). At the same time the move lists are made available when pausing the game so there's not a lot of challenge to memorize the list (and no list is overly long. Around 10 moves a character, some lower, some duplicates (air + ground versions). There's three other elements worth mentioning, There's a super meter that can be spent in a number of ways to change up the fight for the very technical fighters. Second there's a 'Wager' move, that you have to spend to try to cause damage to the opponent. Finally each character has a super move, that if it hits, causes MASSIVE damage to the opponent. It's harder to pull off and takes time to build up but they are the game changers. One last thing that distinguishes the game is the environments. The player can interact with the background to trigger different things to damage their opponent, evade their opponent, or add a weapon to use against their opponents. In addition the players can send their opponents through the walls at times, to add huge damage, and go to a different location. These work to great effect. Sometimes they feel unbalanced or unfair, but they work well the majority of time, and definitely add to the epic battles happening on the screen. Overall Injustice is a great fighter. It's not perfect, and heavily relies on the DC licenses. It has a superman who can somehow lose fights to almost anyone, and an aquaman that is kind of cool, but overall it's a worthy addition to the fighting genre, and heavily packed with a ton of content. Note: I played the Ps4 version in addition the PC version. Both performed similar, the core of my review is based on the Ps4 version but appears the same in the PC version.

I was first recommended Mass Effect out of the blue one day by a good friend who assured me it was 'like Star Trek with guns'. It's not. It's SO MUCH BETTER than that. The Mass Effect games 100% deserves their place as an iconic series. While the first game has a more complicated skill system than its sequels, I personally preferred the ammo-less mechanic used here, where weapons used is throttled by overheating and the subsequent wait for cooldown. This makes Mass Effect 1 the only game in the series where a true sniper class is viable, since in the sequels the scarcity of sniper rifle ammo relegated it to an occasional weapon choice for most of the game. In Mass Effect 1, the sniper rifles were almost the only weapons I used. Mass Effect does have a 'tactical mode' where you can issue commands while paused, similar to the Dragon Age series. The beauty of Mass Effect is that it's not required at all. I all but ignored it for all 3 games and never felt that I was at a disadvantage. Come for the shooter. Stay for the amazing story. Import your saves into Mass Effect 2 and 3 and fall in love with the world and companions you shape around you. The Mass Effect series is the only game series I have played for 2 full playthroughs. There is no doubt I will play it through entirely again in future.

Originally posted on June 28, 2010 Mass Effect is essentially the cross-breed result of mating Bioware's RPG formula with Gears of War's combat system. The game is a console title first and foremost, which makes many of its flaws all the more apparent on the PC, however the art design, and story telling are top notch, and the roleplaying elements (through not as deep as the game would like you to think) are interesting enough Graphics- The game features dated graphics technically speaking, even for the original release date. Incredibly low poly models, low res textures, and mediocre effect (particles) make this game less than awe inspiring visually. However the art design and character models are generally pretty good, especially when in comes to aliens, geth, and other creatures. The animations look quite good, and generally the art design is very creative. Cutscenes look quite good, generally speaking, although the overuse of bloom sometimes is annoying. Yet the game is clearly custom tailored for the 5-year-old hardware of consoles, with irritatingly frequent load screens, jarringly low res skyboxes and other textures, and annoying amounts of loading zones masquerading as elevators. Sound- Generally speaking, the music is superb, with a electronica soundtrack that harkens back to deus ex. The voice acting is also generally good, although there are a few rough spots, and the characters are generally memorable as a result. The sounds for weapons and other effects are also quite nice, providing a space age feel to the combat Gameplay- My biggest problem with this game by far is the gameplay, as Bioware seems to have taken their typical RPG formula (which I have mixed feelings about) and mated it with Gears of War's cover and combat systems ( which I hate). Bioware's formula allows for alot of choices in the story, randomized loot drops, and other RPG staples. It is also notorious for lazy level design. absolute cookie cutter carbon copies of levels litter this game, quickly draining what little flavor the side quests hold for you from the game, as there is one generic mine level, two generic settlement levels, and one generic spaceship/station level that the player encounters AGAIN AND AGAIN throughout the game. At least Bethesda knows their level design, give them credit for that. Bioware's level design flat out sucks. It doesn't end with cookie cutter levels however, for the driving sequences are equally frustrating. Exploring strange new worlds in a rover and finding hidden collectibles (tedious, but an RPG staple) along with side quests sounds fun in theory, but the Mako handles like a physics nightmare. In addition, some of the terrain is modeled with so few polygons and so extremely steeply that it is almost impossible to simply cruise around the planets. Instead the mako climbs impossible angles, flips and does barrel rolls (without taking damage of course) and gets caught on terrain. In addition, the turret has almost no traverse, and you only get half xp from kills in the mako, making the armaments almost useless. Driving quickly became on absolute nightmare for me, and I was using a mouse and keyboard. I can only imagine how those poor saps with controllers felt. Third, the cover system is awful and unnecessary. I hate gears of war, or any third person cover shooter for that matter, on principle. So seeing this system in a game made by people who used to develop RPG's for the PC first is awful. It locks you into objects unnecessarily, makes it difficult to get out, and frequently got me killed, frustrating me to no end. It also leaves levels littered with absurd amounts of cover for you and your enemies to use. Not that this unrealistic feature mattered, as the favorite maneuver of most of the AI in the game is to charge straight at your guns. Other features such as the leveling, perks and squad management worked better, but even those got clunky. For example there is no way to examine your crew member's stats while on the Normandy, so equipping them via the weapons lockers can be very confusing. Inventory management in general is clunky, and needs a menu that is actually designed for the PC. Finally, I found the fact that every member of your squad had one of each weapon, even if they weren't trained in its use, to be very odd, and the fact that armor and weapon stats were not tied to the model or skin of the item gets very confusing. The loot often felt... generic at best. Ultimately, this game has a story that will draw you in and it can be a lot of fun to play, but it is full of irritating gameplay, so much so that I would almost recommend skipping all but a select few of the side missions. It has a large amount of replay value, with many classes available to play as and many ways to resolve a situation, (although not as many as you think, 2 dialog choices often result in Shepard saying the same exact thing, a false representation of a choice), and it will keep you playing for many hours. Just take it for what it is: Consolized.

I was always told that F.E.A.R. was the best of the series and after playing F.E.A.R. 2 I agree, I still have to play the third one though. As I expected, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin was a huge improvement both graphically and gameplay wise. I'd say it's still a great looking game and I could clearly notice how the gun handling was improved. I felt like on the first game the recoil was somewhat too much and needed more recoil compensation on the player end but on F.E.A.R. 2 I think they've 'perfected' the shooting to better suit 'casual players', while I think this is a good thing I understand if others think that the first game had more 'realism', if you can call it that, to the weapons. One thing I still find to be rather 'lazy' about F.E.A.R. 2 is that most of the guns are basicly just new skins of the older ones, you've got the assault rifle, the submachinegun, the 'penetrator' but I gotta admit these new skins look pretty damn nice so I forgive them, one other thing, or maybe it was just me, I'm pretty sure they re-used the enemy voices and player and enemy animations from the previous game, I'm not complaining they did just the right job but I still find it lazy on the developers end. At the end of the day they did a pretty good job in keeping the shooting just as great as in the first game with improved visuals and gun handling, not to mention you can pilot Mechs on this one which I found out to present a nice variety of gameplay but, they did also put some turret segments in the game (I believe two), which I feel they didn't overdone it like some games. Still I think despite of having a great shooting experience, F.E.A.R. 2 wasn't that tense or scary as the first one, I think that's because of the improved graphics everything looks more 'colourful' while in the first game everything looked kinda dark and sinister. In the end I think F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is a fine piece of work and definitely a great shooter with a nice continuation to the F.E.A.R. plot and the ending clearly gives you the clue that's more to come, I'm pretty sure you can't go wrong with F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin, either if you're looking for a great first person shooter single player experience or a first person shooter with a paranormal twist to it, F.E.A.R. 2: Project Origin is clearly the game for you.

Significantly worse than F.E.A.R. yet still functional. It has obviously been dumbed down and aimed at consoles and you can't even bind additional mouse buttons without an outside program. More weapon and enemy variety is always good as well. There are some scripted set pieces and 'vehicle' sections but they're rare enough that they don't get in the way.

The refined sequel to what is already a bit of a modern classic, F.E.A.R. F.E.A.R. 2 improves on everything and as a result, plays much more smoothly than its somewhat clunky predecessor. Graphics are crisp and clear, comparable to Max Payne 2, which means they are still holding up rather well today. Sound is excellent, much better than the first installment. In particular, the score has seen notable improvement. Gameplay still rewards a tactical approach to combat, though you no longer depend on your slow-motion ability quite as much as you used to in F.E.A.R. Gunfight are often winnable even without resorting to slow-motion, though using it definitely helps. F.E.A.R. 2 provides the same type of scares as the first game, so they may sometimes be fairly cheap. Due to the improved visual fidelity, the gore is much more explicite here, however. This game is not for the squeamish. Any shooter fan should definitely pick this up, even if they didn't like or play the first installment.

Despite being a bit dated, IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 is still a top notch flight sim. The game had a number of substantial updates since its release, with the most recent being just last year (2013), though I'm not so certain if the game will see as much now with Battle of Stalingrad on the table. A plus in my book, some aircraft that have multiple crew stations can be manned by human players in multiplayer, so there's a possibility you can even get friends who don't care for flying to join in. If you're looking for a solid World War 2 to 1946ish era flight sim, this is a safe pick and you especially can't really go wrong with it if you get it on sale. If you're new to the flight sim scene, I would suggest trying the A6M but be careful of your dive speed. If you excede 350mph, you could cause damage to the airframe --even to where the wings tear off... Edit: I was just thinking about this review the past few days and it occurred to me that I should mention (emphasize) that this game is a flight sim and not an arcade style flyer. A flight stick is highly recommended for this game because flying with mouse and keyboard is going to give you a pretty lousy experience.

A unique entry to evergrowing roguelike genre and one of the best I’ve played. Dungeon of the Endless skillfully merges both turn and real time based strategy in a way I’ve never seen before. It strikes almost a perfect balance between luck and strategy. It keeps you on an edge but is fair. Things can be chaotic but there's a logic in that. Dungeon of the Endless is rich in playable characters and game modifier accompanied by pleasing visuals. Because of that, I name it a top tier roguelike. Final score : 8/10 The good : - Addictive with “just one more turn” syndrome - Pleasing presentation - Unique gameplay - Fair and balanced but also keeps you on your toes - Variety in simplicity The bad : - UI is not as informative as it should be - Equipment and gear is not as numerous as in other roguelikes - Humor is kind of meh - Lacks a story

Firstly, a TL;DR for the lazy reader: + Great Art and Music + Great lore, for those interested in the Endless setting + Great design and interpretation of the rogue-like genre + For 10 bucks, you can enjoy at least a solid 6-10 hours of gameplay and potentially dozens more. + Multiplayer is finally fixed and well designed. - However, it is heavily team dependant and one player can genuinely kill three others by making rash decisions. With friends, this game should be a blast. - The game’s mechanics may not be for you, read section “Game Mechanics” for more info. - Some minor bugs Read More: Dungeon of the Endless follows the lore of previous games by Amplitude Studios (Endless Space & Endless Legend) and presents it this time, in a “rogue-like” fashion. The objective is simple: Explore the dungeon, search the rooms and then get the dust crystal through swarms of aliens into the teleporter for the next floor. The mechanics of this game are somewhat profound and relatively unique, based on a turn-like system that dispenses new events after a door in the dungeon is opened. This isn’t to be mistaken with the fact that the game is very much in real-time, players will have to make very quick decisions on defensive relocations, retreats and emergency use of skills/medkits. I imagine the most convenient mechanics comparison to be drawn here is to that of Faster Than Light. Game Mechanics: The biggest design component of the game leads me to warn potential buyers to possible disappointment- heed my word. Suppose the main feature of rogue-likes that people enjoy is the risk: reward decisions one has to make. This is tied with the subsequent “snowballing” of a character’s strengths and the increasing challenges; item collections in Risk of Rain, Binding of Isaac. At first glance, Dungeon of the Endless may not meet these expectations, decisions to develop one’s character is often met with only simply a new ability or meagre stat boosts. This isn’t an inherent flaw in the design but rather, a choice made to cater to players having to combine all of the resources: Industry, to build modules for resources and defense, food for character development and medkits, sciences for researching better modules. A player that may only enjoy, say, the character development of a roguelike will be met with disappointment here as one cannot neglect the other aspects of the game in order to succeed- the very same reason why Amplitude has curbed the potential of characters clearing whole floors by themselves. However, when said mechanics are utilised properly the game truly shines. Players will find themselves scrutinising their floor’s layout, optimising where to allocate power and resources, what resources are most required, whether or not to save resources for the next floor, if characters should be replaced by newfound possible companions, the list goes on. Decision making is the core component of the game that gives it drive, anticipation of resources desperately needed, whether it be dust or a replacement for a fallen companion will lead players into a game that forces them to make decisions. Make no mistake, the game is balls to the walls difficult and will not hesitate to stomp on your carefully knitted floor plans whenever it gets the chance. For this, I commend the developers in creating a relatively fresh balance of mechanics in a recently inflated genre of “rogue-likes”. Multiplayer: Multiplayer is also quite entertaining with gameplay identical to that of singleplayer except with one character per player. This leads to less micro-managing and a larger pool of resources, making the game easier only when players can cooperate properly and plan ahead together. The biggest complaint I have about this however, is the lack of a save-multiplayer feature, thus games can often stretch out for multiple hours and leave players exhausted or unwilling to continue. Furthermore, the lack of a host migration system means that if a host leaves the game—you’re screwed. Amplitude must address these features as they are critical to the quality of gameplay and I find myself only playing alone or with a friend instead of with other players. Art & Music: Other than that, the only noteworthy mention of the game is its further development of the Endless lore, which I am a particular fan of and DotE does not fail to impress, new characters and revelations about the world left me relatively keen on the story of the game. Furthermore, secret character interactions are revealed when specific combinations of characters are placed in a party, leading to a more interesting play through and for the eager player, experimentation with compositions. This lore is accompanied by a pixel art style that is of an impressive quality and the usual stature of music that amplitude has impressed me with so far. Though these are subjective and you in particular may not agree with me. Final Judgement: For the singleplayer experience alone, I recommend the game for its listed retail price. On sale, it’s a must-buy. Though multiplayer bogs the game’s overall quality down, Amplitude is known to respond very well to player criticisms and I am confident they will address these issues. Overall a fantastic little game. On my first playthrough, I fought hard to get the crystal to the elevator and in my rash attempt to escape, left my other party members behind to get eaten by aliens. Made me think “Would play again”- and I did, a lot. Update as of 27th April 2015: - There is a save feature for multiplayer now, this was much desired and a great improvement. - However, the community has slowly died down. It is not impossible to find a match depending on the hour of the day, however there are far fewer lobbies than a few months ago. I would recommend searching globally and not just within your region when searching for a game. - Multiplayer overall works well now, however there has been observations of a recent bug that removes items from the characters of certain players whilst they return when traded to others. Hopefully this is fixed by amplitude.

This game brings back a lot of fond memories. I won't deny that the people who love this game very clearly grew up with it as I did, and it was a shame that Aeria cancelled publishing it before we could fully enjoy it. HOWEVER. The memories I have of this game are a prime example of the term 'nostalgia blinded'. I was overjoyed to hear that someone had began publishing the game again, and eagerly downloaded it. Needless to say, I only downloaded the steam version afterwards to write this review. As the game is nothing I remembered it to be. The UI and controls are crazy asinine and clearly haven't been updated since its original publication many years ago. The class system, while diverse, has lots of really dumb out-of-the-way requirements for getting certain classes. The stat system is impossible to figure out before you hit the cap that allows for free resets on your own, hence why the game has to link to the damned wiki in the first place, and even then you're not gonna be 100% happy with your stat build. The story is a product of its time, quickly written and thrown in just for the sake of saying it has one. And the gameplay consists of near nothing but quests containing 'Kill this thing until you're ready to get the quest where you kill its palette-swaps. Maybe get a party and kill a boss or two.' As much as I loved DOMO back in the day, playing it now makes me firmly believe that it should have stayed dead.

When i got ‘Shadow Warrior’ at its release in September 2013, i thought it was one of those titles, which only wraps it’s original game by 3D Realms in a new graphical enviroment. The thing i have totally ignored is that there is an actually well thought shooter behind the cheap one liners and mediocre graphics. You play Lo Wang, a hitman/ninja under contract of Zilla, who is leading a huge corporation, who orders Wang to pick up a sword for two million dollars, but as soon you arrive, everything goes south and you find yourself in a Kill Bill-esc swordfight. At this point the world is overrun by demons and destroying the area you are in, where you end up half dead in a burning house, that leads you to meet Hoji, a mysterious and weird demon, who was with the man you supposed to buy the sword from. You both agree to work together to get the sword back to give him the chance to return to his old home: The Shadow Realm. With a story arc like that, you immediately feel like in an 80s B-movie, which the game perfectly set the tone in this way by starting off the game with Wang sitting in his car, jamming to Stan Bush’s ‘The Touch’ and Flying Wild Hog (the developers) bombarding you with cheap one liners, which Wang not coming up with on his own, rather to his knowledge of comic books and his affection to B movies himself, which I, in my first playthrough attempt, totally ignored, even though it helps the tone of the story a lot, because it still has a chance to change it’s pace to a more serious tone, which it actually did and did well. I got super drawn into the progression of the Wang’s trip to ‘hell’. Since Lo is a ninja, he is good with a blade and since the katana — called the Nobitsura Kage — you were supposed to pick up ends up in your hands, you are going to use it in all its capabilities, which becomes a main portion in the game, where you learn via picking up KI stones over time a bunch of skills. The way to execute those abilities are pretty easy to learn and execute, but being very similar to each other that you may end up looking up which one was which, but did not hurt the overall experience at all. I was very surprised by how fun it was, even though you will never encounter a blade on blade grinding sword fight. Wang is a hitman as well, so he knows how to use guns, which you pick up the typical variety of weapons throughout the game that are upgradable through money that you can pick up in the levels. They feel pretty basic and not really satisfying, but i can forgive that, since they are not the main focus and in context totally fine, but i wished for that extra ‘oomph’, that Shadow Warrior couldnt deliver. You are also able to learn passive abilities, resulting in things like more HP, damage resistance, more stamina and so on by collecting Karma, which you get by killing enemies and by chaining kills together, multipling the score of the staged fights. I really liked the variety of enemies in here, giving every monster and human a distinctive look and feel, keeping ‘annoying’ types at a minimum and thanks to the game’s self awareness can’t hold itself back to comment on them, too, which was a nice move by Flying Wild Hog. But the time you actually have to fight them, it is a fun and challenging experience. The way it introduces new enemies to you is very good to understand, giving you enough time and chances to understand every enemy’s capabilities and weak points. Sadly, even with it’s pretty neat animation work troughout and really good lighting effects, the game will/has not age(d) well, thanks to its pretty basic visuals in the level enviroment department. Some areas feel way too stretched, copy-pasted and boring, which could be the result of trying to hide the many secret areas (that not only are being extra Karma pools or Ki stones, even some levels mapped in the original Shadow Warrior’s early 3D artstyle, giving a nod like some other games did before, but definitely nice to see). Don’t get me wrong. The game looks pretty good, but its not blowing your socks off. The sound design was fine, i did not get angered by bad sound choices here, more a bit confused that the video cutscenes are a bit lower than the actual game, but not by a huge margin. Everything sounds pretty solid, so there is nothing to complain about. All in all, this game is not only an oldschool game with new shoes on, it’s an improvement with very good 2013 gameplay mechanics, an actually very cool and interesting story with a fun main character and sidekick, which lets you forgive it’s mediocre graphics. The only thing that holds me back to play this 9 hours and 30 minutes trip is that i won’t keep the sword in the New Game+ (here called EX mode), which is a huge bummer. Otherwise, if you like skilled based shooters, this one is for you and i can not wait for the second one to arrive.

Okay, the year of 2012 really disappointed me on a number of counts. I was feeling quite forlorn that the gaming industry was beginning its downfall and headed towards an influx of cookie cutter games, each with slightly 'better graphics' or 'one or two new weapons' or 'better killstreaks' (You know what game I'm talking about). You know, it sells, so keep doing what sells, right? As horrible as that sounds. Well, to the point, Sleeping Dogs restored my faith. Square Enix really did an awesome job taking up this project when it got scrapped by the guys doing the True Crime series. This game is like GTA except without so much of the random ♥♥♥♥ to do. It's a bit more serious, a bit more mature. The storyline was great - I'm not going to ruin any of it, but it was awesome albeit a bit too fast. It was a game I finished and I felt that I wanted more. The ending left me a little empty because it felt a little rushed, I mean, you could totally make a Sleeping Dogs 2 or something, definitely. Overall though, this game really, really made up for all the disappointments that year (yes, the whole year). The gameplay is pretty fluid, the fighting can get repetitive after maybe four days straight playing, but it always keeps you on edge. It was very hard to put down. I never found myself bored and, even now, I'll start it up and complete a couple side missions. They really, really did a great job recreating the Hong Kong cityscape and atmosphere. You can't go into most of the buildings, but the world's so big that you won't even want to. The ONLY thing I think I would've done to make this game better is tweak the story a little bit. Just near the end. Everything came together really quick. This could've been a full on, like, 60 hour game if they wanted to. And just... well, playing this game really beats a lot of the crap dramas you see on TV. THAT's how good it was. I beat the game and for a long time after, I felt really empty because nothing else really matched it. There was a sort of... 'What's next?' And that gave this game the move from 'good' and 'great' to 'outstanding'.
Mechanically, it's a decently fun game. Thematically, it's a catastrophy. An example of just how much of a cluster♥♥♥♥ it would be if the GTA games took themselves seriously.

I went into Medal of Honor expecting another gritty, brown, cover-shooting FPS, clicking away until the brown terrorist hiding behind brown rocks stop moving. What you get is, well, that but not nearly as deary and grinding as I had anticipated and even did some things pretty well. Maybe it's because it's been a few years since I've played a single player modern military shooter. First off, the campaign is head scratchingly short. For a series that has always focused on single player it's a little puzzling that so much time and money was put into a 3-5 hour campaign. That being said, short is better than long and grindy. There is a good mix of stealth based and all out war game play, with vehicle and sniper sections scattered through out that keep things fresh. You jump between three view points that tie together nicely whcih prevents the transitions from being jarring. One of the things that I thought they did well was conveying the uncertainty of who is a target and who is a civilian, or even a friendly. I do think they missed an opportunity to put those decisions on the player, as most of those situations occur in either scripted sections or cut scenes, but still, it didn't go unnoticed. There were a few more details that helped lift this game a bit above mediocre. The guns felt varied and solid, although the shotgun is overpowered, and headshots look and sound satisfying. My favorite detail was the sound design. There's this really cool thing when you're standing near a squad member who's speaking and you can hear their voice both through the radio and normally. Sluggish controls, tactical map unit caps, and a real time macrostrategic map of the galaxy make this a pain. Yes, there's a pause button on the galactic map, but you can't do anything while paused like move fleets or build units. It only works on the tactical map. Also, some of the scenario maps seem glitched on tech levels. If you go to advanced settings and reduce the starting tech level while playing on hard, then you start with reduced technology but the computer starts with regular technology. Having X Wings, Y Wings, and basic frigates doesn't really match top of the line Imperial Star Destroyers. There's also no hold position command. You can tell units to stop, but it's very easy to lure or get lured, especially when units won't respond instantly after being lured. This creates a very annoying situation where rocket infantry wreck light tanks, anti-infantry vehicles wreck light infantry, and aircraft become pointless (although aircraft dominate easily until AA weapons are around). In space, it means fighters and bombers won't withdraw from cruisers, and larger ships that are slightly misoriented beacuse they advanced two inches too far take forever to turn around. The game really isn't that bad, but it's like they choked it for no good reason and ruined the experience. If the units were responsive, tactical map unit caps didn't exist, the galactic map was turn based instead of real time, and the pause button let you issue orders while paused, then this would be an easy thumbs up. I have no idea why they ruined their own game with arbitrary restrictions.

Let me preface this by saying if you like puzzle games are have a sharp mind, you may want to check out Braid, and it's hard to say yes or no to whether I recommend this game, purely because it depends on who is looking at the product. I however, didn't have a great experience with it. I went into Braid after hearing a lot of hype and was really let down. Yes, the visuals are fantastic and beautiful, but some of the monster designs are just UGLY. The main enemy (out of only around 3 different varieties) just looks stupid, and another one is just a rabbit that makes a creepy noise before it jumps at you. Sound is alright, although I didn't really find any of the tracks incredibly great. They all do fine as ambience I suppose. Gameplay is alright. The main concept of time control is well executed, and the first world is pretty fair and rewarding. The difficulty has a very steep curve though and after a while the puzzles just seem overly complex and frustrating. Sadly each world is sort of independent of each other, and that's a shame. Instead of continually building off how you can use your powers, each world will basically introduce you to a new way of using your power or a new time concept. In one world, moving right moves time forward and left is backwards; in another you create shadow versions of yourself whenever you rewind time that will perform your old actions. This makes that in every world you have to master a completely new and mostly unrelated way of looking at puzzles. For some, this might be amazing and very rewarding, but as stated previously, the difficulty ramps up way too quick and things just get frustrating. Also, some hidden things are so hard to find you basically NEED to look up a walkthrough to get everything...I guarantee that 50% of people will have to restart the game due to a certain secret being hidden and locked away if you complex the puzzle from the first world. AWFUL design choice there. There's a bit of story that has apparently sparked a lot of discussion, but it didn't really grab me because it's put so separately from gameplay and told disjointedly. You'll basically have a few books you can read a wall of text from at the start of each world, but other than that there's nothing substantial. Whether or not you'll enjoy this game really depends on if you are a puzzle lover and critical thinker. If so, most of my review points probably won't affect you, and you won't get turned off by difficult puzzles. You can take more time to get into the story and I've heard that it is great if you do so, but it never really captured me. Check out a few gameplay videos before you purchase this game.

I have to say, I don't recommend this game. It's a really frustrating game. It is soo nearly a good game. There's soo many games like this, that are just better, but without the irritations: 1) Randomly can't fire, no, I am not in frameshift drive, no the power consumption says only 76% so i am not maxing out the power, yes the weapons are assigned to fire groups. The target is tracked in range, and weapons are deployed. Just cannot fire. Could fire before I upgraded the ship with exactly the same config and weapons, but after removing the upgrades to exactly how it was, the ship can't fire. This has happened with 2 different ships now, it's annoying. Lots of people have this problem and it's not at all obvious what the problem is. If there was some indication of what the issue was that'd be swell. It's not nice to find out you are totally unarmed in the middle of an interdiction. 2) Marking star systems on a map gives you a cursor on the hud. Why then when marking stations on the map, does the hud 'forget' that destination coordinates? 3) Ship upgrades. What the *hell* do the stats mean? Was it just too much trouble to print the current stats of what the currently installed equipment is so you can compare it? Some of the upgrades you've got to stare at the screen for about 5 minutes trying to figure what the hell you get when you upgrade them if you get anything at all. Some upgrades you can actually work it out, because the numbers change, but others, it makes no sense. 4) The game dynamic is such that some missions you get fined for if you can't make the deliveries. For example, I picked up a mission, i took off in the direction and found that my jump drive couldn't make it, so i failed the mission and got fined. Next thing i'm minding my own business running a mission which also has a penalty, and abdul insane comes after me for 400CR. I lose my ship and I lose my cargo and get a fine, I wouldn't mind, but I now have an even larger bounty on me. This feedback loop where it inevitably progressively escalates and you are forced to either lay low for a bit, or just have half the galaxy tailgating you just isn't a good game dynamic, at least not when you are starting off. 5) In games like Naev (for example) races seem to have more unique cultures, technologies and principles. In that respect Elite Dangerous is very 2dimensional in the environments narrative. 6) THE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MENU SYSTEMS. ARGGGGGGGHHHHH. 7) In other elite like games you can chain jumps together automatically. There's a short period in between jumps where for about 20 seconds you are a sitting duck, but having to manually jump every time is tedious. 8) Why do you always drop out of a jump with frameshift on facing and accelerating towards a star? I mean why. Is it the developer's idea to just prevent you ever going to to toilet? What possibly could be the rationale for that? 9) Cube like space stations have no guidance on which entry point you should enter at. I cannot find any markings, so it's always a 50/50 guess, lots of people must fail their missions because of this. 10) There is a huge variation of distance between stars and stations. It would have been nice to skip the b/s and jump directly to a station within a system - given you aren't interdicted and you have enough fuel. In summary this game just don't feel complete. I know it's massive in terms of the procedurally developed environment etc etc. And there are a lot of good points to it, but god damn some of these things are annoying. Additional comments. There's bugs that occur when you're landing, for example if you land, and you go inside the hanger, and you click refuel. The menu will totally lockup and you need to restart the game. Another issue is that since the new changes to the missions, it's now a constant struggle to keep your head above water financially. The smuggling missions have totally disappeared. There's these irritating wait around for 2 hours to meet people in space to collect cargo missions. There's new multi legged missions which means you get faffed around for 4-5 legs while you try and earn a pittance. When people said they wanted more content. They meant they wanted new content in addition to the old content, not instead of, with all the rewards halved! I used to be able to find missions for 1.5 mil. Now I am struggling to find anything over 50k. God only knows what it's like for people just joining the game, where they are earning maybe 1k a mission and losing 4-5k every other run! EDIT: a new update has come out that has solved a lot of these frustrations. Therefore I am giving this game a thumbs up :)

Gameplay is standard but fun and quite addictive. You could compare it to 'Crimsonland' which, most likely took this game as an example. The RIP-Trilogy is not perfect and it's not for everyone but I believe fans of the genre won't be dissapointed.

The Following Statements are solely based on the official Seattle Campaign of the game as i have yet to play any of the user created content for the game. What the drek do i say about Shadowrun : Returns ? I guess what i can say are the following things regarding what i consider to be my Game Of The Year 2013 First lets start with the music it is absolutely phenomenal and really makes me regret not buying the soundtrack edition because it is the kind of music i would probably play a lot of it if it was available on spotify because it is that damn good plus it matches the mood of the game perfectly. Second lets talk about the sweet sweet combat it is so satisfying to get crits when attacking the enemy but i should back up a bit and explain that yes it is turn based combat that has a cover system in place to reduce incoming damage if you are positioned right and it is downright brutal at times but at the same time is very rewarding when you succeed in a fight and with a nice arrange of attacks both ranged and melee as well as a nice assortment of spells and abilities so in short i would say the combat is very good and meaty. Third i would like to discuss the story and probably my most fav thing about the game the dialog options. Okay so in short without spoiling anything regarding the story it is very much a solid Cyberpunk story that is really dark and has some WTF moments that had me in shock during those moments and most importantly hooked and wanting to know what will happen next but even then i may be saying too much so i will be quiet for now regarding the story. Okay now onto one of my favorite parts of the game the Dialog options. It is very well written and sticks true to shadowrun`s tone through and through with terms like drek, slotting in, chummer and my favorite fraggin. Depending on what skills you have you can sometimes avoid a fight entirely or open up dialog options you normally could not without the required skill or receive mission items that may help you later on in the game i mean come on this is a dialog system that while is not as deep as lets say Planescape Torment but is a ♥♥♥♥ ton deeper than any modern “AAA” game to come out in recent years with the exception of Witcher 1 and 2. Fourth lets talk about character creation which while it is nice and they have a decent amount of portraits for you to use and there is a little bit of customization. I really wish there was a lot more to it then the game offers but i think this may be a limitation due to the engine and how the game was made. Conclusion i highly recommend anyone to buy this game if they are a fan of cyberpunk or shadowrun or both i really mean it when i say it is so damn good and at a price of $19.99 how can you not buy it it is practically a steal in my opinion and probably one of the best things of all it has steam workshop integrated into it and there is already a community effort to bring all the Shadowrun source books to Shadowrun : Returns here is a link for that http://www.shadowrunidentity.org/ If i had any complaints about the game it may be the length of the official campaign which took me about 16 hours to complete left me wanting more and i encountered a few minor bugs but nothing major or game breaking. TL/DR : Go buy it now and play it.

Pros: - Nice visuals, awesome portraits, the art style is very fitting and immersive. - The combat system is enjoyable but could use some polish. - Dialogues and NPCs in general are very well written. - The story is part dumb, part engaging. It fits into the setting, altough it somewhat turns downhill towards the second half. The writing is good for the most part though. - The setting, I personally love the setting. Cons: - The combat, despite its solid foundation feels cheap and too easy. - The decking sections are super boring. - The game is waaay too linear for an RPG. It takes away from the awesome dialogues when you know you can't change a drek no matter what you say/do. - The music is rather forgettable. - The spell effects are down right ugly. - The game world is gated behind loading screens and comes in small chunks. In this regard it's similar to Deus Ex - you're being teleported from location to location, thus the world seems small and contained. They did an awesome job of bringing Shadowrun to PC, but sadly it's just isn't that good of a game. Feels more like an interactive novel, an introduction into the world of Shadowrun. The dialogues, the NPCs, the visuals and the cyberpunk distopia, the immersion of being a runner... it's all there and it's a pleasant journey for the fan of the setting. It's just it doesn't feel like you're DOING anything, other than watch the game play itself. It's like this GM friend who's got this really awesome story he wants to tell you... but you can't alter a thing, your PC is but a pawn in his hands and you can only sit, listen and bask in the ambience. And if the story was indeed as good as he promised I would have enjoyed the ride way better. Either way, if the story was better or the gameplay was more polished the score would have been higher. As is the final score sits somewhere around 6-7/10. Still, the game is so cheap these days, and the setting is so awesome you should buy it anyway.

Bought this game because I loved the cRPG style. It did not disappoint, from character creation, to doing the first few areas, I am truly enjoying the game. It has a decent amount of a challenge, making it so you can't just rush headlong into a battle, but gives you a feeling of satisfaction when you are able to beat a boss, or a difficult battle. Every class seems to be balanced in its own little way, and each one feels unique to the others. Some of them are very similar to classes from other RPGs, but at the same time different enough so that you don't feel like you have played them ten times over. The graphics are great, and are exactly what I expect of the genre, if not a little bit better. I tried to play Divinty: Original Sin, but I could just never get into it. This game, has a totally different feel, and is exactly what this genre needed. I hope that we can see more games in this style, and hopefully see some sort of mod community come out for this game. When I finally beat this game, I can then look forward to starting over again, but with a different class/race/background/etc. If you love the cRPG genre, you need to give this a shot. If you still have Baulder's Gate, Icewind Dale, and Neverwinter Nights installed on your PC, then you really need to give this game a shot. It improves on those games, and adds a bunch of aspects that you didn't even know you wanted.

The game is nice. I have 2 remarks – about gameplay and about story. Gameplay. In short: it actually is quite good (but I agree that there are types of people who would not like it). Before buying I have read professional review on top review site (forget which one) that gave the gameplay very bad scores. The reviewer claimed that he was shocked how easy his character dies while his comrades are almost invulnerable. After completing the game I was missing several “intel” locations. So I went online, googled (top result) walkthroughs to find out were the missing “intel” was and redo the chapters to collect the “intel”. As walkthrough was on youtube I watched in disbelief how person doing the walkthrough fights “the end game turrets” mostly simply standing and exchanging fire from afar (and not with long range weapon either). That was ridiculous, because turret is supposed to be almost invulnerable from front and turret is supposed to kill you very fast. So I guess only reason why the walkthrough guy was able to win the firefight was because he probably was using lowest difficulty (or/and probably some cheats). I also suspect that professional reviewer I mentioned in beginning was same type of player who loves to run with the shotgun against fortified position and expects to win. So if you love to slaughter waves of enemies simply by running into them this game is not for you. Me, I personally find that automatic health regeneration makes character incredibly tough. Quite often it is more beneficial to simply absorb fire while you maneuver to better position rather than spending ammunition by shooting back. However you must always make a judgment call which position really is better one and you have to maneuver. I would also note that level design is good. It has surprising variety of mission types. Waves of enemies are quite manageable and enemies never suffer “never ending” syndrome. Learning curve is very ok with first missions (“chapters”) being easy and demanding very limited tactical knowledge that changes latter. I agree that keyboard controls could be better. Story. In short: it ok, not as good as some claim. The story is very good in sense that it forces casual player to think about idea that “enemies” are not bad and do not deserve to die. If this is your first realization that quite often there is truth (right) on both sides, then you would probably go away quite shocked. The most epic moment is also very emotionally done. However to tell the truth this is neither the first time this idea is presented nor this is the best way of presentation. The biggest problem for me was complete lack of choice of action (while in game dialog repeatedly claimed otherwise). I read the interview where developer explained that the bad path was intentionally chosen because in life the good is not rewarded (Here I simplify what he said). While that is technically true. It would be completely untrue in case if in real life you would have option to see the results of your mistaken action and then “reload” and do it differently. If in real life you would have reload button you could easily avoid almost all the bad moral situations presented in game. Actually in real life you can avoid some of them even without “reload” just by applying common sense and prudence. The actions taken by main character was simply childish and idiotic. That broke my “suspense of disbelief” and unlike many other people I felt no real guilt for gameplay actions (but it was emotional nevertheless). However citing the end game “it takes a strong man to deny the reality” – maybe that is the case with me ;-). That said I must note that “bad ending” actually makes the game into non replayable. Why you would want to repeat the suffering once again?

Chaos Domain is an indie game which single handedly illustrates everything that is wrong with AAA game development. I had read the reviews, I had listened to TotalBiscuts WTF Is, I had perused screenshots and checked out gameplay footage. I knew exactly what Chaos Domain was and how bad it was. Yet when I started that first level up, I STILL was disappointed and let down. This game is the posterchild of terrible game design; the controls are crap, the animations are janky, you can only aim while moving in the direction you’re aming, and the entire game looks dreadful in action. I don’t know how they budgeted out the creation of this game, but I have to imagine that 85-90% of the entire development budget went to the visual fidelity of the levels and characters. Aside from those two aspects, everything else in the game is neglected. Even the art assets for the pickups look like they were thrown in at the last minute. I don’t remember where I got this game (I know I didn’t pay for it, thank god) but even going into it expecting garbage, Chaos Domain still managed to not live up to my expectations. High definition textures, dynamic lighting and fancy particle effects don't make a game good, only good gameplay can do that.

Edit: (updated 3/21/16) Coming back to the game after some time, with RTG having added more chapters to the game and, disappointingly, I have to change my review to Not Recommended. The last time I played, I got through a bit of Kian's story before I finally just got fed up and said forget it. I was in the middle of working through a to-do list for a NPC and it just bored me to death. Between that, and another puzzle type task I had just completed, whose solution was so arbitrary, with no logical train of thought leading to it, I decided to step away from the game for a while. I recently decided to play from the beginning again, having played through once before. Figured I'd start again, with a fresh perspective. I don't know if they changed the controls or what, but just getting past the first bit (with the falling girl) was a hair-ripping experience. After several unsuccessful attempts at trying to slow them down, then grab them, I finally said 'Nope. Forget it'. I'd gotten through that bit with complete ease when the game was just released, and it was far more intuitive. So, I think they changed something with the controls or interaction since then, and not for the better. The storyline, dialog, voice acting, everything else is great. If this were an interactive story, my opinion would likely be quite different, as Ragnar Tornquist and co. consistently turn out brilliant work in that capacity. However, as this is a game and intended to be interactive, I feel it falls short. As much as I would have loved to, I can't recommend this. From now on, if I feel I want to visit Stark and Arcadia, I'll just play one of the first two games in the series.

As someone who's played the two games that came before, I was happy to see the kickstarter. Some continuation on the story and maybe even a conclusion. I've been with the game since the kickstarter and the developers haven't disappointed. Regular updates and lots of fine tuning. Although they have chosen for an episodic release, I rather play the game in one go so I've waited until all 5 books were released. The game itself is a worthy successor to the story and offers some nice plot twists. Choices you make actually make an impact on the story and for some of the choices you'll hit yourself in the head later on in the game, even though at the time you thought you made the right call or thinking wouldn't have any repercussions. I'm sure there's a lot of content I haven't even seen yet. There's a pretty decent introduction to the story included in the game, but to grasp the full story you really should play (or watch a let's play) of the earlier games. There are quite a lot of references in the game that are only appreciated if you have played the earlier games. The story is mostly linear with only a few puzzles that require you to wander around and find the right things to do. This is a plus in my case as I love to enjoy the story and not have too many distractions of pointlessly running around until I find the one thing that the developer hoped you'd logically find in order to solve the puzzle. I think a pretty nice balance is found here. The pause introduced in order to solve the puzzle allows you to appreciate the story more once it continues. The graphics are great and the only downside I'd think of would be that there could be more expressions on the faces of the characters during conversations.

Don't be fooled by 68 hours, My main account most likley has several hundred hours of gameplay. This game offers so much, but it's rather difficult to get into, while being incredibly easy to get in to. Starting the game and exploring is fun and you can do it from day one, at first glance it's a fun game, but nothing you'd spent much time on. Now If you look past that, there is actually so much. The leveling system isn't what determines a character. Maxed stats are. In game 'potions' are used as a sort of currency in the trading economy, along with gear and other items. These potions are obtained by defeating difficult enemies and completeing certain dungeons. To problem is, getting this far takes practice, detrmination and grit. Death is inevitable, dont let it set you back. Learning how to rebound from deaths becomes an integral feature as you make characters that are more and more powerful. Even the most powerful characters who have all 8 stats maxed are prone to quick deaths, the game in unforgiving, and requires skill, but offers much in return for those who deliver.

After having played the entirety of this game with a co-op partner, I can hopefully give a helpful review of Kane and Lynch: Dead Men. First of all, lets start with the pros. There's not many of them. The voice acting was tolerable, especially the titular characters, however, there were a few side characters that were just meh. The save point system is great. If you or a teammate dies (and you will, more on this later), it almost always starts you at the point just before you died. The character exploration was fairly limited, but what little backstory you learn of Kane and Lynch is somewhat interesting, even though it never really gets used in the story. And thats it. Now for the cons... The story is abysmal. The loosely connected missions barely have anything to do with each other outside of verbal descriptions between scenes with no visual guidance. It really has a way of disconnecting you from the story. There's no gearing up for anything, it's just a 'we have to do this to get that' and boom, you're doing it. This is more of a gripe than anything, but vertical split screen on a shooter means you will be killed by enemies you run right past because you couldn't see them. Im sure in single player theres not much of an issue but on co op we both died multiple times because of it. The controls are fairly awful on a Xbox 360 gamepad. The shooting feels imprecise, always accelerating just beyond your target. Normally you could just move the left stick a little to compensate, but the cover system, which automatically forces you into cover, will cause you to lose the shot. It's just sloppy all around. All in all, it was a decent co-op game. But if I had to play this alone I probably never would have finished it. I would not recommend this game, but if you really must get it, do yourself a favor and wait for it to go on sale. It's not worth more than three bucks. If you don't have anyone to play this with, then skip it altogether.

Kane and Lynch: Dead Men (Played on the Highest Difficulty) Positives: + A nice array of weapons available, although with this said there definitely could have been more as well. + Funny dialogue between Kane and Lynch which really lightens up missions, I had quite a few laughs. + Decent storyline. + Shooting is fun, but the hit detection is not 100% accurate, which detracts from the experience a little. Negatives: - This is a very short game. I finished it on the highest difficulty in just 6 hours. Only purchase it on sale like I did and never pay full price. - Very linear gameplay, no open world exploration or opportunity to do so. - Bad graphics. Overall Score: 6/10 Kane and Lynch: Dead Men is a fun, short action game which will entertain you. Just be aware, it won't last long at all.

To shorten this, learn about their movements, add a little bit of timing and voila. Otherwise ask the forum for help, there are always a few people willing to help you. Cons :/ -- The pvp system, ranking seems fair, but the netcode is the huge frickin' problem here, not as bad as in Dark Souls 1 (according to my experience) But i mean : You live in Europe... and someone from Malaysia invades your hood.... lag teleports and face stabs you. It sometimes seems impossible. Also there are alot of OP mages and healer nabs. And hundreds of trolls (This actually belongs into the Pro section, since they made me laugh pretty often GIT GUD) -- The DLCs, when you're finished with the main story, you probably wanna play the DLCs such as i did.
