Need for Speed as it should be. Racing against cops and other racers in the sleekest and fastest cars up to date while avoiding traffic in enviroments like forests, highways and deserts. So what are you waiting for? The big open roads are waiting for you.

Need For Speed III: Hot Pursuit was one on my favorite games back in the old Need For Speed days. When they announced the revive of the Hot Pursuit series back in 2010, I was pretty excited. Driving in a high speed chase from the cops was a fun experince to have. Having to be the cop was a great experince to have if you want to be with the law and wrecking racers. There's a big list of cars ranging from everyday cars to one the most exotic and expensive cars in the world. They all have their unique characteristics of thier driving in Seacrest County. From the bulky Dodge Charger SRT8 to the lightweight Koeningsegg CCXR Edition. The county of Seacrest is a beautiful resemblance of four different enviroments mashed together with one of the most exhilerating roads I've seen in a modern Need For Speed game. The sounds in this game is mindbolowing. Where my head just couldn't handle it and I had to stop and catch myself before I pass out. Ok I'm kidding on that but really the vehicle sounds is really amazing. Graphics For a 2010 game, I have to say that this game itself is a pleasuring beauty. All enviroments ranging from the mountains to the desert have a beautiful scenery that keeps the driver in awe while driving in a intense race. The details of each vehicle is really amazing with high tessellation that helps the vehicle look more realistic and more immersive to drive. The carbon fiber on the Koenigsegg CCXR for example is just amazing. The lighting effects is just beautiful from day to night. The weather effects has got to be the best I've seen so far in a Need For Speed game. Seeing the relfection on the wet surface is really fantastic. The textures of the road is just amazing with each road having their own unique style to it. Also since this game is made by Criterion games. It's not surprising that the damage model is just jawdroping from every crash that you witness. The only complaint I do have to say is that theirs no Anti-Aliasing to be found in the game. Gameplay Since this game is supposed to bring back the original Hot Pursuit feel, there's obviously not going to be any customization. Which some people would complain but since all of this was based before Underground 1 and 2 it would make sense. Color picking has been reduced to manufatured paint only which is a bit disapointing. For the driving part, it's pretty fun driving every vehicle since they do have their own unique handling and drifting. What I thought was pretty interesting that the devopers added weight to the driving which makes it more realistic. For instance the Bentley Continental Coupe is a pretty heavy vehicle. It's pretty difficult to swerve the vehicle from left to right since it's a heavy car. For the Pangani Zonda Cinque, it's nimble so the car can swerve easily around traffic and the cops. This new pursuit weapon that Criterion Games added is a pretty cool feature. Each side (racer/cop) has some unique features that only one side can use (For instance cops can call in road blocks or a helicoptor whereas the racer can use either a jammer or turbo). In my opinion they'll seem to be balanced in a nice mannor. Freedrive is a decent experince since the player can use freedrive to test drive the car without having to deal with cops/racer or crashing out. The main downside is that since there's no option for a online freedrive, the replayability of that mode is small. This new social feature, Autolog, is a really nice feature that let's the player challenge their freinds, share photos and disscus. The downside to this is that people that has little to no friends will think that this feature is useless to them, but it's a not a flaw by any means. DLC wise..... well there's no DLC here becuase we know that EA doesn't like PC players that much besides Battlefield. Conclusion This game is a great succesor to the past Hot Pursuit games and I feel like this game is great for any casual or competitive players. PO. Slender: The Arrival was a rather great game. It had a complete story line to lore you in, a beautifully building atmosphere, and the graphics where absolutely STUNNING. There are little few bugs from what I've found(And trust me, the second I get a game, I like trying to break the maps to said game.), and a nice map to free explore. But by far, the best thing I found about Slender: The Arrival, HAD to be it's atmosphere. It had a great build up that left the player on edge, which made the jump scares all the more better. The rustling of the forest around you, the crunching of the leaves, or in the case of the generator level, the sound of footsteps running at you, all help immerse the player. The game uses rather nice functions of forcing the player to do what they don't want to, such as entering a building or going down a hall to grab a note, knowing they'll have to go back and he might be standing there. Although, I will say, the complaint I have about this game is that the enemies themselves often get stuck on objects while coming after you. It subtracts from the game play to know if you angel yourself right or quick turn a corner, you could get them stuck there for a moment. In Slenders case, He'll become unstuck the second you move to far away and instead transport away, but in Kate/Jeff The Killer/ Whoever the one running after you is, They could get stuck there for a good while. This game is best played in the dark, with either surround sound or headphones in for best possible outcome. Overall, I'd give it a 8.9 of 10.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a game that folluws up on the succesfull 'Alan Wake', starting it's story where the DLCs of the latter left of. So you should definitely play the original first, because of spoilers and because that is still better. But is Nightmare good as well? I'd say yes, but for different reasons than the original. Where Alan Wake had a story of horror, confusion and mystery, in Nightmare this is simply not possible anymore, since the player (or at least the Protagonist Alan) already knows what is behind it all. So the game has to go into a different direction. Nightmare has a good and fun combat system, great soundtrack (that raises some of the moments in the game to nothing short of awesome), an interesting story that fully embraces the new possibilities now that Alan knows what is going on, and most importantly one of the best villains in Video Game history: Mr. Scratch. Said villain appears on screen only as a real human played by an actor, who does a marvellous job at looking like the perfect psycho killer. With superpowers. And an army of unholy monsters. Admittedly, the game's world is not that large and the game doesn't take that long to complete (except if you really like the combat and get into the arcade mode), but if you happen to get it on sale, for say under 5 bucks, you should give it a try, especially if you liked the original.

They Breathe is a strange game that can not be categorized into any genre. You play as a frog that jumps into a body of water. Not sure if it is a pond or what. Your goal is to save as many drowning frogs as you can by pushing them into air bubbles until they regain enough to swim away to the surface. I use the word goal lightly as it doesn't really matter if you save them or not. The two enemies is a cow like creature and a jellyfish which will consume you. If a jellyfish consumes a drowning frog it becomes much more powerful. You can defeat these enemies by either waiting until they run out of breath or guiding them into air bubbles. They get stronger and faster when they get a air bubble so it may be better to simply out maneuver them until they drown. Environments are cool and spooky looking the deeper down you go. The game itself actually has a creepy vibe to it which suits it perfectly considering all the animals you will see drown. The moody music you will hear throughout is pretty great too. There isn't really much to talk about this game as it is a very simple game and also about 20 minutes long. It's not an expensive game by any means but that may turn some people off. Not much to do other than dodge enemies and collect bubbles to stay alive. That does lead to some pretty cool moments where you have to decide if your own life is more valuable than the random drowning frog next to you. Even if you die though you will respawn in the last check point which will be just right before an enemy encounter. I don't really see the point of dragging this review out. This is a good and interesting game with a very memorable ending. The short length of the game is both a blessing and a curse. On one hand it keeps the simple gameplay from getting stale but on the other hand it is a 20 minute game. I do think this is a game worth experiencing but do expect an artsy type of game instead of a gameplay focused one. It is certainly unique I'll give it that and it's visually appealing. Though there is no real reason to replay it once you finish so be sure of what you are getting when you purchase this. Recommended to those that want a very short but memorable experience.

No steam Overlay unless you add it as a non-Steam game (lol) and no support for wide screen resolutions... Great game, but this stuff pisses me off. I'm not saying the game is bad. It can be real fun but these things just won't let me enjoy the game at its full. I need the overlay because that's a useful way to communicate with my friends in-game. I've already asked for Ubisoft support. What happens is this: Usually the exes of Steam games are modified so that they HAVE to detect Steam and the license prior to run. Here, Ubisoft went lazy and made a runme.exe (search your binary folder) that reads a runme.data Inside runme.data is specified the name of the exe (in this case R6Vegas_Launcher.exe) that will en up being executed. The runme.exe is the one that holds the Steam license validation... Yes, Ubisoft didn't modify the actual game exe to be compatible with steam, it created another one with the validations that calls the retail one. So if you run the game from Binaries folder Steam won't track your game time. Is it really THAT hard to modify the game exe so it can be fully compatible with steam? Okay the game is old, forget the resolution, (there is patch that changes the congif file online that does the job) give me the overlay with tracking and I'll be able to recommend it.

I've been a fan of the Rainbow Six series since the beginning but after Raven Shield the series headed in a console centric direction. While Vegas has the console feel but still it a great game on the PC. The play commands Logan Keller the new team leader of Rainbow, a international anti-terrorist organization, sent to a Mexican border town to capture Irena Morales who is a terrorist ringleader. Failing to capture Irena, Keller is ordered to head to Las Vegas to handle a new crisis there. The story is on par with any Tom Clancy book or game so it filled with action and a couple plot twists but overall its not memorable. Gameplay takes on new features from previous installments. One is the cover system much like Kill.switch and Gears Of War players can take cover against almost anything and either blind fire to give covering fire or pop up and shoot. Another add in is a regenerative health system that is much like any other game that has one. In previous Rainbow Six games before each mission but with the going more console centric that went away and was replaced a simple order giving control scheme which in Vegas was refined and is pretty simple to give your team members orders to breach, grenade, flash, clear, etc. Sound FX do sound great in the case of the weapon fire and other general FX's and the voice work is good and fit the game well and while the soundtrack is good and fits the game its just the same orchestral work like most games. Overall the game is a great game to experience for fans of the Rainbow Six series. 7/10

Rainbow Six Vegas offers a decent tactical shooter experience by allowing the player multiple ways of dealing with situations in the game (choosing an enterance, method of entry etc.) and allowing the player to regularly select their loadouts of different weapons and equipment. This particular Rainbow Six title falls short on many things however; with poor story character voice acting, clunky controls, incompetent friendly AI, enemy AI with stupidly inhuman reflexes, and an awful damage system which blinds the player when hit and forces him to sit and do nothing for a good few seconds, killing the flow. I personally found this game unjustifiably frustrating a bit too often but after completing the campaign I felt a satisfying sense of accomplishment, a consistent characteristic in the Rainbow Six series. It's a decent shooter and it's something to try if you're looking for a game that doesn't hold your hand.

Any game that requires an AI to prevent micromanagement is needlessly complicated. This game is the poster child for that statement. As it stands after 5 planets are colonized you need to turn over control to the so-called AI. It isn't very intelligent, and will bankrupt you doing stupid things, building stuff that isn't required. It will chew up any asset you have to suit its whims and create a totally negative economy. If I'm going to play a game I want control of what is happening. If the game is so complex that it gets boring to manage, then redesign the game. Otherwise design the human right out of it and let the computer play itself (that will sell well, I'm sure). The only thing I can say about this game is imagine playing chess with three people and two of you are controlling one side, but aren't allowed to speak to each other. You end up getting in each other's way and no coherent strategy can be formed. This is Stellaris in a nutshell. It needs a total overhaul from the ground up.

I read some of the other reviews and the main criticism seems to center around 2 issues. The first being that the game feels and plays a bit rough and seems incomplete. To that I say, give it a month or two, the updates that have come out have already dramatically improved the game, and the quality of the game itself more than makes up for it. Also, these complaints if stacked up against almost any other 'incomplete' game on steam don't really hold water. Go play one of the survival alphas that cost 30 bucks and are so buggy you'd be lucky to successfully do what the devs demonstrated in the trailer, or play whatever new steaming pile of excrement slurped out of treyarch this week for console and come back and talk about how complete stellaris is. The second big complaint is that mid-late game play is redundant, boring, and or lacking content. Well, to some extent I'd have to agree with that criticism, but at the same time I'd say this is the exact same complaint you might level at ck2 or eu4. Everyone who's played eu4 extensively knows of that moment when your empire is so strong that the game becomes easy and you can just bulldoze through entire continents. Stellaris operates much in the same way, so it has many of the same pit falls in terms of playability you encounter in eu4. If you're willing to overlook a bit of early bugginess, and so far a slight lacking in content and you want to play an intricate sci fi empire game with an almost tedious amount of detail this is for you. If you're maybe possibly not entirely sure that genocide is a bad idea and want to murder all of the other species/people you encounter, this game is for you. If you like eu4 and eu4 in space is what you pray to Gaben for every night before you go to bed, well, it has arrived.

Surprisingly good game. It's well designed and intuitive, and it manages to fix what's generally boring about tower defense games, by reversing the roles. I think they call it 'tower offense'. Basically, instead of protecting a core from incoming enemies using lame towers, you actually lead your units down a path (you can modify the path at any time). With the cash you get by picking up minerals, you can either upgrade your current units or buy new ones. During the game, you also have to walk around the battlefield to grab some items, while your units are still moving. Those items function as area effects and you can use them to repair your units or prevent enemy towers from attacking them. The game also does a great job at introducing new elements in every level. It never feels stale or repetitive. It even has a somewhat interesting story, at least for that kind of game. The kind of story that doesn't feel out of place; just short dialogue here and there that subtly introduces new gameplay elements, while giving you an extra incentive to keep playing. Great mix of action and strategy. 7.5 / 10.

I love the simplicity of it: movement, 5 'stances' (overhead, high, mid, low, crouch), a jump button, and an action button. That's it. Using combinations of those controls, you have access to a surprising variety of moves that help you push past a constantly respawning opponent, only to celebrate your victory by jumping into Níðhöggr's waiting maw. The one downside, though, is the price. $15 is crazy. $10 would've been MUCH better. I hope they continue to develop levels/content for this to help justify the price. There's a damn good reason this won so many IGF awards, and I'm glad it finally made it to a full release version. A Tower Attack game?! The most important thing I want to mention here is, Space Run is a tower defense game. A pretty simple one, mind you. But in depth, it's much more than that. While the basic of the game consist of building offensive and defensive weapons to keep your ship alive, as well as thrusters to actually move through space, the active part of combat is much more complex than a simple tower defense game. Every structure comes with 3 upgrade slots that can be purchased with credits earned from previous runs. These upgrades mostly consist of 2 active upgrades and one passive upgrade. The active upgrades range from reorienting weapons, over massive single-time attack to quick-repair. All in all, the tower defense aspect of the game is just one part of it. Using active abilities wiesely, adjsuting to your stubborn cargo and handling all the micro-management, is the really big part of the game. And no, we don't need a pause button or anything, be fast or die, that's it, that's the challenging part of the game. - And really, it's not thaat hard. Space Run is an interesting and fun mix approach that will kepp you well entertained for ~10h if you want to complete it. With the current number of 30 runs, I have to say, I'm not sure if I would've bought it outside the Steam sale however.

At first, I suffered from the same problem as most people with an incredibly low FPS, not performing at a level in order to play. They told me to fix the problem I needed to change the graphics card which the game ran on, from my integrated card to my NVIDIA card. To do this, I went to my graphics card control panel. After this, I click on the 3D settings in order to gain access to program settings which allowed me to switch cards. Also, I updated both of my cards from the device manager. I hope this is helpful for all that are having difficulties. If not, I would recommend contacting their customer support as they delivered quick responses to my emails that solved my problem. Some people say the Spellcrafting system is unoriginal and hollow. It is my belief they have not really delved into it and tried that many combinations. In addition to that, there are more to the spell types you can use (Sigils) than shooting differently colored fireballs or area of effect explosions. Your spells are divided into three categories. Nova, AOE and Targetted and Shields. Novas are explosions that center around you that occur when you block attacks in the nick of time (counters, really) or, with certain types of shields, when you blink on enemies. Targetted spells come in the Missile, Ray or Lob variety. Missiles are projectiles, rays behave more like breaths, being cones of energy, and lobs are like grenades. Your AOE come in the basic area of effect explosion, traps and patches that deal damage over time or apply an effect for the duration of the spell. Your shields dictate how your block behave, whether you can quick-blink or not and how much damage they block and hp they add. Now all that is just for the basic 'mechanics' for your spells, every single type of spells does something different and synergizes accordingly with the other sigils, of which you can carry only 3 but can do some godlike stuff if you study the system a bit and NOT JUST chuck stuff at enemies. For example, you can charge enemies with 'stored' damage from a Lightning AOE and then unleash it all at once with a critical hit (guaranteed if you charge your AOE or Missiles). BUT you can also stack that with breaking free a frozen enemy for more damage, so you could, say, throw a AOE Ice spell on top of that and finish the combo with a quick charged Fire projectile. You just need to craft your spells carefully and wait a bit till you get proper materials, and then you'll suddenly find that your character can indeed be a mighty mage. Now if you're not convinced, here's a spoiler. At the point I'm at (not too far really) I can Synergize Fire with Corruption, and Ice and Fire. Synergy comes from spells above the Legendary Tier, given from fusing (Upgrading) three Legendaries together. What these synergies let me do is, essentially, summon a FIRE GIANT and a tornado of FIRE AND ICE to basically, clear whatever it is I'm fighting at the moment. I don't fell badass, I feel like LIVING GOD. Just play the game, think your ♥♥♥♥ through and you'll get there too! TL;DR: The real attraction to this game is the Magic system, but you need to try and learn it and wait till you get at least some decent crafting materials before you can use some good spells, but once you get there you're not a Wizard, you're a God.

Yet another example of how 'video game reviews' drag down a good game where many hours of blood and sweat went into. The tendency of reviewers to go mad as soon as a game does not reflect the reviewers expectation a 100%, is tiresome. This unprofessional babbling has nothing to do with reviewing objectively any longer. Every one can do it. It is mostly just the expression of a very biased opinion but disguised as a review. One article even rated Thief as alow as 40%.... come on, really? 40%?? This is a highly polished game, with a lot of atmosphere. Even the view of the scenes alone makes it worthwhile to play. How can one seriously rate it as low as a broken game (which 40% would imply - Yet the game is all but broken.) If you expect the freedom of previous Thief games, you will be disappointed. However, if you take the game for what it is, it is still a lot of fun. The tone it sets, and the mood it creates is very dark, distopian and gritty. Its first person movement immerse you well into the actions, and there are a ton of options to customize your difficulty. You can even switch off entire UI elements to immerse yourself even deeper. At times you struggle with the controls, but it is nothing game breaking and I got used to handle it as time passed. Thief's only big mistake is it's rather linear gameplay in the main missions, which is really the only downside of an otherwise great game.

This is a great game. The graphics are terrific and the gameplay is very intriguing. Now diehard Thief fans may not enjoy the changes from the older style Thief games, but for those folks who are willing to keep an open mind or who are new to the Thief genre, this game is a winner. For one thing, there are multiple ways to approach almost any situation. If you want to get through the game completely unseen, it is possible...not easy, but possible. If you are the aggressive type and want to go through killing everyone in sight, well...ravage away. It is a long enough game with a large world so you feel like you have definitely gotten your money's worth if you play all the side missions. The storyline is interesting and the dialogue is very witty in many places. It all depends on how you play the game and what your actions are. This Thief is not as 'dark' as some of the earlier ones and differs in mood from say Thief Gold. I didn't see this as a negative as some other reviewers did. This game was a breath of fresh air after playing some of the earlier games. This is not a criticism of the earlier games...just telling you that they shouldn't be compared directly. This version of Thief is very good on it's own. To believe it should be a direct descendant of the earlier games is to do all of the games a disservice. Evaluate this Thief on its own and I believe you will agree. There is a place for the old ones and the new both in the Thief world. Enjoy...

I'm a long time MGS fan. This is a good game. This is not a Metal Gear SOLID game. That is okay. Metal Gear Rising has entirely different gameplay then any MGS game. If you came into this expecting MGS w/ Raiden (MGS2) Then you will be dissapointed. If you love stealth gameplay, you can try to be stealthy in this game. You can try, but ultimately the game leans towards combat and action, letting your sword do the work over your cunning and stealth. Storywise, this is one of the MGS games where the writing is subpar. The story addresses a LOT of political commentary, as well as moral issues, social commentary, and it TRIES to make you think of the issues. Emphasis on TRIES. The story can be hit and miss depending on your viewpoints on certain subjects. It does address certain tropes such as the 'hero who kills for a purpose.' If you can ignore politics in games and are willing to look past it, then this isn't important. If you like quick fun, MGR can offer you fun and quick gameplay (although the enemies can become quite difficult and annoyingly tanky towards the endgame. Executing a combo or a Zandatsu (Basically ripping out an enemy's spine and consuming it for life force.) can be RIDICULOUSLY SATISFYING. The bosses are all unique and offer a challenge even on normal difficulty. These bosses aren't written as well as say, the Cobra Unit or Dead Cell, but in terms of being unique, these bosses can offer that. Lastly, Raiden. When all the MGS fans saw him in MGS2 instead of Snake, they weren't happy. Raiden has grown up, but he still seems to be the goofy, 'WE MANAGED TO AVOID DROWING.' kinda guy. This is bad because he's no longer trying to be that guy. He's trying to be Jack the Ripper, his pseudonym due to his finesse with a blade and klling capabilities. Sadly, his performance can either be good or laughable. He shouldn't get on your nerves, but you won't take him as seriously as intended. I would give this game a 7/10. TL;DR If Metal Gear Solid was about being a Ninja Samurai who's idea of stealth is killing everyone. I still prefer Metal Gear Solid.

What to say about this game?... Well, first of, It's my first Metal Gear, So althought I know it's far to be like the rest of the Metal Gear games with their stealth mechanics, it's also the first time I come to the saga, which means I didn't got underwhelmed by the fact that it was... different? Come to think of it, Why is that underwhelming? This game isn't a reboot or a remake! The usual Metal Gear Solid will still be made with the their classic stealth mechanic so... Why complain about how this game isn't fully based on stealth? Anyway, I'm getting offtrack, This game is a Hack 'n Slash (Or in other words, a Beat 'em Up with swords) where you play as Raiden... Who I honestly don't know what was his portrayment in the original saga, but I must admit, after playing the game, this game obtained my approval, I like this character, However, the plot in the game is... confusing... Never the less, I'd still say it's a good plot, not one of the best you've ever seen, but at least it bring us something entertaining unlike other games who just throw us the first thing they got in mind, oh! And I really have to mention the soundtrack! It's awesome!! Comepletly, over all the tracks from the bosses, They give us some great rock you just can't stop hearing. Now to the gameplay itself, it's actually being a long time since I enjoyed a Beat 'em... Ahem... I mean, a Hack 'n Slash game like this (Seriously? Why have two names for two genres of games that are basically the same thing?) the controls feel good althought you're gonna have a lot of trouble with the fact that attacking and parring are in the same freaking button! At first that simply annoys you, but after playing it I must say, I think it kind of made the game better, it gave it challenge, and it's not that hard to differenciate one action from the other, the game also has the blade mode, where time goes slower and you remain still to give a lot of cuts to the enemies that tear them to pieces, it's pretty fun cutting somebody in over five hundred shreds, you should try that out! In the end, a great game! I comepletly recomend it to everyone! To Beat 'em up fans at least!... I mean... Hack 'n slash fans.... Seriously! Why the different names!?

This game is a puzzler that features more than puzzling. First, the character (named Woop) is so cute that you can only smile when he's happy as you just completed that damn level that took you so long to finish. With such a great transition, I will add that this game is by no means easy, despite his looks, and completing a level with give you plenty of satisfaction. To go in more details, there are 3 types of levels : - Ones which require your brain (often Sokoban-like block pushing, sometimes guiding monsters to a switch ...). These levels are probably the hardest (some of them I have no clue how it could be possible to solve them) - Ones which require your timing : it is all about going at the right pace, at the right moment (they can be tricky but not actually hard) - Ones which requires your fingers and nerves : just run from the beginning to the end, without stopping will often work. Trouble is that you can't afford the slightest mistake in the whole level as it is instant death (or forever trapped). Of course, whatever the kind of level you play, the ultimate goal is to get a good rank among all the players who have succeded before you (and there are good people out there, so it's not easy to get high in the ranks). What's more ? There is a weekly challenge (ranked as well, of course), and you can create and share your home-made levels (there's an even achievement for that) Well, to be honest, I have to mention the controls : when trying to play for the ranking, you need as few moves as possible, so you'd like to move in a predetermined path you've selected to be the fastest (or sometimes, the only one). That is pretty hard to do : most of the time, Woop will make one more step before turning, and this step will lead you into ... water ! (or magma, or a monster, plenty of ways to die, yay !). Well, that's it ! Pack your brains, hone your skills and challenge the ranking !

Basically, you're moving blocks and skating across ice/conveyor belts to make it to the end of the maze. Chuck Summerville is a renown puzzle designer and this is a reskin of his game from 1989 called Chips Challenge. I will say that the interface -- which was created for iPhones and Android devices -- leaves a lot to be desired. If you die too many times, you'll get a message that for the most part implies that you're an idiot and asks you to skip that level and try again later. Also, there are cutscenes that are activated by stepping on a shirt that is contained in the level -- also ragingly annoying. But if you can get past the handful of interface issues and just focus on the puzzles, this title is a ton of fun.
If you're old like me and you remember Chips Challenge from the early 90's, this game is the spiritual sequel made by the original creator. It still a fantastic puzzle design so I recommend it.

This remaster is excellent! I played the original through once, and absolutely loved it. But I found that there were a few things that could have been done better, such as the view through your gas mask which became hard to see through after a few minutes, and the UI and inventory seemed a bit rough around the edges. With this version, they basically used the UI from Metro Last Light and applied it here. It looks like a slighty refined Metro Last Light, but with the 2033 story and setting, which is exactly the same as the original. I believe they used the Metro LL engine, and basically revamped the lighting and texture detail a bit. The graphics are of course incredible as is Last Light, and is hugely better than the original 2033, especially in the texture side of things. On the performance side, the game runs very well. 4A really, really knows what they are doing in the optimization department as well as the eye candy department! Framerates are smooth and steady and there are enough visual options to tweak so that lower end systems should also run this well (Another complaint I had about the original 2033 was the lack of options to tweak). I set it exactly as I had the original Last Light settings and it runs pretty much identically as that game did. I'm running an FX 8320 @ 4.2 GHz and an R9 280X @ 1170MHz with 8 GB DDR3 1866 RAM. I run all settings maxed except Tesselation, which is set to high. V-Sync is enabled, too. I'm not sure of my exact average FPS but there is no lagging or glitching and it looks very smooth. The game has not crashed or showed signs of any problems at all. 4A did an excellent job with this remaster. I am very happy with this game and also happy to support a top notch developer like them. This game was worth every penny! If you enjoyed the original, you'll enjoy it even more in this form, definitely worth a replay. If you haven't yet played it, then don't hesitate to grab the Redux version!

Trying to get this game working on Windows 7 has given me cancer. Resolution needs to be adjusted via .ini file (not hard). Mouse doesn't lock to window, leaving KBM controls unusable on multi-monitor setups - the window will force-minimize any time something else is clicked. Gamepad controls make no sense: Instead of mapping looking around to a single stick, it puts up/down on an analog stick and rotating left/right on the triggers. Shoot guns with the start button and melee with the back button (wtf?). You can't map any actions to left/right on analog stick. Cancer. Mouse lock workaround: Grab fullscreen window with Windowed Borderless Gaming, open up the game settings, and force mouse lock to game window.

First of all, the game requires a 3rd-party patch to get the controller support into a somewhat usable state and fix the cutscene audio getting cut off at the end. Voice acting is still terrible on all characters, though. The game gets tedious quickly. There are a few main sections, each of which is a seemingly endless sequence of levels that are pretty much all the same. Even the objectives never really change; usually it's 'kill the officers'. Sure, tha Nazis have an evil plan and all that, but... that doesn't add anything. It never felt like a story. Occasionally, the path to progress is hidden; I frequently checked a walkthrough on how to proceed which is a main source of negative score on a game. The game is not encouraging trial-and-error or exploration in areas that have bottomless pits or a lot of environmental damage, since a death requires a restart of the level from the beginning. For that reason, and because the bossfights are tedious to no end, I also preferred to check the walkthrough for them so I could do it correctly. Regardless, I was unable to kill the final boss (Beliar) despite checking walkthroughs -- they just keep shooting at him, but there aren't enough weapons around and he grows quickly in my playthrough, so that never worked. Blades don't seem to do anything, and there is no way to recharge blood rage -- so all attempts ended with me being unable to do anything.

This game divided a lot of fans. It took the whole game for me to figure out what bothered me about it: it was the victim of the franchise's own continuity. The Saints Row series has always been a fan-based formula. If you didn't play the previous games, you missed a LOT of the context of the later ones. It was always a smaller, zanier alternative to Grand Theft Auto for people who wanted a different kind of writing. Each game in turn played off the same fundamentals of gameplay in order to make that happen, and except for the backstory and characters, all of it was thrown out for this game. That's what ♥♥♥♥♥♥ people off. It's a good game, but it really shouldn't have Saints Row in the title. Logistically, there was nowhere left for the series to go, entrapped by what people expected. They couldn't make another game where you just take over another city, because they've made that game THREE TIMES BEFORE. So, like the bomb in the closet during The Stand, the problem was solved by blowing it all to hell. What's left is still a pretty good game, but it has basically crushed what was important about the old games into powder. Upgrades are still necessary, but you will probably never use gang members. You COULD customize your guns, but you don't have to. You COULD drive around in vehicles, but you don't have to. You COULD make lots of money, but you don't have to. Almost nothing about what was important in the core gameplay in the previous titles is important anymore. All that being said, you're still going to have a good time. It's certainly a good game, just not so much a good Saints Row game.

It's like Grand Theft Auto and Prototype had a badass love child. First mission has you taking out terrorists and disarming a Nuclear Missile in the air to Aerosmith's 'I Don't Want To Miss a Thing.' After it's standard Saints Row: run around, shoot the baddies, etc., soon leading to your character gaining super powers in which the Prototype aspect comes into play. Leap tall buildings in a single bound, sprint through the city faster than an Attrazione. Shoot fire and ice from your hands, fly around like Peter Pan (well more like glide but whattaya gonna do?) and kill aliens with some cool new weapons. It's a bit of a letdown that Steelport is recycled from Saints Row: The Third, but the powers leave you feeling more like a god than a king. I personally find that a plus but I've heard others say it's too over powered, it's really to each their own. Overall, I'd have to give Saints Row IV 7/10.

I played Saints Row: Mass Erect back when it first came out, on PS3. I haven't played the PC version yet, but I can tell you what I experienced on PS3: The culmination of years of over-the-top action, crude humor, and the-♥♥♥♥-is-a-writer plot twists. There are a lot of people who say this game went overboard, that Saints Row: The Third was better. While the latter camp may have a point, the former doesn't know what the ♥♥♥♥ they're talking about. This is Saints Row, ♥♥♥♥♥es. There IS no overboard. We crossed the line so many times that it's smudged to hell and back. Saints Row IV takes everything you loved about the series up to this point and injects it with an alien invasion, presidential hijinx, superpowers, combat mechs, hover tanks, bizzarre weapons (including the almighty dubstep gun) a metric ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of Matrix, Mass Effect and They Live references, brings back almost every character ever seen in the series, throws a couple new ones in the form of a sexy English operative and a snarky robot orb, and generally just blows what you thought you knew about sandbox crime sims out your ♥♥♥. Everything Grand Theft Auto V got wrong was done right in this game months earlier. The combat is relentless, ridiculous and always entertaining, and all the side content is worked into the ordinary game flow, especially if you're shooting for the best ending. I like to think each Saints Row is the previous one on a whole lot of drugs. If that is true, then hide Saints Row IV from the DEA before you give zombie Ronald Reagan a heart attack. I loved this game so much that it netted me my first and only Platinum Trophy. Take a trip back to the Row and take a whiff of that purple haze once again, you won't regret it.

A decent addition to the 'fake roguelike' genre (a nice name for it might be rogue-like-like.) I would recommend it as it has most of the elements that fans of the genre like including permadeath, random upgrades, random dungeons, and a retro feel. The only problem that keeps me from loving this game is that it feels very slow, but only on the players end. The dungeons side on the other hand will seem very fast and can kill you in just seconds with the crazy amount of enemies on the screen (which is no problem at all of course.) The issue is that killing the enemies seems so slow sometimes with your cannon gun and tiny little dagger. Yes, you can upgrade both of those, but sometimes you wont get upgrades through out the dungeon if you are unlucky and it will just make things slower. One may argue 'that's what rogue-likes are all about. They are going to be tough.' This isn't really that kind of game. In this sort of game you want quick difficult gameplay where the upgrades make you feel like you are progressing even if the game is getting more tough. A few floors in and i'm doing the same damage. The only buffs I have make me immune to fire or that the chests wont be empty (yet you can still get unlucky and recieve nothing.) The game is fun. Just seems slow. ♥♥♥♥ing awesome electronica music, solid platforming, colourful backgrounds, and girls moaning at every checkpoint. What more could you want out of a platformer? ... well, I guess the answer to that is a game that isn't slow, buggy, and filled with pointless gimmicks to make up for the lack of anything unique. Electronic Super Joy is a game that has a lot of potential and looks like it'll be great, but falls flat on its face once you dive in. Let me explain why. The first thing was my controller just didn't have the right buttons mapped. Now this isn't an unknown problem for the gamepad I use if I'm not using x360ce. I'm guessing x360ce for some reason doesn't work for this game which is a real bummer and put all my controls everywhere. Considering out of over 100 games I've played with this gamepad using x360ce and this is the first one that's given me problems I'm going to have to count that as an obnoxious negative. Anyways, once I got going.. It sounded amazing. This game has some great music. I can't say much more. It wasn't memorable though. Not necessarily a downside, but lets just say I let the game idle on the title screen for an hour without bothering to mute it in order to get the trading cards.. after turning it off, I couldn't remember the track I had been listening to the whole time. Speaking of the title, it doesn't loop properly and just fades out before replaying. I wouldn't be surprised if other music in the game was the same way. Regardless, the music did sound great. I loved the style and it was very energetic. Visually.. its kind of.. boring. Yeah. Its boring. Look, I like my share fair of retro pixelated graphics but this game's art is plain lazy. Yeah, the backgrounds are colourful but they're not much more than basic colours thrown together.. Throw some black blocks everywhere and that's all there is to it. The character you play is just some black pixels. Uncreative and more forgettable than one of those games where you play a blob. Alright, so the gameplay. The control.. was... Okay, well I immediately thought the game felt slow. It feels like a game that should have a run button. Imagine playing Super Meat Boy or Mario without ever using the run button. That's what this game always feels like. Speaking of Mario, imagine playing Mario and dying everytime you jump on an enemy. Yep. You can't kill enemies by jumping on them in this game. Instead, you have to jump and then use an attack in mid-air that slams you down on to the enemy. Honestly, it just feels pointless and would be better off with a standard jump-to-kill method. So its a platforming game.. with a lot of platforms that seemed to always be above bottomless pits. You jump here, you jump there. It worked and felt pretty solid. But the levels had some kind of silly gimmicks. There were things that launched you in the air and teleportals that were cool. Though one problem was the levels are set up so sometimes a teleportal entrance requires you to run a direction that'll immediately kill you after you teleport unless you completely let go of the movement button. A bit annoying, but not that big of a deal. Also, how many levels will the screen constantly scroll in? Those are in a lot of games, but just in my first few levels it was all I was seeing. It wouldn't be so annoying if the game was a bit faster but it just isn't due to the lack of being able to run. Most of the gimmicks were just plain bad. In one level, the visuals were so crazy that it gave me a headache and made me dizzy. It was a pain to try and play through all that was going on. Hard to explain over this, but if you end up playing the game you'll see what I mean.. and you won't like it. As for the actual difficulty, the game was tough but it didn't feel overly hard. However, being tough early on makes it seem like it could easily be one of those games with a stupidly hard difficulty curve late-game. Unless it has a flat difficulty curve. The things that felt hard weren't even pure user error, but failing from silly gimmicks that felt forced in to try and make this game more unique. The game seemed kind of buggy. One level the music went absolutely apeship and was just a huge distorted wall of noise. At first I was questioning if it was intentional but the longer it went on and the worse it got I knew it couldn't be. It just sounded absolutely horrible and cringe-worthy. Do I think people could like this game? Definitely. Do I think its a bad game? Not at all. But I feel it has a lot of problems and just isn't too great. It has potential and could easily be turned into something awesome, but when has a released game ever been completely reworked? Its been a long while since I played this game, so maybe its changed for the better now.. but because of how awful my first experience was with it I won't be giving it another try. If you really want to then its worth checking out I guess to see if you might like it, but I don't recommend it. There are so many other platformers out there that do all this game does and more while doing it much better.

Street Fighter X Tekken had so much potential. It really did, and it's actually a pretty fun game in short bursts. I bought this one back at launch and I don't necessarily regret it, since I do enjoy this game a lot, but it's not one I'd recommend. The main problem lies in the game's lack of replayability. If this game were made 5 years prior, all of the DLC for this game would have been unlockable content, prolonging the life of the gameplay considerably. However, that would almost be too logical in this day and age, so everything, EVERYTHING that could possibly be DLC is DLC in this game. No unlockable characters or costumes here. Just pay up and they're yours! If you can get the 12 character DLC pack on sale then that'd be worth it, but then you're giving money to Capcom for all the wrong reasons. I wouldn't bother at this point. To make matters worse, the game will taunt you for not having DLC, showing very clearly what you're yet to 'unlock'. Aside from the DLC issue, the fact that THERE'S NOTHING TO DO once you've beaten the arcade mode a couple of times, seen all the endings, and gone for a few rounds of online play, the game actually has a solid selection of playable characters, with or without the additional 12-character DLC pack, and the tag team mechanics satisfy both the urge for a serious fighter in SSFIV and a more over-the-top fighter in MvC all in one game, which is pretty cool. The Tekken characters in SF style offer a breath of fresh air with Capcom's own charming take on these classic characters, and they're all loads of fun to play as. Not to mention how good the soundtrack is! In fact, I rather like this game for what it is, but I'm disappointed for what it could have been. It's kind of underwhelming, especially after all the hype. If you're a more casual fighting game fan like myself, then you'll probably get some enjoyment out of it, but it doesn't feel quite as deep and refined as some of Capcom's other fighters and there's little to keep you coming back. It's definitely simplified to a noticeable degree, which seems to be a conscious design decision, but it feels like it could be a little more technical. On the plus side, at least it's easy to pick up and play. I mean, yeah, it's still totally fun, but with the DLC issues, questionable mechanics, the lack of long-term support from Capcom (especially for the PC version which is behind on several patches), and the fact that NOBODY FREAKING PLAYS IT, I really cannot recommend this game at all. Just wait for Ultra IV to come out, and hope that Namco's promised Tekken X Street Fighter is a lot more compelling. But hey, at least it has Trading Cards!

Let me start off by saying that the Counter-Strike pack is a stand-alone product. You don't need the original Half-Life to play this game. In the retail package you get a full version of CS as well as Team Fortress Classic, Opposing Force multiplayer, and the Wanted, Redemption and Firearms mods. The entire pack is overflowing with multiplayer fun, but, of course, the real focus of the retail release is Counter-Strike. There is a single-player component to CS and, while it provides a good primer, this mod is all about online action. You basically play a game of cat and mouse, with the mouse being a terrorist group and the cat a squad of counter-terrorists. As a terrorist, you're goal is to plant a bomb at a specific location or hold a group of hostages. As a counter-terrorist, it's your duty to defuse said bomb or rescue the ill-fated hostages. Taking out all players on the opposing side will also assure your victory. CS is an action lover's dream, with games lasting only four or five minutes (if that in some cases) because, unlike Half-Life, one shot to the head can mean instant death. CS is the perfect mix between fast-action and realistic damage. You can't just absorb bullet after bullet and expect to walk away. Working as a team is a must and, while you're in the game, taking the lone wolf approach will often get you killed...and fast. It's the team-based tactics that make CS so fun. I can't stress how important it is in this game to act as a team. If your team is on the defensive side you'll all benefit by creating a cohesive strategy. If you team is on the offensive side, you will all benefit by sticking closely together as well. I'm sure you've seen movies or television show demonstrating this 'Conga Line' style of infiltration. Well, that's exactly how your team will have to act. This creates a fantastic game balance that will keep you coming back for more. It'll also keep you from thinking about your school work, your job, and interaction with your loved ones, and often work around the IGN offices will be put on hold so we can clog our network with CS. Visually the game will not disappoint. While the Half-Life engine isn't the prettiest beast out there, there is plenty of animation that creates a smooth look and feel, and the gun models are some of the most realistic looking of any shooter available. The environmental textures look realistic enough and complement the provided camouflage well enough for you to be hidden, but not be invisible. As in real life, the distinguishable difference between good guy and bad guy is a little difficult, but the balance to this is if you can't tell who it is then you probably won't be able to hit him with your gun. Now, if you've purchased sniper rifle, you should have plenty of scope magnification to tell the difference between terrorist or counter-terrorist, but otherwise you may be taking out a team member from afar. As good as it is, a couple of features of this game really stood out as frustrating... at first. But over a period of time they actually became enhancements to online multiplayer gaming. One feature is buying your weapons at the start of each round. This takes a little getting used to at first since, in most shooters, you just run around picking up weapons at your heart's content. Usually by the time you figured out which guns, grenades, and armor you were going to take in your early games, the bad guys would come over and kill you. But a couple of tries later, after getting the gist of things, you're off in no time. The other feature that took some getting used to was the 'wait and watch' feature after you get killed. Once you sustain a lethal injury, you have to wait for the next round to start before you can join in again -- you don't just spawn again and start shooting. This actually adds a ton of anxiety to your efforts of staying alive and completing your objective. But like I mentioned before, the rounds are short, so you shouldn't have to wait too long before you can jump in the action again. Not surprisingly, the user interface is very Half-Life-esque. Gamers who have played Half-Life or any of the other mods for the game will have no trouble with the menu system. Even for the first time user the interface is easy to use or fumble through. The only thing that even slightly tripped us up in the interface is the 'Update' on the server page. First-time users may be confused into thinking this meant update my version of CS. Not true, it actually means update the list of game servers. But the rest of the interface is easy to understand and even easier to navigate. Just about the only aspect of this game that we could make negative comments about is the sound. Sure, the realistic guns sounds are spot on, we just wish the same amount of attention to detail was given to the rest of the sound in the game. Some levels have lighting and thunder. When the thunder crashes it sounds a little wimpy. We were hoping for some deeper bass and clearer sounding claps from the lightning. In most of the level the user can go inside or out side of buildings, the sound of their footsteps should also change to reflect what type of surface they are walking on. The sound of footsteps getting closer and closer could also have been improved. As it stands now, it's hard to tell how far down the hallway or street a bad guy is from you by sound alone. So how long does the magic last? Well we've been playing this game for over a year now and we still can't get enough of it. Are we tired of it? Hell no! We're still surprised by how fun this game is. This game actually made some of us squeal like little school-girls after getting sniped from an unexpected angle on high. On the other hand some of us were drawn to stand up and scream obscenities at the monitor. I guess we'll just have to get them next time! In a nutshell, if you're looking for the next step in online first person shooters, then look no further. CS is fast paced, intense, and satisfying--this game will not disappoint. This is truly one of the best mods for one of the all time greatest first person shooters ever, and the retail package of CS is simply bursting with multiplayer goodness. If you like to play shooters online, get this pack!

Alright so, where to begin? I guess I should start off by saying this game is the ♥♥♥♥. It's amazing. Now yes, everyone in this game is a furry of sorts but that's no big deal. You remember all them entertaining animal shows you watched as a kid? Winnie The Pooh, Franklin The Turtle, etc. Now imagine those dumbazzes wielding a legendary blade ripping through hoards and armies of monsters/bigger dumbazzes and having an outstanding back story and front story, giggity. Honestly this is one of the best games I've played in a long time. What I'm trying to say is, I honestly don't know why you're sitting there playing Garry's Mod/TF2 when you could be playing some mother ♥♥♥♥in' Dust! Don't have money? Finger ♥♥♥♥ a dolla 15 out your mom or some ♥♥♥♥. get it. Ashes to Ashes. Dust to Dust, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

I wish Steam had an 'Ehhhh...' option. Let's start with the good - Dust looks great, controls well, has a passable soundtrack, and the writing can be quite funny at times. I laughed often at the deuteragonist Fidget's lines, and while she was entirely grating at first introduction by the middle of the game I only found her likeable. Unfortunately, main man Dust himself never improved much. He goes back and forth between being some edgy amnesiac dude to bland to a bleeding heart. He doesn't improve in motivation or reasoning, even after his exposition scenes. The villain meanwhile twirls his mustache at every turn while literally slaughtering men, women, and children alike. Fun. This game never really marketed itself more than a simple beat-em-up, but the mechanics here are beyond simple. You have essentially four attacks - a ground clear, a ground slam, an air knock-up, and some attack where you spin through the air. Fidget also has the ability to shoot projectiles which are amplified by your spin attack, but there's very little difference between the 3 options and they don't interact with your other attacks in any way besides juggling enemies. This wouldn't be a problem if the game was varied in other ways... but it's not. Enemies are basically all reskins of each other and the best way to play is button mashing due to the number of mobs that can clutter your screen. The game has a parry mechanic, but outside of it happening randomly the only times you bother to make use of it are for enemies designed to require its use. In fact, none of the attacks in your repertoire feel particularly natural to use - they all seem as effective as one another and there's no combo system to speak of. There is some degree of animation canceling utilized via crouching, but again it's pointless to use given how Dust requires absolutely zero strategy or mechanics to speak of. Level design is passable at best and at worst makes you want to tear your hair out. Levels are simply too long for what they offer. Like the gameplay, they're repetitive and on the rare occasion things are mixed up, it's in an annoying fashion. I have absolutely zero idea why anyone would think that hazards that essentially explode randomly would be a good idea, much less to cover entire sections of levels with them. And surround them with spike traps. I certainly love having three hazards explode at once, leaving no opportunity to dodge, only to send me into conveniently placed spikes so that I may die without option. Fun. Anyway, regardless of all these multiple faults I did, I suppose, have some fun with Dust . Despite the terrible story, the repetitive gameplay, and the occasionally annoying level design, the game did offer some honestly cool moments. The animations and sprite effects when dealing with a group of enemies can look amazing, and stuff like grabbing a guy with your sword then slamming him into a group of enemies takes a long time to get old. With that, I'd recommend Dust to the younger gamer. It's something I would have loved at a young age, where flashy effects and simple gameplay were the bee's knees, but for anyone else I'd probably pass.

Developers have made some improvements to the optimization of BO3, with that I can give this a more helpful review. The game still needs a bit of tweaking with optimization but it is certainly playable well enough at this point. Gameplay is what you would expect it to be as in who enters the crosshair first tends to lose and I am not too sure of the hitscan it seems every so often the finishing shot appears to not even hit the player and theres a slight delay on who actually wins in a fire fight. And perks and upgrades are exactly what you would assume they would be in a COD game. There are a few things that will win over a player for this game however. The maps, I think, are really well designed and have a good charm to most of them that make you want to play on them. While green seems to be the new brown there is much more color to each map that breathes some fresh air into the series. It's also nice to see maps with swimmable water and designed with wall running physics in mind. The player physics have certainly improved and gives players some choices of escaping or persueing in situations with the crouch dash, double jump, and wall running abilities. The only negative side is how exposed a player is while wall running and feels a bit tacky with the lack of speed a player is running during the animation. Characters also get different choices of player specialization skills that can spot enemies, absorb or repel damage from gear, create a AOE burst of damage near the player and more to give it some extra abilities a player can use in certain situations. The maps and the new character mechanics will win over players into feeling this is a worthwhile game for a change. Pick it up if it's on sale I wouldn't recommend the retail price though.

Ninja Theory has taken a Classic Original Playstation title and gave it a controversial respin. If you liked the previous installments that you'll like this one too, however if you have a closed mind and don't like change.. Well then maybe you should pass on this fantastic game and miss out. In order to truely enjoy this game i'd recommend using an Xbox 360 Controller, a Logitech Wireless Gamepad F710, or a newly usable Xbox One Controller for PC. If you plan to use either Xbox controller you will need to get the Microsoft Drivers off their site, but honestly it's worth it. Well, here we go: DmC is a reboot to the Devil May Cry series, set in the present day, with new weapons and a new setting for New Dante. You join forces with New Vergil and Kat a human Wicca who uses her Wiccan spells to help Dante traverse Limbo (The Land Between the Demon world and the Human world). You spend the course of the game acquiring new weapons, abilities, and powerups much as you did in the previous games. The standard game play can be seen as 'easier' than previous Devil May Cry games, but as in the older games you can always step it up to Dante Must Die!, Heaven or Hell, and Hell or Hell modes. Which are far more challenging and provide that sought after level of difficulty. The Vergil's Downfall DLC provides some great follow up content to the main game and fills in some missing information relating to Vergil and Dante's past and future. I look forward to DmC: Devil May Cry 2, but in the meantime I plan on playing until I max out everything and getting to that sweet 90% completion rate. You may ask yourself why I said 90%, well then you obviously have never played Hell or Hell mode.. All in all, this game is fantastic and does the series a much needed change of pace. Ignore the neigh sayers and pick up a copy!

Having just spent 150+ hours playing Dragon Age: Inquisition, I was ready for another epic fantasy adventure game. This certainly fit the bill. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is the first game of this series I've played and I'm quite impressed. In spite of the complaints about the graphics being downgraded from the original demos, they're beautiful. I like the skill advancement, and the magic in the game is simple, but useful. Two nice improvements over DA:I -- horseback riding is actually useful and semi-realistic, and you can actually swim in this game! The card game, Gwent, is a nice addition and easy to pick up as well. Finally, there are a TON of side-quests and there is enough variation between them that they still feel fresh after 21 hours of playtime. My only complaint about the game centers around actions on items--such as igniting a torch or examining an object. You have to be standing in front of and facing the object. Not on top of it, or in front of it facing sideways. Facing it about an arms-length away. This wouldn't be as much of an issue if The Witcher would turn on a dime; however, he feels the need to take a step forward, one to the right, then another to the right again to make a complete 180. Otherwise, the game is excellent and deserves all of the accolades it's received.

Imagine Endless Space combined with a fantasy-style civilization and you'll have this game. There's going to be a lot of comparisons to Civilization here. The largest and most obvious difference happens before you even start the game. Instead of 'customizing' your civilization a la Civ:BE, or just randomly picking one from Civ 5, you have the option of picking a prebuilt race or making your own using a point-buy system. The differences are huge and actually define the race, instead of being restricted to a unique unit or hardly game-changing mechanic. You can play as the dead dudes who are sealed inside their armor who live off of dust, granting a huge bonus to income and negating the need for food, or play as the wandering merchants who can literally move their cities around the map if needed. Once you fire up the game, you start with a military and a settler, much like Civilization. The difference, however, is the fact you are restricted to colonizing a 'region' instead of just placing a bunch of cities in a crazy pattern to try and min/max your coverage. Strategic and Luxury resources don’t even have to be inside your city limits. Instead you build a building on them, no matter where they are in the region. Instead of harvesting and 'having' x resource, you now harvest a certain amount of x resource a turn. This makes it extremely hard to go back to Civilization because I like this system so much better. The armies in the game are exactly the same as Endless Space. You have a limit based on your technology on how many units you can fit into an 'army' and you can assign a hero to guide them. Combat turns into a miniature battleground like a stage from many other games, and has a miniature system that is serviceable and interesting in its own right. Units themselves are interesting. Instead of having a crazy large selection of units (civilization), every cavitation has 4-6 units. Each unit can be customized greatly, though, by choosing weapons, armor, and accessories depending on your level of technology. All in all I'd definitely pick this one up if you're a fan of the genre, and I'd recommend it twice as much if you loved Endless Space and wanted to see a land-based version.

Most people will play Outlast with the expectation that it terrifies them. They'll play it because a friend sent it as a cruel gift, or because they know it'll be hilarious for others to watch on YouTube. The appeal of fear is pretty obvious, but if you're like me, horror games are never all that frightening. Still, I find myself playing horror games from time-to-time to see if they excell in other areas. In that respect, Outlast is an excellent game. Underneath all the frequent (and often unavoidable) jump-scares and prolific gore, Outlast is a game with expertly-crafted mechanics, an intriguing (if convoluted) story to tell, and stunning visuals. You'll find yourself legitimately curious about what secrets Mount Massive Asylum holds. Unlike most survival horror games, Outlast doesn't bog the player down with a tedious inventory system or intentionally-unresponsive mechanics. Instead, the player quickly and fluidly navigates a labyrinthine environment, using only a night-vision camera to help see in the dark. If you're a fan of horror games, then you've already played this. But if you never bother with games that just focus on being scary, I recommend you still give this one a try. Not because Outlast will frighten you, but because it doesn't sacrifice gameplay in favor of cheap scares for the easily-spooked.

Cons: The puzzles are not engaging or difficult. The only thing that takes time is figuring out how to actually interact with them. The gameplay is boring. The power mechanics are boring AND slow AND are unreliable AND SOME OF THE 'PUZZLES' RELY ON YOU BEING FAST AND ACCURATE WITH THEM LIKE WHY!? The levels are boring. Most of the models don't even look like they belong in the same game. The sound will randomly BLAST you during completely random moments no matter how low you have it turned. I destroy one block? Sound is fine. The next block? Horrible ear death. No matter how DESPERATELY I tried to immerse myself in the story and enjoy it...it was boring and I had to take frequent breaks in order to force myself to pay attention. I just didn't care at all, it felt so forced and generic. The lighting is so unbearable. Every area is so dark that you can't see any detail whatsoever. They obviously did this to discourage you from looking around so you wouldn't realize how empty the game is. This point is proven when you FINALLY get respite from darkness imprisoning you in the form of a sunny level...and the level is barren and uninteresting. When I say 'empty' I don't mean short either. They have added levels since this games release, and even show you where you missed collectibles to encourage you to go back to try and find them...but I couldn't even make it through all of the levels ONCE, why would i want to do it AGAIN? Its empty because there's just nothing to it. Just another bland 'transcendental' puzzle game with absolutely nothing remarkable or special about it. The game tries so hard to be transcendental I almost feel bad for it. I didn't notice any game breaking bugs like some of the other reviewers, so maybe they ironed them out? Even then, its not worth your time to play this chore of a game. I did notice one time when I could sequence break the game, but it didn't matter because I would have been without an essential power for the next part. Pros: At least the way you interact with the world was almost creative...maybe if they would have let you interact with anything besides the extremely context sensitive puzzle components this would have turned out to be a cooler mechanic Other thoughts: You get an achievement for like everything you do in this game. Did they literally just add fluff achievements to try and make the game look like it had actual content? Was Elysia really the most creative name they could think of for their program? How many times do I need to hear that word before it dies. At least Dust: An Elysian Tale was cute and fun and interesting. AND IT WAS 2D. I LIKED THE GRAPHICS OF A 2D PLATFORM SIDESCROLLER MORE THAN A FULLY MODELED 3D GAME WHAT DOES THAT SAY!? I've seen some of the positive reviews of this game saying how they are going to play it forever and ever and it makes me wonder if these people are masochists or something? I am willing to give A LOT of breaks to indy companies. Short game, low resolution, muddy sound, bugs, limited animation...thats all okay you didn't have a huge budget. But for the love of god at least make your art UNIQUE, your levels INTERESTING, your story ENGAGING, and your gameplay FUN. You don't need to have a huge production value to make a great game, plenty of indy companies have made worse looking games that still CAPTIVATE people with their art direction and story. I've read a lot of the reviews in order to help me formulate what I want to say, and let me tell you I completely disagree with so many of them. The graphics are not interesting or beautiful AT ALL. Its all VERY generic. Sometimes I feel like the critics and users that review these games somehow got a different version. If you want a game that centers around a simulated universe or consciousness...go play SOMA, it may be a horror game but you'll certainly enjoy it more than this. This game just feels so generic I am literally FORCING myself to try and enjoy it. I really wish I could say I at least finished the game before giving it a review but I just can't force myself to play this anymore. I would literally rather go to work for a 12 hour shift than play this game at this point. If you would like a more clearly written and worded review, go look at the Metacritic review by Destructoid. I'm a massive fan of these type of simulator games. I decided to give this game a try, and after a few hours of learning their engine I started my own city. These cities can get absolutely massive. water drought is a factor, traffic will obstruct emergency vehicles, and much more. You REALLY have to take the time and think about why you're doing what you're doing, and how it could negatively impact your city. This is a phenominal game, and the fact that I can add workshop features makes it even better. Do not hesitate to purchase this game.

Ever since simcity-4, city simulation has become more off a hobby for me than just occasional game play. Over the years I have created many custom buildings (mainly Paris and medieval themes) and mods (amongst other the Jupiter (weather) and the Aurora mods) for simcity-4. Simcity 2013 was a major disappointment on all accounts. I have been fortunate to have been invited to test Cities Skylines' modding tools during the beta phase for the past couple of months. And during that time I have also been able to play the game. Cities Skylines exceeds my expectations. The potential that can be unlocked by the community and by DLCs provided by CO is unbelievable. I am absolutely overwhelmed by how great this game is. Additionally, I have gained the utmost respect for CO. It is unbelievable what a small team of creative people can do. Aside from developing a fantastic game, CO actually listens to the community to the best of their abilities. Bound by an NDA, it has been challenging for me not being able to respond to all the comments, questions, critisicm, (sometimes unjust) speculation on the forums. And I kept thinking if only you could get to play the game for half an hour and - like me - become captivated by studying the little CIMS in their daily routine, or laying out the most amazing road interchanges. Finally a game I can enjoy again without having to shoot someone. Off course some I do share some of the criticism that also has been shared on the forums. I could even create a list of a dozen or more features that I would like to see changed or improved. But all that is driven by my enthusiasm for this game, and there is a time a place for everything. So for now I am just giving this game a 10/10.

If you're new to FPSes, don't bother with this one. You will die constantly and accomplish nothing useful other than being cannon fodder for long time players. The learning curve is less a curve and more a 100ft high wall, and the bare tutorial you get does not even scratch the surface of it. Vehicle controls are unintuitive, which is just as well because, until you get some upgrades, driving or piloting any vehicle just makes you a bigger target for other players. Speaking of other players - all their weapons will splatter you in a couple of hits at most, and yours will feel woefully underpowered in comparison (because they are). In short - Planetside 2 is a game that hates new players and wants them to suffer. It is a game where, if you want to have fun, you need to spend an unknown number of hours feeling frustrated, angry, and useless first, while every long time player with far better guns who knows the game inside and out murders you repeatedly. The big massively multiplayer battles? They must have sounded like a good idea on paper, but in practice they just hammer home how utterly irrelevant you are. There are two solutions to this, if you still want to punish yourself. The first is to join a large platoon and hope that they carry you until you learn enough and earn enough certification points to survive more than a few seconds and, y'know, actually start having fun. The second is to throw money at SOE, predictably enough, to buy the upgrades you need. I wanted to give it a chance, really I did, but all I can think now is thank the gods I didn't pay for the truly god-awful experience I had. That's nine hours of rage-inducing, stress-filled insanity that I am NEVER getting back. Hardcore FPS players will worship at Planetside 2's feet, but casual players need to avoid this one like the plague and go back to TF2. Personally I am deleting it from my HDD and I will curse its name forevermore.

Here are just some of the things you can do in Assassin's Creed 4: climb a tower, hunt a whale, hide in a haystack, steer a ship in a storm, stick a sword through a man's eye socket, shoot an iguana, stab a shark, stand atop a church balcony and sprinkle coins onto the people below, regardless of their beliefs. But you can't just crouch when you want to, which seems a bit odd for a game that spins around sneaking, subterfuge and poking holes in the heads of a secret war between assassins and templars. The struggle for supremacy intersects with old-fashioned analogue piracy in Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag, which lets you sail across the massive caribbean, swim in its perfectly turquoise waters and make any treasure your own. Not having a squat button in the middle of a meticulous recreation of Havana is the ultimate first-world, 18th century problem. You do, however, bend your knees and lower your stance automatically as soon as you enter a bush, and the good news is these stealth shrubs are everywhere. Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag is a more honestly designed game than the last, appearing cognizant of where it needs to lay down some rug-shrubs to cover up the seams between – how many systems is it now? There's sword-fighting, pickpocketing, free-running, air assassinating, diving, sailing, eavesdropping, harpooning; all slave to another massive, richly rendered slice of history. And it's all the better for designers understanding the monster they've created.

The crafting system is unique too, and IMHO well done, thought there are pieces that stilll need to be added, like the ability to craft jewelry. Eventhough it's not quite as open world as a standard Elder scrolls game, it still feels like one to an extent, and I would have no problem recomemnding the game to a friend.
