If somebody asked me to describe Murdered: Soul Suspect in one word, I would say: Unfinished. It's evident from the start that this game was rushed out the door too early in order to meet a deadline. Many things that you'd expect from a modern, full-priced AAA game are not present here. I knew something was up even before I jumped into the actual game. The menu was just a static image. There were no flashy effects when you highlighted any of the options. No bells and whistles whatsoever. Of course, none of that is actually necessary, but it is odd to see a big-budget game cut corners like that. Unfortunately, this was just the tip of the iceberg. After the game's opening cutscene, you're immediately tasked with investigating a crime scene. Games like Ace Attorney and L.A. Noire have already demonstrated excellent examples of how to simulate actual detective work, so it's pretty baffling to me that Murdered: Soul Suspect would take the most basic, and un-intuitive route possible. You point. You click. You win. There's almost zero deductive reasoning involved in investigating these crime scenes. Gathering evidence presents no challenge, since the 'clues' are ridiculously easy to spot in the environment. It's depressing that the biggest problem I ran into when solving the mystery behind these crime scenes was my tendency to overthink them. Turns out, the most obvious solution is ALWAYS the right one. Once you figure that out, the rest of the game is a cakewalk. So what else is there? Well, your ghostly character can possess people. This is a great idea on paper, but your enthusiasm will quickly wane once you realize that you can't actually control your posessee's. However, you can read their minds. Better than nothing, I suppose, but you'll be in for a rude awakening once you find that NPCs in the town only have a handful of phrases to recite, none of which are actually relevant to the investigation at hand. What could've been an excellent and inventive way to acquire information about the details of your case is squandered by the complete ineptitude of the developers. Soul Suspect isn't entirely without merit though. The story held my attention for the duration of the game, and even though the characters are archetypes that we've already seen before from the detective/mystery genre, it still managed to be a moderately intriguing tale. The pay-off is also decent, with a twist ending that even M. Night Shyamalan would be proud of. What saddens me the most is that Murdered: Soul Suspect is a very solid idea, and it could've easily been a great game with a little more TLC. It's painful to see a game with this much wasted potential. I liked the ideas here, but the execution left a lot to be desired. I'd love to see a sequel to this game where these ideas are more expanded upon, but as it stands, Murdered: Soul Suspect is half-baked, and it shows.

The Zone: A mysterious place inhabited by twisted creatures and men, where physics itself is bent, and the environment distorted. A place beset with violence, amplified by greed and bad choices. There are no black people or females in The Zone. Only white men with bad accents and terrible running posture.

In this game you roam around a bleak landscape and dying horribly either to mutants, bullets, or radiation. And you will die because this game is pretty brutal in its difficulty. It also is filled with NPC's who hate the player character and tell you to go away and will likely shoot at you if you take too long. It's also pretty good. It's post-apocalypse and almost a survival horror game where you have to worry constantly about lurking threats that will most certainly kill you if you are not careful. Also it has a pretty decent story, though one you can easily ignore due to the massive amounts of side-quests there are. In short... it's kinda like a Russian Fallout, though set in Ukraine. It's quite similar to Metro 2033 in its atmosphere, though this game is an FPSRPG rather than just a straight shooter like that game is. This is the first in a series of three games (sadly there won't likely be anymore since the devs are dead), so if this series interests you at all, then this would be the likely starting point. Have fun! :D

Alright, this game for me would be a 9.5/10. This game is an immersive, free roam survival, and it does a damn good job at it. The storyline is one you can really wrap your head around. The gameplay throughout the story is intense action and fun at the same time. The game has a realistic fighting system with bleeding effects and radiation. There's also the mutants that you can fight with. If the story isn't good enough for you, there's tons of side missions and free roam exploration. You can even win favor from different factions in the game and get special weapons and suits from them only. The only problem is in this game you can't join factions and control them without mods. So if you like large free roam survival games, then get this.

I really liked this game. Open world FPS with survival elements and light horror. You have to manage your hunger and continually scavenge for ammo and better weapons. This is a big factor in the early game but towards the end you may find you have tons of everything if you explore well, diminishing the importance of all this somewhat. The game's atmosphere is the biggest selling point. Wandering the Zone is quite a joy with the ambient noise of nature, cycling weather effects, a constant sense of danger from either human enemies, mutants or anomalies and a day/night cycle. The nights are dark and full of terrors. The AI groups interact with each other dynamically and the world feels like it keeps turning regardless of your own actions. You could return later to people you've done quests for only to find them surrounded by bandit corpses and being eaten by wild dogs. The ending kind of dips into one man army territory as you fight through endless hordes of enemy soldiers, but that would be my only proper criticism. The game does suffer a little bit with crashing and bugs but nothing particularly serious after being patched. It does look a bit dated now as well, particularly people's faces, but mods go a long way towards making it easier on the eyes. ------ There's a pretty good modding scene for all the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games. Recommended mods for first time playthrough; Zone Reclamation Project:- Required bug fixes and optional tweaks. Absolute Nature:- Environmental texture upgrades. Absolute Structures:- Texture upgrades for buildings and vehicles. Atmosfear:- Improved weather system. I played with just the Autumn Aurora 2.1 mod which is a combination of the above with a couple gameplay tweaks, new guns and other added stuff. Be aware though that when I played the mod had a serious bug with corrupting your saves if your quest log gets too full, so I had to pick and choose side quests a bit, keep multiple backup saves and do a bit more running back and forwards.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a timeless classic in my opinion. I'm sure many agree with me - it was my first venture into computer gaming many years ago (2008 is when I picked it up originally, I believe). Set in and around the area of Chernobyl (obviously), the world is open for you to explore and discover your identity, as you are an amnesiac. The games' structure is pretty evenly paced for the most part, however there is a very, very steep learning curve at the beginning if you are used to run-and-gun style games (particularly the first mission, where you are outnumbered and unequipped to handle the situation if you don't use tactics). You'll encounter everything from run-of-the-mill thugs and highly trained soldiers, all the way down to mutated beasts and telekenetic monsters throughout your journey. Overall, the game is a bit buggy to this day, and most people enjoying this title won't be computer-savvy enough to iron out some of the fixes possible. However, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a fantastic open-world adventure set within the confines of Russias' 'Exclusion Zone'.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is one of those special games that punches way above its weight class. It seeks to be an open-world, open-ended FPS/RPG with fluid relations between characters, emergent behavior in the wilds, and a compelling story and setting underpinning the whole thing. Those are lofty goals for any game, much less one from unproven developers back in 2007. What's shocking, then, is just how much it gets right even by modern standards. In the world of S.T.A.L.K.E.R., the Chernobyl disaster spiraled outward to create the Zone, a harsh land ruled by mutated creatures, spatial anomalies, and mercenaries seeking to capitalize on the chaos. You play one such S.T.A.L.K.E.R. sans memories, sent back into the Zone to kill a mysterious figure close to the epicenter of it all. Along the way you'll forge alliances with other wanderers, discover threats far worse than mutated wildlife, and maybe come face to face with the source of the disaster itself. I wouldn't bank on that last one without some serious effort, though. Instead of discreet levels, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is made up of maps that connect to form one contiguous world. Starting near the border of the Zone, you'll journey through radioactive swamps, underground bunkers, ghost towns, and more as you complete jobs for the other inhabitants. Sometimes that'll mean finding a stash of bizarre artifacts, and other times it'll mean gunning down a band of killers in their hideout. There's plenty to do in the Zone even without a specific mission, as you can loot corpses, hunt hidden stashes, and locate artifacts by navigating the treacherous anomalies that can crush, shock, or maim you with little warning. All of this is accomplished from a first-person perspective, but don't expect the run-and-gun action of... anything, really. The combat in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is very much its own thing, a perpetually harrowing affair of dancing around cover, emptying magazines to only land one shot, and pumping dozens of bullets into charging beasts. Weapons in the Zone are inaccurate, difficult to use, and seemingly do no damage until you land a headshot that kills in an instant. I imagine it's more like real-world firefights than anyone would admit, but that doesn't necessarily make it fun to be eaten alive by wild dogs who dodged or shrugged off a dozen rounds. You'll want to avoid combat as much as possible, at least at first, and luckily there's a robust and effective stealth system to make use of. This system tracks your light level, posture, noises made, and even gives you bolts you can toss to cause distractions (or trigger anomalies). There's a pretty big emphasis on stats across the board, really. Your character has resistances to all kinds of injury as well as a radiation level to monitor, your inventory has weight and conditions to consider, and every single NPC in the game has a reputation rating with you. There aren't always systems that address these stats directly, but they do represent significant depth to the simulation. Attention to detail extends to the environments, and it is here that you'll find S.T.A.L.K.E.R.'s greatest strength. For a nearly ten-year-old game, the Zone looks amazing, with crumbling buildings and thick underbrush and rolling clouds blotting out the sun. There's a palpable sense of decay and instability wherever you go, and it only grows more intense as you approach the heart of the Zone. Every dark corner can hide a creature that wants your blood or an anomaly that can rend you in an instant, demanding caution and tense attention even in the daylight hours. And don't get me started on the underground bunkers... some of the most effective horror encounters I've experienced in gaming have come in the subterranean halls of the Zone. I've spent a lot of time extolling the virtues of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. because they are many, but not without a price. It is an ambitious indie game after all, and that means all sorts of potential glitches and instability whenever you load in. Sometimes the AI breaks down, sometimes items vanish from the ground, and sometimes the thing will just crash when you least expect it. Beyond that there are definitely balance issues with the weapons and combat, exacerbated by missions with no real difficulty curve to them that might send you into a hostile mercenary camp before you find anything more formidable than a sawed-off. The rough translated text might actually be the worst offender, hiding key information and names behind English one step above Google Translate in some cases. The Zone is a harsh and unforgiving place, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. exemplifies it right down to the code. It's going to take you a long time and multiple tries to acclimate to its unique style, and turning to modding isn't a bad idea if the base game is just too daunting or janky. But once you come to grips with the combat and start learning the many ways to die in the Zone, you're in for one hell of a ride. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. does immersion and atmosphere better than almost any FPS, presenting you with a rich, frightening, living world that will fight you every step of the way.

Metro 2033 is an FPS with a lot of character. One of the best single player FPS experiences I've played, this game is incredibly immersive and well done. The graphics are spectacular, making the post-apocolyptic wasteland of the metro tunnels quite beautiful. In keeping with the theme of post-apocolyptia, I STRONGLY reccomend playing this game on a 'Ranger' difficulty - this increases bullet damage and reduces the amount of amunition found in the game. It enriches the already extremely immersive world and you'll find your heart pounding in many survival situations that other shooters can't match. The level design is also a plus, making the world feel expansive yet keeping the barren feel of the setting. The only con I have is there's no quicksave feature, you'll repeat many little annoying parts after you die. Pros: Graphics World Creation Immersion Level Design Cons: No Quicksave Excellent campaign, definitely worth a playthrough. The lack of a quicksave really hurts the game. B+

I agree a game should throw you curve balls, but I don't see how this part of the game is supposed to be fun while challenging, more like challenging and frustrating... that was too much for me, I quit after dying for the 5th time because I was wasting my precious bullets taken 2 at a time or could not hit them with my knife.

Perhaps it's the quantity of hours which I've spent playing Chivalry, but it's transcended the left click spamathon which it initially appeared to me. Duel is the true saving grave of this game, allowing genuine skill and experience to shine out. Against an equal or superior opponent, the combat is gloriously stressful, being slowly beaten back, watching your stamina bar diminish and diminish. Timing is vital, as well as footwork and positioning - being an inch out of range can make or break a duel. Duelling against an inferior opponent is pure satisfaction in gaming form, the initial charge towards your opponent with the smug knowledge that they are already a dead man walking is glorious. Throwing in a few cheerful apologetic emotes, and with one final swing, slash, smash, tear, stab, punch, kick, or maniacal laugh, you annihilate your opponent and cast him down before you. *Rematch*

Alice: Madness Returns Game Details Published by: Electronic Arts Developed by: Spicy Horse Genre: Action/Adventure Release Date: 17 Jun, 2011 Completionist Gameplay: 22 Hours “Alice Liddell, believing herself responsible for a fire that consumed her home and her family, escapes into a twisted version of Wonderland. While held at Rutledge Asylum for treatment, Alice was able to conquer her doubts, and eventually was released from the ward. Alice, now 19 years old, resides at an orphanage in Victorian London, under the care of Doctor Angus Bumby, a psychiatrist who uses hypnotism to help his child patients forget their memories. Though she believes herself cured of her madness, Alice still suffers from hallucinations of Wonderland..' The Gameplay Alice: Madness Returns is an action platformer that presents itself with a creepy, dark and creative atmosphere. Wonderland is inhabited by squirming leaches, firebreathing dolls and evil looking teacups, creating a twisted and surreal vibe. As you float and jump through an eerie dollhouse, you can drop bombs, shrink down to a miniscule size or dodge ceiling spikes ready to slam down on you. Unfortunately, the gameplay doesn’t evolve much from the start. This causes the game to become quite repetitive, especially when often, your task is to go and fetch something for another character. If it were not for the distinct and peculiar backgrounds, you might be tricked into thinking you’ve been playing the same level since the start. However, throughout the game there are plenty of hidden secrets motivating the player to fully explore every grotesque nook and cranny. There are enough hidden secrets to make it worth inspecting Madness Returns' grotesque nooks. Alice:Madness Returns does try to change the gameplay up. There are ramps to slide on, an underwater combat scene, puzzles to solve, and a giant dolls head to control. Unfortunately, oftentimes the camera gets in the way of doing these things. There are awkward transitions going in and out of third person, and side views are generally useless. Instead of a heart-pounding flee from a giant executioner, it feels like Alice is just jogging towards the camera. You’ll certainly be glad of the change of tempo, but it leaves a lot to be desired. Melee is the best part of the combat system in Alice:Madness Returns. It feels light, fast, and incredibly deadly. My favourite melee weapon would have to be the Vorpal Blade. Alice will flutter in and around her enemies, slashing them to bits and leaving a trail of butterflies behind. Unfortunately, ranged combat isn’t as fun. The controls for ranged combat lock your camera in place and the targeting system is a little frustrating to use. Unfortunately, this makes many of the battles you will face in this game almost impossible, especially when you are facing multiple enemies. The Soundtrack The soundtrack in Alice: Madness Returns is spot on in setting the mood. The voice acting is good. Nothing spectacular, nothing terrible, as it can get a little repetitive, especially during the longer levels. The Experience If you buy the DLC, there are some stunning dresses you can wear throughout the game. The Fleshmaiden is a direct example of this. While wearing this, Alice’s pupils are white, her legs are bloodstained and the actual dress itself is a mesh of bloody flesh and tendons. The story of this game will be left in your mind for weeks after you’ve played it. It is engaging and a dark twist on your childhood memory of Alice in Wonderland, and you’ll probably never be able to read it the same way again. Overall Verdict While the gameplay can be a little repetitive, I honestly think this game is worth it for the dark, realistic take on a fairytale. If you'd like to read more reviews from me, join my steam group!

The death of her whole family in a house fire and her subsequent internment in a psychiatric hospital have left Alice's life in a sorry state. She sees a psychiatrist to forget about that dreadful event, but she's can't take her mind off it. Her Wonderland, once a safe haven, is in ruins, overrun by corruption. Alice will go on a journey to find out what happened to her past and to her mind. The setting of the game is in a series of chapters each in a different region of Wonderland. Each has a unique art style and atmosphere and its own set of enemies. Each region is gorgeous, coherent, and full of detail, I often stopped for a few seconds to enjoy the scenic view from a vantage point. The chapters are long but do not feel repetitive, as they change progressively and playing through a chapters feels like going somewhere rather than more of the same. The little bonus objectives in each level help make them less linear. One exception is the 'playing cards' region, which was bland and uninteresting. There is only so much you can build with playing cards. Thankfully that level was also the shortest. The gameplay can be cut in two parts roughly equal (or maybe three but I'll come to that later): platforming and combat. The platforming takes elements from classics of the genre. Alice can triple jump and float through the air for a while; there are drifting platforms, air currents, switches and levers, roses to regain life and items to collect that act like coins to buy weapon upgrades. The game often times felt like Peach playing Super Mario 64. Overall the controls respond well but that aspect of the game is nothing exceptional. The tendency of the game to take over the camera can make this a bit frustrating at times. The combat for most enemies except the weakest ones is based on a mechanism of defenses that you have to get around of before you can deal damage. You can break the defenses through a strong frontal blow, or attacking from the back, or simply waiting for the enemy to lower its guard. You will get 4 weapons that fall in very distinct categories of short/long range and fast/slow. The game does not require you to perform any combos or to take down the enemies in a particular way, except the defense breaking mentioned above, combat is just simple and fun which is a positive for me. The difficulty curve was good, and playing on hard and getting the weapon upgrades at a reasonable pace (I got the last upgrade on the second to last chapter) the fights were challenging without being frustrating until the end. Maybe slightly easier if anything. The third part to gameplay that I was mentioning before is minigames. The game is riddled with them, and it is a strong negative for me. You can skip some of them but not all, and they felt like a huge waste of time. You will have to play slider puzzles (skippable but you have to find the pieces first), chess puzzles (skippable), riddles (optional), and the worst of all 'doll head marble platformer' (non-skippable). In this minigame you control a doll head that you have to make go through a level in the style of Sonic the Hedgehog. The camera is non-controllable and unreliable. This can be fun if you liked Marble Madness but this is not what I expected when buying the game, and it felt frustrating and unnecessary. The story is sick and depraved, perhaps as one could expect from the title of this game. Once the game had revealed all the pieces the big picture was frankly disturbing to me, including some aspects that are not revealed explicitely and left to the imagination, but at this point in the game I was imagining the worst. The story of what happened to Alice is divulged piece by piece in cinematics between the chapters, however in each level there are a number of 'memories' that you can pick up and that will reveal a bit of the backstory in the form of a quote by one of the characters, so you may be able to figure out what's going on before the end. Those memories that you have to find will also give you more detail about the personality of the characters than you would know from the cinematics alone, and that can help flesh out a story that is a bit on the light side. In conclusion I leave an overall positive review of the game, the flaws exist and there are some big ones but the good points and in particular the graphics design overcome them largely.

It gives you choice without just throwing options at you. You decide how you want to handle the situation, but you can't help everyone. So who are you going to save? reviews: From the beginning to the very end, Trails in the Sky FC ( First Chapter ) is a mix of really warmful feelings with a tiny bit of darker elements. The main story itself is simple and has been seen quite a lot already.However, it is the entire cast of characters who make it such an enjoyment to fulfill the role of a couple of young bracers in the Kingdom of Liberl. Estelle and Joshua, the two main characters, works very well together. And that complicity,until the very end of FC, with each chapter introducing new characters to team up with, each playing an important part in the whole story, will bring you a great deal of good emotions ! But that's not all, FC standing for First Chapter, there is of course a second chapter coming, and it seems FC is just a prelude to emotionally prepare the player for the last minutes of the game and what is to come in SC. You'll have to play the game to understand. While FC truly shine thanks to its characters and their story, it is still a rpg, meaning a combat system. It is classic but quite good, thought some combats are a bit long and leveling is needed from time to time. The item and magic system ifsa bit unusual and feel underused. It is still rather simple an easy to use, but be aware of you spending, because you can quickly run out of money if you don't farm a bit. Add to all that the technical part, lovely visuals, graphims, cute chara design, and a great soundtrack. Yes it is now one of my favorite rpg. So in a few months hopefully; the second chapter of Trail in the Sky should be released, which is supposed to complete the main story. Feeling heartbroken by the end of FC, considering its ending, such a cliffhanger and all that has been left unexplored. So hopefully again. the wait shouldn't be too long before going back adventuring with my favorite bracers and their friends.

I always have the most difficulty talking about a game I am completely enamored with, but The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky is one of the best games I've played. I have only played a handful of JRPGs such as Valkyria Chronicles, another of my favorites (most of which, including LoH aren't traditional JRPGs) however the appeal of this game, along with the likes of Valkyria Chronicles, is the connection to the characters, supported by a terrific battle system that emphasizes strategy and preparation. What makes this game special, for me, is the dialogue and the characters. So much care and thought is put into the writing and the cadence of the dialogue, that it really reads like a comic or a manga where, even though you read the dialogue, the intonations of the characters come across to make them real people with values, strengths and weaknesses, and not simply there to move things along. LoH takes its time, as well it should. Too often, things are thrust into an 'end of the world' scenario in video games that compels a forward momentum with the main quest, but LoH meanders. It is a tale about the journey, and not so much the final boss battle, to the point that the game is more than the sum of its mechanics. This is rare, in a video game, I think. Lesser games use the story as window-dressing for its mechanics, but things like putting on the school play, while little more than 'cutscenes' are given weight and gravitas that it is clear, to me, that the developers consider it just as important as the battle system. The battle system, too, is a lot of fun and while I don't have much to say about it, I do like the balance it achieves in terms of giving each character its own style, while still allowing a certain degree of customization with the Orbment system. I'm reiterating myself, but the meat is in the writing, and there is always the impression that Estelle & Co. are making their own personal journies within the greater macrocosm of a mysterious political world that is shifting with tectonic unease... pieces on the board are moving, and the beauty is being able to step inside the shoes of Estelle's perspective (who is really the main character, at least of this chapter), and be lost, grappling with the pieces of the puzzle. A balancing of the microcosmic, personal concerns with the larger, political and altruistic values is something that LoH manages to achieve, to the point that the game feels... well, like a full course meal. This is food for the soul, you could say. From the technical perspective, the music is terrific and enhances the atmosphere and connection to the diegesis. I had a few CTDs when I first installed, but IIRC, there was a patch and since then I have had no problems in my 55 hrs with the game. 10/10

Real boxing is a split decision for me. On one hand, I want to recommend it as I have had a bit of fun with it. But on the other hand, there are a few things that keep me from whole heartedly recommending it. The graphics are good enough and the animation is fine. The customization of your fighter, although limited, is a nice touch. The gameplay though, drags down the score. The hit detection is not refined. I counter attack and miss about half the time. I stand in front of my opponent and jab, but wait, he didn't move and neither did I, yet I didn't even touch him. I try to move backwards to regain stamina but instead I move up or down. I attempt to dodge, but the button didn't register, again. I have a hard time with a fighter, go back and fight easier opponents, train then go back and knock him out first round. Yeah, that's realistic. The leveling up system is kind of broken. I have ideas on how to improve it, but let's face it, I'm not a developer, my 'improvements' might just break the game. But don't let all these negative comments drive you off. It can be fun. When it is an actual battle and you win by unanimous decision, it's a great feeling. Or if you are taking on someone who has better stats than you, somehow play it smart and end up knocking them out in the third round with only a blip of health left, it is rewarding. The game does the feeling of the fights right, the atmosphere, it just falls short in the gameplay department. It has so much potential, but potential that is ultimately being wasted unless the developer picks it up again. It's time for the developer to get out of the corner, listen to your trainer and then give it one more go. With a few improvements, this game would be a great title and worth well more than the 4.99 that I picked it up for. Give it a shot if you're a boxing fan, but don't expect too much out of it. On the plus side, it is a great excuse to listen to some Dropkick Murphys .

First, let me get this out of the way: I am a big Castlevania fan. I got into the series during the GBA days (for the record I was about thirteen when Circle of the Moon came out). I played it, I played Harmony of Dissonance, Aria of Sorrow, both the DS Castlevania games, and yes... I wish they'd go back to those... but that doesn't mean this is a bad game. The voice acting is good, the combat is fun and engaging, the level design is interesting (especially the bits in Dracula's castle), and it has some of the most imaginative bosses I've seen (the Toymaker is a special favorite). ... it just doesn't play like a Castlevania game. Its neat to play as Dracula, its neat to have to fight as a vampire and use vampiric powers, and damn if I didn't let out a laugh when I saw what happened to that Chupacabra ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from the first game. ... but it feels more like God of War. Its by no means a bad game! I had fun with it! The giant robot fight at the beginning was lovably nuts and the fight against Death was really intense and actually almost killed me more than a few times. ... but it just doesn't feel like a Castlevania game. So, go into it not thinking of it as a Castlevania game. Think of it as a game where you play an ancient vampire who was awoken to fight off invaders to his realm and who has to learn to act and fight in a modern day world and regain his powers after his long slumber. Its great, its a hell of a lot of fun. Its just... not really a 'Castlevania' game.

A nice continuation of the Rapture storyline from the original game. While Andrew Ryan's laissez-faire objectivist dystopia was so farfetched and ludicrous that it couldn't possibly succeed, I find Sofia Lamb's collectivist 'Family' a much sterner ideological challenge. Indeed, for most of the game I couldn't escape the feeling that I was the bad guy in all this! Nonetheless, you ARE just trying to rescue your daughter, who turns out to be a Big Sister and can easily tear you limb from limb if she desired (luckily, you get on better than that). The splicers remain similar, but the addition of the powerful Brute Splicer certainly changes things (as a Big Daddy, it is your job to meet the challenge). The story was reasonably good, and the characters interesting. Combat remains more or less unchanged, except for some relatively minor weapon swaps (like a more powerful shotgun, and the addition of the Rivet Gun used by Rosie) and the fact that you can now wield Plasmids and a weapon at the same time. The resulting control scheme actually confused me a little bit, despite what one might think. But this is a relatively insignificant issue. Thank goodness the Plasmids are unchanged. If anything, they are now more powerful than they were in Bioshock. Telepathy and Incinerate remain good choices, while Hypnotize will help turn some of the nastier enemies of the game into powerful allies (like the afore-mentioned Brute Splicers, who wear bowler hats and speak with a funny East London accent). Hacking has significantly changed, and they got rid of that stupid pipe-dream puzzle in favor of something more simple. I appreciated the underwater scenes with Subject Delta, and thought it cool that the developers gave us the chance to snag some ADAM slugs on the seabed; after all, they ARE crucial to the story! One final point: the combination of melee and Electro-shock Plasmid is still the best. Hands down. Electro-shock is now more powerful than ever, with a storm of lightning worthy of Emperor Palpatine (POWER! UN-LIMITED POWER!!!!!!!) at your command. This, combined with your fully-upgraded drill (which protects you with a shield when it spins up) can take down even the toughest Big Sister. I swear by that combination! I guarantee it! 9.7/10

I regret to say, stay away from this game. While the game itself is awesome, it is not really enjoyable unless by 'enjoyable' you understand piling up random crashes. I have actually finished the game because in my first playthrough, it would only occasionally crash (at random), but the crashes got more frequent until it became impossible for me to even reach the main menu. Now, if I were the only one to have encountered this issue, I could still recommend the game to you, but the internet, including the Steam forums, is full of people with all kinds of OS's and hardware setups who have encountered -- and continue to do so -- the same issue. It is not fun to play a game, regardless of how good it may be, if you need to worry all the time that it may crash any second. By the way, none of the suggested solutions I have found (and there are quite a few) have helped. Once again, it pains me not to be able to recommend a great game (with respect to the artwork and the gameplay) like this, but I need to make clear one more time: the technical issues spoil the fun completely. Update: I may finally have found the solution to the crashes. Apparently, though I need to retry this with the DLC, the crashing issues are simply caused by the auto-save's tendency to get corrupted. If this happens, not only will the game crash, but it will also prevent you from getting to the main menu. So far, the following procedure has proved reliable: (1) When going to a new level, the game will automatically create an auto-save file. Wait for it to finish this, a message will be displayed, reading, 'Game saved.' (2) Press Esc in order to go to the menu. (3) Create a manual save file. (4) Press Esc again and delete the auto-save file. I kept doing this throughout my latest playthrough and had no crashes after deleting the auto-save file for the first time. The next step will be to test this on the DLC Minerva's Den. An update will follow soon. If the method described above should prove applicable to the DLC as well, I am going to change my review to a recommendation.

Fortunately, they don't make up a majority of playtime, but since (as you'd expect) the game ends with one, it's pretty anticlimactic. Secondly, and a slightly bigger problem, the difficulty scales poorly. Early in the game, with not much of a car, no skills, and weak attributes, survival is a real struggle. By late game, you're a superpowered killing machine. The sweet spot between the two is vanishingly small, though. It may work out better if you don't (as I did) complete a lot of optional side quests along the way, or if you leave them for the end. These problems do nothing to sully the fact that the game lets you wander a post-apocalyptic wasteland blowing the hell out of War Boys. Highly recommended. (The game's pretty as hell, too.)

Fun little Shoot 'Em Up that uses your own music to generate the waves of incoming enemies. You only have a small play zone to maneuver, with enemies coming in from the sides & top of your screen making for some intense close combat game play. The responsivness of your ship with the mouse is great giving you minute control over your position & graphically the enemies & weapons fire is easy to distinguish even when there is a lot going on, on-screen. Each song completed will grant you a random weapons upgrade drop, with a chance of a rare drop. These can be purchased (& upgraded) to increase your firepower of the four weapons slots on your ship & you can even change the angle of fire for each slot to customise your layout further which is cool. This is needed as you progress up the difficulty levels & to kill the random bosses needed to complete the story mode. Scoring is combo based, so the more you can kill in sequence (with less enemies escaping), will grant higher scores but stay nimble as each death will cost you a score penalty. Each kill also drops a bonus '♫' to pickup, granting health, power-ups & score increases so you need to be quick & get them all before they disappear for the best scores. I found all but the top two difficulty levels relatively easy; each difficulty level unlocks after killing three bosses. This can take some time making the start of the game feel rather dull to grind out the first few bosses, but if you stick with it, it becomes far more enjoyable later. For me, I just got a little tipsy off a few ciders, cranked up the volume & enjoyed some of my favorite tracks which certainly helped make the initial grind pass by much quicker :p . Although your music generates the enemies, you don't really get a sense of any pattern to the beat which would have been nice. For example, sometimes it goes into 'hardcore mode' in parts of songs you wouldn't expect & this seems to increase in frequency the higher the difficulty you go. It's not a big issue though, as you do get the feeling of randomness in the waves so each run feels different. Regardless of the few shortcomings, if you love your music & your shoot 'em ups it is very easy to waste away a few hours in ♪ Symphony ♪ liberating your music! TL;DR: If you like your music collection and shoot'em up games, you'll like this game. The gameplay, I have to say, isn't all that innovative - shoot'em ups have been done over and over for decades, but this one is a little different. The music recognition system varies up the gameplay a lot - slow and calm songs will make enemies appear in an orderly fashion, fast and complex songs will make enemies appear quickly from all around, putting your hand-eye coordination to the test. The music recognition isn't perfect, but does its job - the gameplay gets more frantic with higher tempo, special enemies appear at fitting moments, and the subwoofer weapon fires stronger the louder a song's bass line is. You can play any song at any difficulty level, unlocking higher difficulty levels over time. This way, the game is easy the first time you pick it up, but can turn into a bullet hell shooter by the end. Plus, it has that 'just one more level' effect that makes it addictive - you want to find out how this song is gonna look like, what item that song will get you, etc. The graphics of the game aren't technologically mind-blowing, but look gorgeous and sparkling with colors. The music, of course, is the best there is - your own ;). The few tracks that are included are nothing special and you'll need to add more to unlock more and better weapons. Personally, I sometimes think of this game as an advanced music visualizer, not only displaying pretty shapes, but also allowing you to interact with music. I think of it less as a shooting challenge, and more as a fun way to listen to music.

(At least I have yet to seen it) - Graphics are neat, pretty, and simple. Cons: - There is only so much to the game before some finds it too repetitive to be entertained from. - No unicode support. Be prepared to see lots of rectangles if the name is not in English. - You will play so many different songs of your choice, but you get so many similar weapons. - NO SEARCH BUTTON for songs. *Evil laughs at people who have millions of songs* - While boss battles add an interesting touch to the game, it can be rather distasteful when you're rocking out to a nice song and suddenly this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss comes in and wrecks it all. Still, it's interesting. I must strongly emphasize that these are all my opinions on Symphony for as long as I have played (3.6hours at point of writing this review). You may agree or disagree, but ultimately, reviews are only there as a suggestion as to whether you may or may not like the game, and to understand how it seems to work from others' point of view. There are more cons than pros in this review, and yet it does not mean I dislike it. It fits just right into what I was trying to find, something slack and casual that can keep my hands busy if not real work while I listen to the music. Should you feel the price is not the worth, then do buy it on sale and try it then. For that, I enjoy playing Symphony and I do recommend to you.

Beat Hazard and Audiosurf both have this and it makes life so much easier. On top of that, the controller support in the menus is also rather poor, with the 'cursor' frequently going exactly where you DON'T want it to. It honestly feels like a mobile port the UI is so awful. Beat Hazard has a mobile port and the UI for that game isn't even this bad. There isn't even a way to search for songs I've found, so have fun scrolling down the list for eternity. Pick this up ONLY if they ever fix the interface. The UI is just so cumbersome it makes the entire game unenjoyable.

This game is pretty cool. While little more than a 'find the hidden object' game with a first person perspective, the production value and the strong narrative make that experience enjoyable. The gameplay is super simple for the most part: find the 'ribbons' in the level in order to continue through the story. You can also solve simple puzzles to help you find hidden clues and narrative points, but it is mostly finding the 'ribbons'. This game is not mechanically rich, which is not a bad thing but simply the truth. If you want a gameplay focused game, look elsewhere. But I have to say, the environments are really cool. The intention was to make them look like they were painted and for the most part the effect is good enough. The level design also helps sell the painted environments, with homes that look lived in and mine shafts that look intimidating. In a game that is as mechanically simple as Ether One it is crucial that the visuals are extremely interesting in order to keep the players interest. The good news is that for the most part the world stays fun to explore and because of that it was always fun to look for the hidden ribbons. The story is probably the best aspect of the game though. It tells a highly personal tale about experimental research on a person who is losing their memory. There are twists and turns like all good stories have and I won't go into anymore details than that because I think it is best to know as little as possible about the story going in. I liked it. If you like narrative driven games like Gone Home then this is worth a shot.

Ether One seems to be the kind of game you love or you hate, and personally I loved it. Ether One's environment is a very slow-paced and nostalgic one (the game's about memories after all), and the puzzles are really esoteric. Honestly I think you have to be okay with looking up some answers and not determined to figure it all out yourself to fully enjoy it, and for people who would argue that defeats the point of a game, y'know, yeah. But Ether One's environment and story was worth it to me without necessarily being able to pro through the whole thing myself. It's absolutely gorgeous, the music really makes the isolation and nostalgia stick, and there's so much to explore. The difficulty of the puzzles encourages you to examine the whole environment very carefully and methodically, and having a physical space to stop and think things through and examine everything you've collected is really nice. However, I can't really recommend the Deluxe version. I ran into a pretty well known game-breaking bug on that, which was addressed in the original version. So they may eventually fix both of them, but I'd really only pick up the Deluxe version if you're already in love with the game and want to support it. A side note too, if first person games really unsettle you (like they do me), then there are some frightening and unnerving points here and there. Especially the beginning of the game was kind of overwhelming to me the first time, but other than those few points I found it to be a very peaceful game. You're alone in the environment, but you don't get stalked or terrorized, and there's a safe space you can return to at any point with a single keypress; on top of it, from there you can travel to a different location immediately. So unless that's a serious problem for you I wouldn't let the opening sequence deter you. Finally, the story is a sad one. There's a silver lining, but seriously it's a clearly dementia-related downer, go in prepared.

I like what they've tried to do and how they've tried to do it, and wish more developers would start with the story and let that inform everything else. It is well written and well told. You can technically complete the game without attempting the puzzles, but that's like listening to a radio on mute. If the developers can improve in that area, everything else was of a high quality, and I have high hopes for their future output.

This game was phenomenal. If you enjoy first person adventure games with puzzles, then you'll likely enjoy this game. I will do my best to avoid spoilers, the only one i'm mentioning here is literally explained in the first moments of the game (the entire premise of the game is based on it). You are delving into the mind of a person suffering from Dementia with Lewy bodies. You play as 'The Restorer' who is searching through this person's memories. You explore beautiful worlds, but they seem to be a bit off. Things are scattered about, the world is devoid of other human beings, and you are wandering about trying to put the pieces back together. In doing so you learn more about this person, about their life, about their struggles with the disease. What you'll find is an interesting look into the mind of a dimentia patient, and it is an absolute wonder. One word of recommendation. Look up how to get there if you have too, but do the Brimclif Mines BEFORE you do the Village. The area isn't intentionally hidden, but it seems to be common for people to run right past it. In chronological terms, the mine took place before the village.

Alpha Runner is a very RELAXING ... RAGE QUIT game. Two words I never thought I would put in the same sentence. This is all thanks to its groovy musical score that drowns you out in the background, while you die a quad zillion amount of times. The story is you’re an Alpha runner and your goal in life is to be a Beta runner. Get it Alpha, Beta, bad joke I know, but I couldn't resist. Being serious now, it's a platformer where you’re biggest and hardest achievement goal is to try and get 200 squares which appear on platforms that will eventually disappear as you stand on them. Also you must avoid spikes, rotating saw blades and dropping hammers. Unfortunately the game still feels like it is in Beta and this is because the developer ( http://lightsoutgames.com/ ) never seems to have a clear vision of where he was going with all this. It more looks like a product of a person who just wanted to make a game for the sake of wanting to make a game. For instance your character after a minute or so of traversing platforms will start to hold a umbrella which will spawn in, this is because there was a mini game where you had to avoid rain drops as well as continue to traverse the landscape of disappearing platforms and spikes, but the developer received a LOT of backlash about this concept and removed it, but kept the umbrella in for no reason. Also each time you die you get a different character, some characters have different abilities, one character can double jump, another character has greater speed, another character has an exaggerated jump, but some characters have no abilities what so ever and seem to be a product of a developer out of ideas. Options are really limited. For instance you can only mute sound, not turn in game sound down which can be bad for those that want to record. There are also three different modes... 1) Normal: As described above the objective is to try and get 200 squares. This took me a long time, there is an xp levelling up system and the more you level up the harder the traps get and the quicker the platforms disappear. Eventually at level 22 I was able to achieve the 200 mark all thanks to the red system which usually only gives you spikes and the Astronaut guy which has an elongated jump and allows you some time to plan ahead. The higher your level the more complicated the two mini games are in normal mode. One mini game involves you being a spaceship destroying all the other spaceships by shooting at them in the opposite direction until you come across the Mother ship which requires you to shoot at it travelling in the same direction. The other mini game requires you to hit one of three keys at the same moment the prop tells you to alas a saw blade spawns in. You must keep doing it even though it gets faster and faster until the exit door appears. These are the only two mini games in Alpha Runner and again seem to be a product of a guy only wanting to make a game for the sake of making a game and someone who didn't have a clear vision of what he was trying to achieve. 2) Speed run: Here you get a certain number of platforms and traps to try and get the quickest time on. Problem with this is that even though the number of platforms are always the same. Their layout and traps aren't each time you log out and log in it. So one lay out which allowed me to do it 28 seconds another lay out would not allow it. So what is the point of it all if it isn't consistent? 3) MLG: It's the same as normal mode but after a minute or so it will flip upside down, it flips upside down even in the mini games. No one plays this as it is too hard and the game does not give you any time whatsoever to adjust. A poorly designed mode that does not favour the gamer, hence no gamer is really ever that interested in it. 4) There is also a practice mode where you can turn traps on or off, but again this mode never adds to the achievement scoring and seems rather pointless in practicing in it. So why do I give this a thumbs up then in comparison to a weak envisioned platformer slaphazzardly put together, because in normal mode it is a really challenging and rewarding experience when you eventually are skilled enough to get your little guy to that 200 mark, and as stated before it is the most relaxing rage quit game I have ever played all thanks to a soundtrack which is the most fitting soundtrack I have ever heard for a game. Below is me showing you the various modes. Notice my best score 247! Are you game? https://youtu.be/5-_OP1pQQK8 Suggestions for developer... * Each character should have a different ability. * Get rid of the Umbrella. * More mini games. * If I’m able to opt out of the space mini game I should be able to opt out of the saw blade mini game. * MLG give the gamer more time to adapt to the world flipping upside down. * Background should change more the further you go, trees, waterfalls, comets, fireworks etc. * Speed run should be consistent in its layout. * A mode with an ending.

In all honesty, 'Dungeons' tries too hard to be a spoof of the old 'Dungeon Keeper' games to really stand on its own merits. If you liked Kalypso's previous game 'Ceville', then you'll probably enjoy 'Dungeons' on your first playthrough or two, but the game gets pretty repetitive even during the campaign. If you played the 'Dungeon Keeper' games, you'll probably find yourself wishing you were playing those games instead. This is not to say that 'Dungeons' isn't fun, but it doesn't have nearly the same level of detail and control that older games had. You can't, for example, pick up creatures, or create complex dungeons with many different rooms. The concession 'Dungeons' makes to customability is to add in lots and lots of 'gimmicks', which are decorative items that have the added benefit of making your Dark Lord stronger. 'Dungeons' is the smaller, pudgier, comic-relief sidekick of 'Dungeon Keeper 2'. If you like humor as a substitute for play, then go ahead and get 'Dungeons'.

400.app_name: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
reviews: Ask yourself... how does a game primarily tested and reviewed by players who recieved it for free end up with ~60% positive rating that has done nothing but decline since release? If you got this for free, awesome. Skyrim is a good game that once modded becomes even better. If you didn't, don't buy it. It is the quintessential cash grab when the Legendary Edition of Skyrim can be found for $10-15 and isn't ultimately any different outside of the 64 bit engine. And unless you're a heavy modder (in which case you probably got this for free anyways) that just isn't enough to warrant a purchase. There are a great many problems with this game. Microstuttering? Check. Awful TAA from Fallout 4? Check. Ultrawide support? No. FOV slider, or an option for motion blur that doesn't require an ini tweak? Yeah, you didn't need or want any of that, did you? Still locked to 60 fps, which while minor is annoying for those of us snobs who pay a premium for high-end hardware and expect our games to match. All of the bugs that existed in the original Skyrim? Totally untouched, don't worry! Bethesda is going to let modders fix what's wrong... again. Don't believe me? Check the top screenshots for this game. Bethesda's willingness to allow the community to resolve any problems with their games instead of fixing their own titles is pretty gross. If any of you think that it is acceptable for a company to release a title knowing about literally hundreds of bugs in the game but not do anything about it because the community will fix it for them... well, that is why this kind of thing happens. People like that let it. It would not have been hard to integrate the fixes seen in USLEEP or its separate parts into the core game, and I know it wouldn't have been expensive because Bethesda legally owns the intellectual rights to any mods published for Skyrim that have used the Creation Kit. No excuses, guys. This is laziness, pure and simple. I recommend you avoid paying for this, since obviously Bethesda isn't ever going to fix their games themselves and that kind of business attitude towards loyal customers should never, ever be rewarded with your money. And frankly, if you disagree with that statement, you're a major part of the problem. Consider the manuevering that Bethesda is doing to get everyone to rely on their mod service. Has everyone forgotten that they still want to implement paid mods in the future?

It runs like a No Man's Fallout or something. Where I could get 50fps on a mid-range with Skyrim on ultra, I barely get 15 on low with SSE. All the bugs are still there, as can be expected. Stick to OG Skyrim. It's better. Oh! And icing on the cake! Achievements are disabled with mods!

A bittersweet tale accompanied by beautiful artwork and soundtrack, Transistor truly is a gem that should be played by many. It excels on many levels, and has definitely become one of my favorite games up to date. The story of Red, a singer gone mute, and her companion sword, the Transistor, is told with just the right amount of ambiguity and subtle cues. Decidedly leaving some questions open while you play, Transistor invites you to piece it together yourself - the little hints regarding Red's background and how she ended up on her own are stunning to put together. Paced just right, it is truly a unique experience for the player. The gameplay, too, is quite fun. The mixture between turn-based strategy and action helps the player to find their own rhythm - a rapid, high-risk approach, or a carefully planned out attack: It is up to the player. Furthermore, the RPG elements of this game are very entertaining. Even though I found myself very comfortable with a certain set of functions early on, the game encouraged me to try out new combinations both through story and challenge incentives. I have to say that I am glad that they did, for I've long left my original set behind. And now with New Game+, one can explore even more of its versatility! And of course, Transistor stands out as a visually stunning, and audibly well told tale that was to be expected from Supergiant Games. Like Bastion, all assets have the beautiful 2D quality to them, and take it to the next level. Jen Zee's art direction is impeccable and truly comes to shine in this beautiful game. Darren Korb's soundtrack complements the visual side of it with a jazzy and relaxed style, truly emphasizing the artwork of the game. Transistor is a game that every gamer should have in their library. Every aspect of it is outstanding - gameplay, visuals, soundtrack and storytelling - and thus makes it a gem worth having.

Aesthetically stunning. Playwise, covers some of the same ground as Bastion (a running commentary on your actions from a third party, managing weapon slots for optimal loadouts, a bittersweet story that's not quiiiite as profound as it seems to think it is), but is a bit more 'on rails' than its predecessor. Still, it's glorious to look at, the soundtrack is spectacular, and definitely worth your time and money.

I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game! I would go as far to say it is one of the best space battle RTS out there. The combat feels like 40k ships going at it. Eldar ships are fragile but very fast. Chaos Ships are frail but rely on long ranged weapons to slaughter in the name of the dark gods! Imperial Ships are strong overall but lack any reliable ranged weapons like what chaos has (The Nova Cannon is powerful but aint that reliable) Orks are Orks, they ram you and if that dont work they shoot you with rocks or shards of scrap. Very durable ships though. Raming feels like raming, it hits hard but it's risky Heavily customisable ships (only complaint is that you cant customise the apperance without aligning with a sub-faction) The ships maneuver like ships, dont expect them to go anywhere quickly (unless they arer eldar) However there are a few things which weigh it down... The 2D plain which the ships are contrained to, if it were real 40k ship combat, ships would b eable to maneuver in all directions. (I understand why it's 2D and its honestly just a minor gripe) The abilities are not that effective or intresting... When is a chaos ship gonna get close enough to deal damage with the mark of nurgle? I also find it repeatative with the objective types... Most of the time it will either be kill the enemy or kill the convoy. The size of the fleet also disgruntles me... I want a true sized armada with multiple battleships and plenty of cruisers... Like the naval battles in the books. A true black crusade consists of more than a few cruisers and a battleship. Would be intresting to see what the devs do after the tau if anything at all... Would be intresting to see how tyranid hive fleets would fight aswell as the necrons...

At first you might get paired against harder opponents so you have to warp out as soon as you can and minimize the losses while gaining some points and experience. I also play LoL and even in a game with such a massive audience you get frustrating matching sometimes but you have to wait 20min to surr. This game has massively smaller audience so it is to be expected but here you can warp out after 2min. Also people are great, usually there is little communication but it's often in character and friendly. Overall, a great game 9/10

This is a game about space battles in the Warhammer 40k universe. As such it isn't really a SciFi game, but rather a SciFantasy game that plays like tall ships combat in space. If you ever played Battlefleet Gothic, the tabletop game, then this is a great videogame version. Not all mechanics were ported over (e.g. solar winds for Eldar), but the factions all feel and play noticably different. The campaign also captures the WH40k feeling to a t. Sadly it is only available as the Imperial Navy. For everyone else there is a pseudo campaign mode that chains random missions together and allows you to level an Admiral. There's also multiplayer, which I did not try. Apparently the balance can be quite wonky. I recommend this game for anyone who is a 40k fan!

So lets start by making a decent review of a game that could have had everything to be a great game and instead is a disgrace of a Space RTS that offends even the most casual of player's eyes and brains. I am a hardcore fan of the War40K series, i used to play the tabletop, bought the few games that came out ( yes even turds like this one) and i can proudly say i have almost every book that the Black Library brought out to date. Does this make me a Pro Reviewer or some authority in what comes to appreciation of games? No. But i do have an extensive background in IT ranging from programming and having been involved in some titles to currently being a sort of Specialist for companies with problems.. yes i identify and sort out problems in exchange for money. ( yes im a capitalist pig and i enjoy every second of it ) So without more preamble my opinion on this game... ... its CRAP. The UE4 engine is a beautifull engine, only that Tindalos is a very ugly dev team, dont get me wrong the game in itself is interesting in some aspects, small details like ship textures and animations are well made, the only problem is that the maps are rubbish, and by saying they are rubbish i mean imagine yourself a A4 piece of paper with some colourfull background imprinted on it, then smack a white gride accross that lovely piece of paper and start placing figurines of ships moving in a 2D environment, yep you got it, thats BFG Armada for you, repeated every single mission, every map is more or less the same, recycled with some objects to make it look diferent but very much the same with the same elements and the same background, in other words, this dev team hasn't put an ounce of imagination and effort to make the game in itself appealing and pleasing to the eye. The game modes are pretty much the same you can expect from the maps, you are either a defender or attacker and face Orks, Elder, Chaos, seditious forces and have besides of the fact of choice which force you want to take on to keep the campaign rolling in your favour not much else to help you with. Bear in mind that the campaign was balanced around the awfull extended Beta phase Multiplayer bringing all the unbalance, bugs, quirks and issues along with it. As game modes you have, - Assassination - which works pretty ok - Convoy - God help you if you face Eldar or Orks whatever position you are - Siege - Meh... - Cruiser clash - smack figurines against figurines against one another over the A4 paper and start roling dice - Retrieve data - God help you again... Probably theres one mode im forgetting but then again its nothing you are missing out on since the game revolves around the rinse and repeat mechanism i explained above. The races, well fellow Imperial loyalists , you dream of bringing the Emperor's light to the galaxy? Crush Chaos and the Xenos assailing the imperium with your mighty fleets? Think again, while the Emperium is the jack of all trades its also the most difficult race to achieve anything with, the Imperials lack speed, range, adequate tools and get beat by amout everything else in the game, yes even in the campaign, remember this game was balanced around multiplayer. Chaos - Long range, favours of the dark gods, crush Imperium die to everyone else. ( and its also a load of rubbish the way they were implemented lorewise, Table Top they make sense, but book wise, well its an offence ) Orks - WAAAAAGH!!! ... errr no. You do have tractor beams, can boost your ships in a similar way that the eldar do and are deadly are close range. The issue is getting in range with them, once you get to grips on a ship you can pretty much anihilate it but then again not all of us want to play the same thing over and over again.. or play Orks for that matter, Orks remain the only race where i believe people with brains can actually succeed in MP, which in itself is good and ultimately sad at the same moment. If you like lotsa guns and a funky gameplay style of grabbing people, ramming and shooting then Orks are your race. Eldar - the swiss knife of MP and the bane of Tindalos, or a bucket of idiocy on display. Eldar are like a sniper riding a motorbike zapping you from range and peeling away before you can do anything, its one of the races that needed a profound balance work but never got to because Tindalos cant keep deadlines and sorta rushed eldar out . These guys are the long range of long range fighters in the game and no one can catch them except for a good ork player with brains and even then its not a garanteed win for the Ork while for the Eldar player its more or less of a FU and IWIN in 90% of the fights kinda sign. I have played the Multiplayer, while the Imperium revolves around spamming Nova canons and doing not much else and every other race doing what i described above the game doesnt bring anything else new, you pick a race, win renown, build up your ships and get splattered with 300 points game modes where you cant bring anything meaningfull to the table.. or get into 600 gp games and get anihilated by people with already countless hours and every excel spreadsheet available just to get a garanteed win. Also a word of caution, if you think someone is cheating, it probably is, other than finding the odd 6 battleship player ( which i encountered quite a few times ) , there is the player using one Battlecruiser that somehow just does not die to anything, or the player with perma invis ships, yes there is alot of polish work to be done by Tindalos. The game is, -Prone to freeze and ensures you a reboot -Prone to crash out of nowhere -Prone to consume insane ammounts of resources over nothing ( and i have 2 good rigs ) - Filled with bugs. There is one good point about this game and its the fact you can use Renown to equip your ships and customise them, only you cant always use them when you need and just because you have a good strat rolling unless you use the flavour of the month race you cant do jack. Another point, the descriptions for the guns, modules, ships and about everything are an aberration, so be prepared to go trough countless spread sheets and grow a Korean accent. This game is not about fleet fights also, its about micro management where who clicks the fastest wins, forget the Cogitator mode , you want to win? Get yourself some Korean finger enhancements and start clicking away. Conclusion: I am of the option that games should catter to everyone, to some more then others naturally but they should grant this feeling of joy and satisfaction, provide you immersion in a alternative world where you can have fun and forget your wife and worries for a good couple of hours. Battlefleet Gothic fails at providing fun, its buggy, its unfinished, its unbalanced in all aspects and lacks the depth and respect that a Warhammer 40K title should have. Tindalos proved to me at least that they are not up to the task of programming games, perhaps a calculator or a rudimentary solitaire game in Pascal or qBasic but not something of this dimension. Remember this launch was delayed to iron out bugs and bring out balance, instead it came out with all the old problems and some more attached. If you are a hardcore 40K fan then this game might appeal to you for the sake of having another WAR40k title in your library, if not spare yourself the money and the trouble and keep away from every game Tindalos develops. PS. Why does Games Workshop grant licenses to such midgets that cant even hammer a nail on a wall without breaking the house is a question that bogles even the mightiest of minds on this planet, but alas, perhaps we can see a gem like DoWII somewhere in the future.

First of all, let me tell you that i've played this game on both PS4( friends house) and PC( My game) The difference between consoles and PC version are obvious: Lagg. Some may say there are more glitches in the PC version then the console version, but that may not be true. The reason why less glitches and bugs may be encountered in consoles in comparison to PC is that most are caused by the lagg, example: The scale down a building pretty fast once you got the hang of the new parkour controls, when suddenly your game laggs for maybe 3 seconds. When the mists of lagg clear and you're eager to continue, you notice Arno floats mid-air in his gliding position, not able to move or anything. Starting Coöp or fast traveling may fix this, yet if you're in the begin missions, this may turn you into a rage devil.( consult a doctor before raging, tables will be flipped.) A pro about the PC version is that the online experience is free of cost, in comparison to PS4 and XboxOne. Lagg doesn't occur for me most of the times(mind you that the only thing not being 'optimal' is my vid card.) making the online experience one of the best gameplay features of Unity. Just for those who would still consider buying it. I strongly suggest you don't when your pc can't handle the weight this game will bring with it. If your video card is from Nvidia, is a ' generation too less' and it's the only thing not optimal for Unity, you might want to take the risk to try it, if you're willing to go through 30 minutes of hell first in the begin missions. Conclusion: For the average old gen pc user, i don't recommend buying it. For those with a 'weaker' vid card, i'm suggesting you consider well before taking the risk to try it. But a life without risk, is a life not lived.

As far as free-to-play titles, Gear Up is a fantastic vehicle shooter. It’s audience is players seeking instant gratification through combat, who would rather forgo the tediousness of voxel-building to jump right into a frag fest; the type of player who plays Minecraft for the combat. There are an extensive number of possible module combinations, and it's easy to build new vehicles as it’s like slapping Lego’s together. The toy-box atmosphere, simple controls, and variety of vehicle combinations create a lasting experience that leave an impression. If you prefer chiseling away at the perfect combination of parts try Robocraft, or similar. But if you're a player who likes to smash robots together and watch them explode, then start playing Gear Up.

A helpful review I previously wrote a gear up review stating that its a great game, and the usual blah blah everyone sees, I decided I'd try to be a bit more helpful as I've been seeing a few newbies to the game. I'm going to do this in sections to help organize (I suck at writing out stuff) Parts/G points First off, parts are not your source of how good you are, yes there are some slightly unfair parts that can cause rage, but for the most part they are balanced. If i'm a bit bored, or there are a lot of new players abroad, I tend to go basic tank, and I still tend to rek some scrubs, because when compared to some other typical layouts the basic (scout) tank is pretty good. So don't always see someone using some big fancy gun and go 'Wow, if I start using that, I'll be that good', cuz that ain't it sugar. Just practice with what you have and then try one new thing, don't always buy something just because you think it'll make you 'better'. The people you meet There are several types of people in this game that you will meet quite quickly, not all are as nice, or as helpful as I can be. First, the 'Basics' as I call them, people you know just started, either based on rank or the parts they have. Typically consisting of all scout but one part or two, and usually using a machine gun or heavy cannon, they are usually high health but really slow and don't know what they're doing (they pick some big heavy body thinking that it will keep them alive, heh, if only it were that easy). There are the snipers, all shapes and sizes, from the flying ones that have just enough health to not get one hit by heavy snipers, the fast little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with no health at all, or the spiders that get somewhere cheesy and pick off basics, they all can get very annoying, but luckly it only takes one or two hits with something higher damage to destroy them. The Heavies, the big ones with like 300+ health and a lust for explosives and fast bullets, not fairly common, but they can ruin your day. The Gunners, fast guys with around 100 health and a need for speed, along with a passion for machine guns, they tend to zoom in F*** S*** up and run off for health and ammo, they are the type to rely on weapons as their skill, and don't confuse them with harpooners and lazer'ers Harpooner/lazer.. er These type are pretty simmilar to the Gunners, except they actually have some decent skill, they tend to use the harpoon gun , or the vintage laser and assorted secondaries, which require pinpoint accuracy, and a steady freaking hand (with how fast they go, they need to account for their movment, your movment, obsticals, and gravity with the harpoons), and if they are as good as I make them out to be (and usually they are) they will kill you... again and again. The Maps Well there isn't much to say, there are several maps, some with optional night time, and most of them are pretty cut and clear, the open ones are fun for snipers and slower based combat, the duck and cover ones are better if you like quick kills and nasty 3+ person skirmishes, and the skate park ones are for some sick moves and rad jumps... bruh You can pick three at a time when making a game and so long as someone is in the game it will keep cycling the three indefinitly, but there is no G coin/exp gain from just you in a match, even if you have a score, but someone leaves, you wont get any gain (sorry for you farming type) Health, ammo, and power ups, oh my The three aformentioned things are found everywhere on maps (almost redundanly so), and are pretty simple, health packs give you 25 health, ammo packs refill ALL ammo (every single gun and secondary, even if empty will totally refill), power ups have two effects, blue shields will reduce damage taken by 1.5X and visa versa with red rockets (yeah I have no clue where they pulled that idea from, damn swedes) will increase your damage by 1.5X, and if combind you get a fun purple...y glow Weapons Well, I figure you can guess what that means, there are several type, lets delve them Bullet/laser GUN, run o' the mill machine guns, with a quick travel time and low to fair damage (this includes the description of the lasers that fire like a gun) and really good reload times Snipers/laser BEAMS, instant travel time, fair to INSANE damage (up to 113 with the desecrator and 1.5X dmg) but nil on reload Shotty/fire Flame throwers, and the shotgun, oh god, what can I say, MASSIVE damage over short time, but no range, pick something fast nimble and good god make sure you can turn fast Missle The ole' standbye, whether lobbed or launched they do good damage, have a range of decent to F*** all short, but deals decent to insane damage, and has really good reload times for the damage So wrap up anyone? It is a easy to pick up, hard to learn, impossible to master game of goofy tank battles and endless mayhem. I recommend that everyone try it, its free and fun as all getout obligatory Used super dmg cannon on super light tank, got 1.5x dmg, killed the light tank next to me along with myself 11/9 would aloha snackbar again
