Having just finished, I don't know where to start with this game. I would say that the game was very refreshing playing an evil character. Unlike most RPGs, this wasn't kicking puppies and stealing candy from babies. Tyranny did a fantastic job of exploring different types of evil, from “I’m just following orders” to bat-♥♥♥♥ crazy ♥♥♥♥♥♥ murderer. You could even scrape together something that vaguely resembled kindness. From a story point of view, this game had tons of choices. It’s hard to explain just how many meaning choices they fit into the storyline. This is where the game really shines, most every choice has some meaningful impact later in the game. I don’t mean choices like “do you want the red banner or the green?” These range from NPCs responding to decisions, sometimes with lots of anger, in later dialogues to major story altering changes. The combat system seemed a little lacking compared to Pillars of Eternity, but I am not sure I can tell you why. The rune based build you own spells system was very well executed and a lot of fun to experiment with. Overall I would say combat was solid but not great, but that’s not why you should play Tyranny. The combat was really just an excuse for the enriched storyline. The one big complaint I had was this game has a very unsatisfying ending. This is made up for partially by an appendix that tells you what happens after the events of the game and what everyone goes on to do with their lives. I would agree that this game deserves RPG of the year for 2016.

I am a big fan of RPGs. I played Wizardy 1 nearly twenty-five years ago, and trekked through Wasteland 2 just last month. So I am familiar with isometric third-person games. But I am very sorry to say, I just did not like this Tyranny at all. That’s not to say it does not have positive strengths. I will just touch on these because they are covered better and more completely in some of the other many, many favourable reviews of the game. You can find those elsewhere. I liked the music, the atmosphere and the game design. These are immersive and persuasive. The music, in particular, is different from the usual generic synth sports show-theme. Cello-based, it remind me very much of the music for the equally atmospheric Arcanum game. The story too is – or at least appears to be – complex and rich. This vastly helped by the sophisticated faction system. Every decision you make gains favour with one gang, tribe, general and army and makes you hostile to their opposite number. On the face of it, this is a clever idea. Except… you eventually find that you have to ‘game’ the system to gain the benefits of faction favour (which gain you special abilities) rather than making decisions based on character or story. And this takes me to a more serious – for me – objection to the game. Specifically, the dialogue and voice acting are awful. It’s clunky. It’s cliché’d. Really staid and vapid. And it cuts the balls off the faction-story arcs the player is trying to follow. The dialogue is obviously written by writers of fanfic rather than real writers who have read and learned from other great authors of fantasy and medieval work. Try to imagine ‘Game of Thrones’ or ‘The Walking Dead’ with dialogue by the scripters of ‘The Young & The Restless’. To make it worse, the actors they’ve chosen for the voice stings are all flat, modern and midwestern American. That can work in a fantasy setting – just listen to the voices of the Witcher cast – but here, in what is a supposed to be a cod medieval setting, they sound fake and jarring. There are other problems with the game: While the landscapes, as mentioned before, are attractive, they are small – easily explored and rather samey. The combat system is neither intuitive nor interesting to master. You cannot queue up multiple actions which makes fighting enemies a chore of micromanagement. Finally, while the game is based on the proposition that for once player choices do make sense and do contribute to changing the game, one finds this doesn’t really matter. One still ends up fetching this, fighting that and confronting the same old kind of boss. There’s no problem with that if done with style, intelligence and character, as in Baldur’s Gate, for example. But it is a problem here since Tyranny is, at the end of the day, incredibly bland. Tyranny could and should have been better, a fantasy game where the fantasy was just too flat and boring to save a rather ordinary game.

Simply put, Bioshock is a really good single player FPS. I will only go over a few things that I loved about this game. Pros: -Rapture has a really interesting and uneasy atmosphere to it, making exploration for supplies and recorders worth it. - Using the environment around you, different ammo types, and a good variety of enemies makes combat fun and tactical. - Plasmids are very fun to use in combination with your guns to spice up the combat.\ - Tenenbaum is one of my favorite characters, but I'm not sure why. I just love her character. - Saving the little sisters instead of harvesting them is one of the best feelings in a video game I've ever had. - The big reveal when you meet Andrew Ryan is very memorable in making you question your actions up to that point. - All weapons can stay useful even to the very end of the game. - It has a good game length ( a good 15-18 hours to complete) Cons: - After Fontaine's betrayal, the game really slows down into a boring slog. I fell asleep at my desk twice trying to get myself to finish the big daddy suit. - The final boss fight is incredibly easy. There is no challenge to it or mix-up of tactics. Just keep shooting until you drain his adam. - Your reward at the end of the game is a pretty generic 30 second cutscene that depends on your choice to harvest of save the little sisters (hell, the neutral and the bad ending are just the same scene, just with different narrative tones), so I felt like my choices never had much weight or impact on the story. TL, DR: Bioshock is a good game that will give you a good amount of content and gameplay. Despite some flaws towards the end, it is still a good game. Try getting it on sale (especially if you can get the Bioshock bundle.)

This game is freaking huge; it has the kind of scope and scale that you very rarely see in any game. You are given the option to effectively start with the space equivelent of a backpack and a shed, from which you can work your way up to owning an enormous fleet (and when i say enormous, i mean both numerous ships AND proportionally vast construction - there are ships so large they can't actually dock with any stations because they'd crush it!) entire sectors of space filled with your supply stations and factories, able to smash entire sectors into submission with brute force or starve them into poverty with strategic cordons of ships to block trade routes. HOWEVER - This. All. Takes. Time. Alot of time! Be warned: if you choose the slowest start it could be a good 30hours or so before you can even afford to buy another ship. This is not a game you can just dip into for five minutes - it needs focus and attention, but I for one think the time is worth it :)

Okay, so it's scary. REALLY scary. Fantastic atmosphere, both visually and aurally...very tense...but is it LOGICAL?! Firstly, there's the usual 'you've been given a really, really super-dangerous job for next-to-no pay' premise...so in spite of them never clearly stating as such, I'm assuming that all of these post-FNAF games are set in third world countries, where life is cheap and you'd basically murder your grandmother for spare change. I mean, I accepted the premise of the first Five Nights at Freddy's as much as anyone, but the sixtieth time around this kind of set-up is pushing its luck just a tad, don't ya think? Secondly, I do everything the game tells me to. Run here to stop generator A, B, C, or D from running down, solve (admittedly well-done) mini-puzzles at the laptop when required, and try my best to hang around in the designated 'safe-spot' for the rest of the time (quite how the laptop knows the exact place in the house to stand to avoid ghostly victimisation I have no fricking idea, but I'm happy enough to accept that I know ♥♥♥♥-all about modern technological capabilities). And STILL I die, again and again and again. I don't know WHY I do, but I do. There's a bit in the game's instructions which says something about Sophie occasionally attacking because she simply 'doesn't like you'. Well, apparently she ♥♥♥♥ing HATED ME, because she assailed me left, right, and centre. No reprieve. No logic. Just sudden, random, rampant doom. Don't get me wrong, I actually quite liked this one. There's something at least slightly more assured about it than the likes of, say, Emily Wants to Play. But I'm getting a bit sick of this recent run of horror games where sheer, dumb-arsed LUCK seems to play such a large part in how long you survive before the next fatal 'jump-scare' comes your way. I'm sure a plethora of fan-boys and fan-girls will slap up guides in no time, telling me what you have to do at each and every different hour and blah-blah-blah, but unless I can actually work this ♥♥♥♥ out for myself, it's not exactly LOGICAL, is it now? I honestly look forward to all you people proving me wrong, at which point I'll revise this review and the below-given rating. Please, tell me how my faculties are flawed, and by that I don't mean write ♥♥♥♥ like 'dude, everyone knows that 11pm is the time when Sophie attacks you if you hang around too long at generator C', because unless the game clearly tells me this, IT ISN'T LOGICAL. Please, thumb me down and tell me I'm wrong, but also tell me WHY I'm wrong. Hell, even the first FNAF plays reasonably fair for at least the first few nights, but this game gave me almost no delusion of 'control' over my fate whatsoever. I've played a LOT of horror games in my time. And almost all the 'old' ones - I'm even talking up to Outlast and Alien: Isolation here! - give you sufficient indication of what you have to do to survive, then the rest is up to you. This super-recent, post-FNAF breed of game seems to believe that '♥♥♥♥ happens' can pass for good game design. I beg to differ. Having said all this, I think the dev of this game shows tremendous potential, he just needs to emulate a better - nay, FAIRER - kind of game in future. This is far from the worst of its species, but it's also not the best, and until someone (including Scott Cawthon himself) makes a game as good as Freddy's the first, we really should just put a cork in all games of this type for the time being, whad'ya say? (Or failing that, ♥♥♥♥wits like me could just stop buying them, haha.) Looking forward to that veritable assault of 'tips' from all you super-savvy fan-persons out there... Verdict: 6.5/10. UPDATE: Well, here we are a bit over a month later, and credit where credit is due...this dev has laboured long and hard to give the gaming public a much improved experience. And, I'm pleased to say, he's MOSTLY succeeded. We now have two difficulty levels - though the easier of the two is still much too hard in my humble opinion - and while the 'random' death element has been ostensibly removed, and 'cheap' deaths are far less common, I still can't help but feel that there are moments when you're damned-if-you-do-and-damned-if-you-don't, and I certainly still feel that save-points are too few and far between (once every hour would be more than challenging enough, especially for the allegedly 'easy' version of the game). Whichever way you look at it, I'm happy to concede that this is by far one of the best games of its type - i.e. the some-strategy/some-luck/jumpscare-game-with-minimal-mechanics sub-genre - though it would appear that the first Five Nights at Freddy's is destined to remain the king of its kind. As with that game, however, I'm probably destined to never find the nerve and/or patience to fully 'beat' this one, but in light of the dev's improvements I'm more than happy to adjust my rating to read (drum roll, please): REVISED VERDICT: 7.5/10. SECOND UPDATE: Well, I gotta hand it to Eddie the dev...after the initial doubts of myself and many other reviewers, he's worked long and hard at this little game of his, and he's finally managed to make it fair to the point where even the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ likes of yours truly can now complete the darned thing (granted, on the easiest difficulty)! I'm now willing to go on record and state that this is, in my opinion, a rival for the second-best game of its type, after the first Five Nights at Freddy's. Congrats, sir, and I hope you get some kind of Dev of the Year award for this commendable effort. ♥♥♥♥ing good game...finally. RE-REVISED VERDICT: 9/10 (by far the biggest score hike I've given a game...EVER).

In its previous life, The Ball was a charming and free mod for Unreal Tournament III. Very minimal thinking is required for the first 2/3 of the game. At best, The Ball is a beautiful, but extremely mediocre and repetitive bore-fest. It's only until the final 1/3 of the game that the developers decide to mix things up with new enemies and unique ball modifications. But by then, a chunk of their audience will have already lost interest. There is just a certain quality consumers expect from retail games. As a free mod, The Ball might exceed every gamer's expectation. But, as a retail product, it lacks the ingredients to make it challenging, exciting, and fun. Grade: C

The Ball is a first person action-adventure game featuring a full single-player experience built on Epic’s Unreal™ Engine 3 technology. As a swashbuckling archaeologist working on the slopes of a dormant volcano somewhere in Mexico, you get stuck in a cavern. It doesn’t take long before you realize this is more than just a cave. You reveal ancient ruins that have been hidden from outsiders for centuries and discover a mysterious artifact, a gold and metal shelled Ball. As you progress towards solving the mystery of this amazing place you must unlock the secrets of the Ball and learn to control this ancient artifact. Venturing deeper into the volcano, you reveal some of mankind’s greatest secrets and you will start to encounter not just puzzles and traps, but also various strange creatures – the guardians of this mystery. These creatures have to be overcome, using only the Ball to defend you.

I have owned this game for years, and played it a lot . I'd say a good third of that gameplay is from my currently-in-progress guide. If you've come here from The Solus Project, you should note that TSP is The Ball's spiritual successor. It is not a direct sequel. While you can safely play TSP without ever having played The Ball, I highly recommend playing The Ball first. Having now played both, I can see very direct connections that both make more sense, and are more exciting to find, if you are already familiar with certain things from The Ball. The Ball gets compared to Portal for obvious reasons: It's a puzzle game with simple tools that began as a mod and became a standalone by popular demand. This is fairly light, as far as puzzle games go. You aren't going to spend hours screaming in frustration, but that doesn't mean the solution to everything will be immeidately apparent. The Ball experiments with a few different mechanics, but doesn't dwell on any of them for too long. Nothing hangs around for long enough to get old - unless you have a distaste for Aztec aesthetics, in which case you may want to check out the screenshots above. Some sections of this game are relaxed and can be taken at your own pace. Others require a modicum of haste. I can't quite define why I'm so enamoured with The Ball. It has a simple charm. It does what it needs to do (puzzles, adventure) and doesn't add anything unnecessary on top - but there are extra things to explore (secrets and bonus levels) should you choose to. The story isn't particularly complex, and you do have to go out of your way to learn all of it, but the basics are literally impossible to miss. If you enjoyed Portal for the exploration and puzzles, you'll probably enjoy The Ball. If you're seeking The Solus Project 0.1, you might be disappointed, but I would still recommend picking this up on sale.

Knights of the Old Republic II is, even though sadly unfinished, a decent game with a wonderful story. A decent game because, well, the combat sucks. It sucked in the original Knights and it sucks on this sequel (though the new greatly unbalanced abilities make it go faster most of time.) It basically amounts to selecting Force Storm, clicking on it four times and watching the movie that is combat. To add to this, levels are very small (Its pretty graphics, at the time, did not allow for big levels in the Xbox). But yeah, that doesn't really matter. What matters is its story and characters. The story is a deconstruction of the Star Wars setting. While Knights 1 had a very black and white morality, same as the Star Wars movies, the sequel is shades of grey in that regard. It regards the fighting between Jedi and Sith as useless, since the balance of the Force must be kept. Your character is a wound in the Force, a former Jedi who has had their connection competely severed with it, and only know, about 5 years later, is it coming back. Your master (and one of my favourite characters in gaming), Kreia, has unique views of the Force, borne from her writer's (Chris Avellone) views on the Star Wars setting, and every conversation with her is interesting. Should you follow what she teaches you, you will find yourself at the beginning veering towards the Dark Side of the Force, only then to be criticized by her for being evil just for the sake of being evil. The game offers a satisfying Dark Side route unlike the first game's 'being a psycho just because'. The other characters are also great. Unfortunately, Obsidian got rushed (as always) to put the game out on Christmas, and the ending doesn't provide a very good conclusion. Even with the restoration mod, it still feels unfinished. Even if you don't like Star Wars, I'd recommend this game. Unless you really hate lightsabers.

Just download the Restored Content Mod, and all is well :).

Been a Star Wars fan for a long time and KOTOR II in my opinion is the best out of Star Wars video games. This new update they've implemented has been very much needed for a long time. I'm not going to list the improvements, because I think of this as a reboot of the game. That's how big this update is for this game. I mean, it no longer crashes on start up on modern computers. Just that bug fix would've made me happy so I wouldn't have to search the internet for 6 hours to figure out how to make it work. (sigh) Now to the actual gameplay: Much like Fallout, but in the Star Wars universe, but with less customization of the character. Like Fallout, you can make good decisions and bad decisions, but instead of karma, it's the side of the force you're on. (Important in late game) FANTASTIC STORYLINE: Obviously I'm not gonna put spoilers in here, but the story telling of Bethesda is 10/10 once again. This game is both RPG, and a realtime strategy game, all in third person. Who should I attack, with whom should I attack, what do I attack with, when do I heal, when should I use the force? So many variables to think about. Many different force powers are in this game, and when certain powers are combined with a certain character setup, (levels of strength, charisma, wisdom, etc.) they can become very powerful. EVERY PLAYTHROUGH WILL BE DIFFERENT. Unless of course you do the same combination of things everytime, but that's boring. That's just a handful of things that are good about this game. With that said, if you're a graphics snob, you're gonna have a bad time because, yes, this game is over 10 years old; and even with this update there are still some bugs that happen, but I haven't had any bug experiences that make me lose game progress unless I have forgotten to save in a while. Basically, if you are a fan of Fallout and a fan of Star Wars, this is a must-have game for you, but when it comes down to whether you should buy it or not, that is a decision you have to make for yourself. I'm not gonna be 'that guy' to tell you to buy or not buy this game. Hopefully I've helped you make that decision. RebelBubba out.

I've got this game for free during winter event and i didn't want to complain much but... its not that good. I've reserved playing this game until it was done, though i did get a glimpse of it month's ago and quite frankly i don't see a lot of changes, except perhaps intro video. Each part of the game lasts for about 5-10 minutes because game engine just can't handle bigger levels. It can barely handle even those tiny portions of the game filled with few enemies and items to smash and throw about. Character animations are non existent, from running to talking it looks unpleasant, like it was made years ago. I would rather play it in first person view just to avoid seeing those weird running stickmen hands and legs. In fact - it should've been first person, like Dark Messiah. Though i guess we would have to stare at those horrible, motionless, low polygon npc faces then... sigh. There are bugs, there are slowdowns, the story doesn't make any sense whatsoever, with unknown names, places and characters introduced for no specific purpose. Oh that person cared for someone and betrayed us? Its fine - he's dead now. Lizards want humans dead? Humans saved by birds? Birds gone away? Long faces whatstheirnames saved humans again? Why is it so unnecessarily complicated, convoluted and why do you pour so much info in the first 5 minutes of the game? Surely there are better ways to present the world and its story than that? There's also a disconnect between scenes, music, sounds and characters which almost gives me one of those 'omg how did it make onto steam?!?' vibes. Its not THAT bad, but at times you can almost feel bad coding, graphics, animations and characters voices misaligning into something resembling 'Garry's Incident' or 'Slaughtering Grounds'. Though, i will mention it again - its not THAT bad. I suppose what i am trying to say - its not finished. Its unpolished. Its bugged, its laggy, the dialogues are horrendous and the animations (except levitation, which looks pretty neat) will make your eyes bleed. The game is just too ambitious for its own good. Bigger levels, first person view, scratch the story, make it a sandbox with terraforming, telekinesis, fireballs. Heck - a multiplayer arena with all of those same spells would've been amazing. Sadly - no one is playing this game in co-op, the server list is empty. I suppose i could've overlooked bad story if the game had bigger levels and better animations, or i could've overlooked tiny levels and bad animations if the story was amazing but (and i am sorry for that) - i can't recommend this. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ UPD: I really wish there was an option for a 'neutral' rating. While i would not personally recommend this game, i feel that voting down the game you got for free might be a little bit unfair. Thankfully the developers are nice and understanding and a lot of people disagree with my opinion, so this particular review shouldn't be a problem for those who still want to try that game. Its just an opinion after all.

Elsword is an older MMORPG where you play as one of 10+ characters and go on a journey to defeat demons. The gameplay is a bit sticky at first, but you can easily get used to it. The PVE is a bit boring at times, but the PVP is where it really shines. It acts as sort of a fencing type game where if you land a hit, you need to know how to chain into other attacks. The characters each have their own personalities, and are unique in some ways or another. The game has equal fanservice between characters aswell, mostly leaning more towards males, but overall it isn't that kind've sexualization you see in other games. The music is pretty catchy at some parts, and isn't too bad, but like other games, you'll eventually want to turn it off. I keep mine on because I can ignore it. I have played every souls game for at least 100 hours each and I must say this game lives up to the quality I've come to expect. All the core mechanics are here: Range, melee, magic builds and hybrids, stamina management, equipment/weight management, fashion, and my beloved parrying to name a few so I felt right at home. I love the tweaks they made to this system as well, you get 2 weapon sets to adjust, and when one is equipped, the other doesn't effect your weight. Also parrying animations are legit and can distance other opponents. There are different combos you can perform from standard X, X, X ground combo to X,Y,(X or Y repeated) air combos. Using magic is really satisfying as well in my experience whether you need to zone or distance yourself. Initially I didn't feel very drawn in to the world until I discovered that this game has something no other souls game has. Something I hold very dear to my heart and is becoming harder to find in any games these days. That thing is local co op. I had already played an hour before my older brother picked up the sticks and joined me, so I made a new mage/dex build while he went holy knight. We have been hooked ever since, I love how dynamic our methods in fighting can become as we increase our abilities to crush our foes. There is just nothing like playing along side a sibling or good friend in a game that requires both of you to always be on your toes. It is harder with two people and that is just the way we want it. Now I haven't been exposed to Metroid or Castlevania so I can't use those as reference, but I love the way maps are designed for platforming, moving up and down, it all feels really smooth. Exploration is great as your field of view won't show you everything and you never know what you will find next. If my brother would die late in a stage's progression, I would have to make a choice to either return to a sanctuary and revive him or keep moving forward hoping I find a new one. Sometimes I found one, sometimes I came across a boss who wanted nothing more than to rip me to shreds. Oh and bosses have more than 1 phase like Dark Souls 3/Bloodborne. All in all I highly recommend this game co op or not, it makes you work for success, and feel like a total badass while you do it. We are still learning a lot and have a long way to go, and I can definitely see the replay value this game has to offer. I give Salt and Sanctuary 3 thumbs up, 5 gold stars, and a burrito from your favorite mexican restaurant.

This is 'Dark Souls' meets 'Castlevania: Symphony of the Night'. The game isn't perfect, due to a few odd bugs here and there, but it's nothing game breaking. With Salt and Sanctuary, these small budget indie developers have done something that the multi-million dollar 'triple-A' gaming companies have been unable to do: create a game that *feels* like it belongs in the Dark Souls game franchise, along with Demon's Soul and BloodBorne. It's amazing, and well worth looking into if you are a fan of that series.

426.app_name: Sword of the Stars II: Enhanced Edition
reviews: Overall a good game. When first released the game was unplayable yes but now it is extremely playable. My only gripes are the radically changed command system lack of ability to change map sizes (without a third party program) compared to SotS prime. My problem with the command system is that instead of just pressing “M” to move a fleet now you have to assign a “mission”. My other issue is that when you “set up” a game you don’t have the ability to customize the maps like in SotS. I really liked being able to set minimum distance between stars, star count etc but again with a 3rd party program you can do just that. However all is not bad. The new Loa race is fun to play, especially considering I can’t think of another game that lets you play as an AI race. Another bonus is now you start off with cruisers instead of destroyers, you can still have destroyers but they are now drones carried on special hulls and act as little more than a meat shield. Another benefit of SotS2 is that the tech tree is full but your ability to research tech is dependent on feasibility studies. But this means that even with a 1% chance of feasibility you still have a chance to research and get the tech. Some people complain about the 'end turn' times. Trust me those will save you much headache later down the line as while you have that period of time of nothing it gives you a chance to reflect about overall strategy. This game also has a throw you to the wolves learning system. Many players have created guides though so you aren't completely screwed but If you enjoy learning by yourself it can be quite enjoyable. Highly recommended

This game is an abomination against all that is good. Many people may have fond memories of Sword of the Stars I, which is a fun game. Sadly, this game will only serve to tarnish your memories of fun and joy and replace them with anger, sadness, and a sense of puzzlement as to what could have possibly possessed the developers to make such a steaming pile of feces. The game is filled with....curious...design decisions. Such as the opening techs taking 30+ turns to research. Or the fact that designing a new warship requires you to destroy half your treasury to change one gun. Neither of these problems were present in the original game, The UI is confusing and bad, and even the free expansion pack does not serve to improve it. Avoid this game and go play the original game or Galactic Civilizations.

On the plus side, the tactical battles are very pretty and the way ships take damage is great. On the negative side, the strategic level is a mess. You can't just tell ships to go someplace, you have assign them to a fleet commanded by your limited number of admirals and generate a mission to go to a place. It's hard to describe exactly but it's very counter intutive and feels 'backwards'. You also can't ships in reserve on a fleet like in it's predecessor so even if you have a numerical advantage in ships since you're limited by what admirals can command. If you want to crush an enemy with your industrial might, the previously stated issues make it a logistical nightmare. If it was possible to mod this game into something more resembling the previous Sword of the Stars it'd be a pretty good game, as it stands I can't recommend it because it is simply so tedious to play.

NOTE: Played a lot offline so low playtime! Having self taught this game to myself and a group of friends, I have a good perspective on this game to the majority of people only playing this card game for the first time. Positives: 1) Good Clean UI and very helpful card highlighting - Memorising which card matches with which is abit hard for many people (November especially) and this game allows you to play without having to memorise, which is great for getting players right in. 2) AI is fierce - A problem this game might have face would be an AI that just matches cards randomly but as far as I have seen the AI has been great so far. It capitalises on you being greedy and punishes you for it a lot. 3) Brilliant Tutorial - I made slides to teach this game to my friends. This game has it all written down and the limits of the what moves you can make and identifying the Yaku immediately helps it with beginners a lot. I think anyone looking to learn Hanafuda should start with the game. Negatives: 1) House Rules? - The game at one stage said the game is played accross Japan with house rules and It would be GREAT if they had that here, especially with their collection mode which honestly needs a bit of more substance for it to have more replay value. 2) Multiplayer - This game badly needs this for the game community to expand. I have actual Hanafuda cards so I can get by without it but having this multiplayer function would be brilliant for this game. 3) One Trick AI - The AI is great and all but its play has little variance. Gets Yaku, 2 cards left? Stops. Gets 3 Brights? Chances are, stops. I have played with my friends and seen ridiculous draws like throwing down a Chrysanthenum card to only pick up a sake cup that just flipped open into double viewing combo (Moon, Sakura and Sake Cup). I don't see the AI having the balls to do that. I know making AI is hard but having some variance in AI, like one that plays more safely, another that plays aggressively will add so much depth into this game. Looking at the collection mode, I feel that the game missed some chances to make it a Brilliant game because having all those individuals across Japan you can play against might be like some AI gauntlet with each with local house rules or differing AI. That would have been a strong feature that adds a lot of replayability but overall I love when traditional games like this get to see the light of day on Steam and gain a wider audience. Overall, I would reccomend this game to people who like traditional games that have a lot of luck involved but also a bit of skill.

A very faithful rendition of Koi-Koi with a fairly smart A.I. opponent. The UI and presentation is about as beautiful and simplistic as the Hanafuda deck itself. You can jump in for a match instantly with Quick Play or try Collection Mode, which is a sort of 'campaign' like mode where you choose a region of Japan and face an opponent in a game of Koi-Koi. The main focus of this mode is to collect postcards that depict beautiful photographs taken in the region you chose previously. Overall, it's simply Koi-Koi, and that's all you really need a game like this to be. It's presented in a lovely way and there's even a tutorial for new players. The game goes as far as highlighting possible matches for yakus, and even a complete list of both the cards and yakus for you to look over at a glance. If you are new to Koi-Koi and are interested in learning to play it, or a long time fan of the age old playing card game, it's certainly worth picking up!

-A Total Middle of the Road Experience- Putrefaction is one of those games that makes me wish the Steam reviews section had a rating that was right in the middle. I've played through Putrefaction on 'normal' once, dabbled in survival and have a game on the 'hard' setting started. The game is enjoyable enough but not wholly recommendable either. On the other hand, it was pretty fun while it lasted. Unlike a game I really, really enjoy and am encouraged to come back and play all of the difficulties, Putrefaction feels like a chore already to start over. In the game you play as an unnamed operative who is sent in to clean up a monster-creating infection in some underground stronghold beneath a mountain. That is as much story as you're going to get. This game probably has less story/atmosphere than Doom I, Quake I and the first Serious Sam. In this game you get equipped with a fun selection of various guns and blast your way through levels crammed with ugly baddies. There's no voice-acting or other distractions to keep you from the task at hand. This game makes even Doom and Quake seem complicated as there are no secrets to be found, keycards or otherwise. As much as I love a back to basics game, this one feels like a totally dry piece of toast with no jam or butter added for flavor. The shooting is fine for the most part. Sometimes things will hiccup graphically but overall I had very little trouble there. The guns are cool, satisfying to use and do some Soldier of Fortune-esque gore damage to the monsters. Monster A.I. on the other hand is dumber than dirt for the most part. You can jump on top of a box if you're having any trouble (and it wasn't very difficult on normal overall), and just pick off ranged enemies while the landlubbers dumbly run up against it...trying to nail you yet being too stupid to figure out how. At least those classic games had beasties that each had their own way of making their demise a pain in the butt. Thankfully some small enemies, ones with guns, a type that rolls, a self-destructor, etc. shake things up slightly from all of the goons that run straight at you (and they are plentiful). There's a pair of boss fights to further spice things up and they were fun enough to fight if rather unoriginal. Sound is unremarkable, the shooting is alright although the monster sounds are rather laughable and shouldn't scare anyone under the age of 10. Control is a little loose, not enough to cause alot of cheap deaths, but don't be surprised if one or two occur. When you need to dodge out of the way of anything, you'll find that you have to plan your movements because Mr. Unnamed Operative skipped the space marine diet/exercise regimen. Jumping is wonky which really isn't a problem as there isn't really any pesky platforming segments. You just shoot, blast, shoot, blast, rinse, repeat. I would say I got more enjoyment out of Dead Effect in recent times than this. Simplicity in gaming is a beautiful thing and I'm always down try these new school takes on old school gaming. The problem here is that it's so very linear. With no secrets to find, no overly challenging or memorable battles, respsawning monsters that block your progression and such point A to B gameplay, it becomes very mundane very quickly. Throwback games are fun, but there has to be some salt, pepper or touch of seasoning to make sure you don't end up 'boring' instead of 'old school.' That's the biggest problem here. I'll break it down into some pros and cons... Pros -Simple, mostly fun old school shooting -Plenty of monsters to fight -Solid selection of guns and most are fun to use -The way guns gore the monsters is entertaining -Boss fights were decent Cons -No secrets, little variety, very plain, bland levels, etc. -Ho-hum graphics (but good enough for what it is) -Unremarkable sound -Controls slightly wonky -Pretty short -Doesn't encourage much replay even with a survival mode and different difficulties -Almost zero of its own personality as a game Overall, depending on how much you are into first person shooters or not will determine if you need to play this. I'm glad I did but I'm not sure I'll get much past my 6/10 achievements and a normal completion. Most every game I own I play through more than once. For whatever reason, it's a struggle to want to progress on hard with absolutely nothing to find because the game is so bare bones. I'm impressed what a single person was able to develop here and Oleg shows lots of potential for future gaming projects but I don't think he's quite found his whole groove yet. I'm going to have to say this one is a pass unless it pops up for less than $5. Rating: 5.0/10 UPDATE: I did find some glitches on hard. I fell through the first level no less than 2 times near the end right when I was about to finish. I dropped the score and uninstalled the game. Yeah, this one is a definite pass unless you got extra cash sitting around.

For someone like me who already found Uplink to be too unrealistic this game is just no good. It's basically a script-kiddie simulator and a very short one aswell (finished in 3.5h). Although I deleted my logs throughout the entire game I never felt threatened or in danger in any way. When you start hacking there might show up a trace but once you finished hacking you can just disconnect, reconnect and the trace goes away. This is something that was solved much better in Uplink where all your credentials became useless and the system locked itself up again once you disconnected. The game shows you whether there is a proxy or firewall and it's super straightforward how you counter these things. There are coloured bars for the ports and you have that one specific program that just brakes that port. Throughout the entire game I felt like a script should replace what I was doing because there was absolutely no thought involved in doing it. The only 'challenge' might be to choose the right program depending on how much RAM you have left. But since there are only about 5 programs it's pretty easy to memorize how much RAM each one uses so you know which you can use simultaneously. I have to give props to the devs for putting so much detail into every single server and all these mails written to and by totaly useless characters which the player could easily miss. I can't stop the feeling that they only added these details since the gameplay itself is so trivial. Even though I bought it during the current sale it feels like a ripoff. Don't do scripts, kids.

The game's weird and obtuse, and that'd be perfectly fine if it didn't have a game over. If you do something wrong, the game will penalize you the same way every other game does, by forcing you restart a section. What you do in it is avoid ghosts as you go from room to room fixing lights hoping something useful will appear. You win the level after a few minutes elapse. Getting caught by a ghost or hiding from them will force you to wait longer. You may also find a clock that makes time go faster, so you'll have to wait less. The word wait is essential to this game and that may give you a clue of how much fun it is. The rules are unclear, which is fine, even welcomed, but in the first thirty minutes or so you'll understand them. The real problem, however, is that enemies may spawn on top of you as you're climbing down a ladder. They may appear with no warning from a door as you're busy opening it. It seems they're programmed to spawn randomly, with no regards to the player's current position. More than once an enemy appeared blocking the only exit, and I had no choice but to be caught. There is some (very little) strategy involved in winning, but it's offset by randomness. If you're unlucky, you'll have to redo the level. That'd be okay if the core gameplay wasn't repetitive and mechanic. All you do is go from room to room, hold X for a few seconds to fix the light. Then, you may or may not get the choice to wait a few seconds to see if an object appears. That's it. Most of what you do to progress involves waiting or holding a button for a few seconds. You may also choose to take risks and go to an area where a ghost may be in, but at a certain point you'll have nothing else to do but to venture into these areas and hope a ghost doesn't spawn on your face. You may also force ghosts to disappear, or objects to appear, by leaving and entering a floor/room repeatedly. Which isn't engaging at all and just feels like you're abusing the game. You can also choose to do everything really slowly and remain in safe areas for as long as you want to wait for the time to pass. Often you'll see unusual things that you don't fully comprehend, and if you try to interact with them you'll be forced to restart a level. For an instance, you'll see an eye on the wall, the game will tell you how to interact with it. If you do, you'll be taken to a place where all you do is walk, then you'll have to restart the level. Then there's another section to the game where all you do is fix all the lights and walk in a forest, there's no risk involved in any of it, no challenge either. Once again, that'd be fine. I like walking simulators, I like weird games. But the section just keeps repeating itself.

I've never played a 'Graviteam' made game before, so I'm totally unfamiliar with this developer. I have played Battlefront published games like the original Combat Mission series from 15 years ago or so. This game is somewhat comparible in style, however it is more or less a live action game after the pieces are set. This is not a RTS type of game like Company of Heroes, it's really a battlefield simulator with a God's eye view of everything and the ability to pause and speed up. Unfortunately, the developer sort of dumps you straight into a main menu with a couple of large scenarios right off the bat. If you're inexperienced, don't try to play these, use the quick battle option and you will find several tutorial type of scenarios to run. These are extremely sensitive to deviation from the instructions. If you misunderstand an instruction or click the wrong button, you will probably have to start it over again to complete it. Fortunatly, these scenarios are small enough to avoid overwhelming a new player. The game interface is quite difficult to understand and the overall presentation is not well thought out. However it is configuable and if you're willing to spend some time watching experienced players play this game on Youtube, it is not an insurmountable task to get to a point where you find it playable. The sound quality is fair, but not great, I get a bit of popping and crackling with button clicks and other actions that is annoying with headphones on. The music was aweful and I had to turn it off within munites of playing my first scenario. The graphics would have been cutting edge 10 years ago; today they are passable. The game play is actually quite fun. There is a setup phase, then a battle phase. The setup of your forces is a bit simplified, however there is a decent amount of complexity and you can do an adequate level of fine tuning of positions. The line of site tool is extremely valuable, especially during the deployment phase. Once the battle begins, your task is mainly scanning your God's eye around the battlefield and prioritizing targets or adjusting force maneuvers/positions. You never control anything directly, you can issues orders. There is a great deal of complexity and some battles are so large, that micromanagement would make the game too tedious. If you're looking for a good WWII battlefield simulation with lots of complexity and accuracy to details, you will like this. This is not the type of game most would enjoy or take the time to understand, but as a wargaming veteran, I am enjoying it.

Rochard never gained enough traction because of its small marketing efforts and smaller demographic, which is a shame because it's the quintessential small, charming indie puzzle platformer game with personality and care. This was one of the earliest games to utilize the Unity Engine. It benefits from it, and will feel current for many years. Highlights

Honestly, this game will suck you in with nice atmosphere music for you to enjoy solving puzzle, You could also enjoy the story, if you can. I find the ending suck , waiting for the next game. Meanwhile, you could spend your tons of free times in this game and feel brilliand about it.

This game is under rated. And really fun. Its a 2D puzzle platformer with a little combat. But its so much more. The puzzle dynamic isn't very hard core like Braid, and is not at all frustrating. The combat at times is challenging, however the checkpoint system will allow you to experiment. The story is a little weak (especially with the way the game concludes teasing a Rochard 2) but the voice acting is really good and makes you care about the world. The soundtrack is stunning both in game and out, and the sound design is pretty decent with its audio ques. I played this game with an PS4 pad and it is probably the most responsive game i have played using a controller. I highly recomend this game to anyone looking to play a platformer that isn't too long. Note - If you are visually impared, you can play this game. There is a bit of text when identifying interactable objects within each level, but it really isn't important. There is also a color dynamic which may be a little tricky, but not tricky enough for you to just figure out. Also in a couple of levels the camera zooms out a little too much, so playing this on a small screen may bbe a little tricky. The art style provides plenty of contrast for you to distinguish your position in each level, and the audio ques are good.

PROS: - Great indie game that actually isn't indie quality; level design, art direction, soundtrack, and pretty much everything is high quality. - Clean physics engine integrated with the game mechanics; gravity gun, which must have been inspired by Half-Life 2 , but what games aren't influenced by Half-Life and Portal series these days? - Moderately challenging Puzzles; perfect casual genre as stated on Steam Store page. - Awesome music is never overused and it is only played in the very right moments for the best atmospheric experiences. - The game has cartoony graphics and style, and overall lighthearted vibe but there are emotionally touching moments; Zander. D: - The story is clichéd. However, it does not matter because games do not always have to be original and groundbreaking in every aspects to be fun. You have to fight and stop the corrupt corporate mastermind who is trying to take over the universe, or something like that; the story flows and fits just fine with overall tone of the game and the execution is also great. CONS: - I really can't think of any cons. Final Remarks: Even though Rochard is categorized as indie genre, all work is done by professionals and you will know what I mean once you get your hands on this game. You should expect Bastion kind of quality minus a big budget and Warner Bros.. DLC Review: Hard Times Soundtrack and Artbook . RECOMMENDED .

It's not a terrible game, but it falls short of its predecessors. The Dungeon Master and Eye of the Beholder series were much better games than this one. Let me list the good and bad points: -- Good -- - The graphics are sharp. Thumbs up in this department. - The monsters actually behave differently depending on their type, giving you the idea that they aren't just sacks of hitpoints charging at you. - A lot of secrets to uncover. - Most levels have a healing crystal that will instantly heal your party and resurrect fallen members. -- Bad -- - The magic system is terrible. Both DM and EOB had a rich magic system with a lot of useful spells, both combat and utility. This game has essentially 6 or 7 spells. (There are actually more than this, but in essence a fire arrow spell is the exact same as a lighting/poison/frost arrow, so I am calling it one spell.) Of these, the only real utility spell is a light spell. No healing spells, no create food spells, no detect secrets spells - nothing. This was my #1 biggest complaint with this game. - The puzzles are mostly of the 'hit a switch and race to this location to hit another one' variety. I want puzzles that test my cunning, not my reflexes. - Most of the monsters in the game are about impossible to stand toe-to-toe with. The game relies heavily on the 'attack and sidestep' school of combat. It's wasn't fun in EOB, and it isn't fun here. I understand it for a boss fight, but here it is necessary with most monsters, at least until you are way over their level. - THERE ARE NO HOTKEYS! You have to use your mouse to manually click each party member's weapon in order to attack. Come on guys - even Might and Magic had combat hotkeys! This is annoying with melee attacks, but downright aggravating when it comes to magic. To cast a spell, you have to right-click your wand, select the runes (up to 3), and then click again. Want to cast that spell again? Ok, 5 more clicks coming right up. All this while trying to sidestep and manage 3 other party members' melee attacks. My recommendation is go back and play DM or EOB. They are much better (although uglier) games.

Every now and then there comes a game that tries to revisit genres that have fallen by the wayside as the video game industry continues to change and grow. Dungeon crawler games, for the most part, happen to be one of those genres. So when I first saw images for Legend of Grimrock I couldn’t help but be excited. When I was a kid I spent a lot of time playing the old dungeon crawler games. I still vividly remember such titles as Dungeon Master and Dungeon Master II: The Legend of Skullkeep. Given how much time I spent playing those games, and loving every minute of it, I was hoping that this new game would live up to the games in whose footsteps it was following. I’ll tell you right now, I have not been disappointed. Legend of Grimrock is everything it is supposed to be. It is an old-style dungeon crawler modernized for today’s gaming world. While such a game can be limited in terms of graphics and art style, Almost Human, the indie developer behind the title, has executed it perfectly. The game looks great and the various creatures’ appearances are fantastic given the limits of the genre. Read the rest of my review at Press2Reset: http://press2reset.com/reviews/review-legend-of-grimrock/

I mainly writing this review for the nomination, but it is a flat out awesome title. A fair bit of nostalgia is wrapped up in that, but I still think it is a staple game for the survival-horror genre, and definitely one you can't miss as a fan of the series or game type. The visuals, as one might expect from a remaster, are crisp and look fantastic. The mechanics are better than ever, with the option of going with the classics, or a new, smoother set of controls for new players, or those who just flat out hate tank type movement controls. And the audio holds up, even if the dialogue is chessy as hell, but hey, thats RE. I played the original back in 1998 when Dual Shock had just become a fad in my area. That said and considering how stale most horror games have become these days I went in expecting to get bored within the first 30 minutes. But then 3 game play hours later and I was still glued to my screen. This is what horror should be like, the intrigue, the constant dread, the curiosity that overpowers your sense of fear, pushing you through the odds to want to know what's happening. I already know most of the storyline owing to the fact that I played the original, but that doesn't stop me from being absorbed into this. Instead of looking to others to 'fix' Resident Evil, Capcom should just turn back a few pages and read their own old notes. There was no need to jump on the PT bandwagon to make Texas Chainsaw Massacre Simulator meet Outlast. Right here...RIGHT HERE is the holy grail of horror. You're playing as a fully trained commando with the ability to shove grenades down zombies' throats and explode their innards out and even that isn't enough to stop the fear. There are barely any jumpscares here because the game doesn't need to rely on them, the fear follows you around and stays with you whether it be caused by you running short on health or simply anticipating something terrible to happen yourself or the camera angles making you feel that you're being watched all the time rather than you watching your character move. Horror doesn't need to be first person to work, this here is the testimony to that. A masterpiece. A Classic Masterpiece made even better by the reworks.

Okay, you all know this is as much for that Steam Contest as it is heartfelt -- but since i have given most of you this game over time, you know it is true. GHOST MASTER was one of those hidden gems that I have replayed god knows how many times and still has a lot of legs today. It is joyous, funny, and occasionally frustrating -- but an amazing strategy title that is funny and well designed and at $5 or less you can't go wrong. . .

FULL DISCLOSURE: I played this during my childhood when it was first released and therefore this game is very nostalgic for me . Disclosure over: I have never played and will likely never play another game like Ghost Master. It takes a very unique concept and runs as far as it could have been taken given the games budget. You play through several maps either scaring everyone away or completing objectives (or both). The act of terrorizing away mortals from their homes is suprisingly enjoyable, and the objectives vary the gameplay nicely. Unfortuantly, the game is short, but each level has immense replay value through trying to unlock new ghosts and attempting to reach a triple pumpkin time. There are also bugs and glitches, but they are rarely game breaking and are not enough to make this game not worth five dollars. Also, this game is constantly discounted to 74 cents, a bargain price for a game of this quality.

Ghost Master is a game most people have never heard of. In fact, even during its release in 2003 it never received much publicity or commercialism. This is because it wasn't really a 'big project' in the first place. Basically no one ever heard of Sick Puppies, the developing company, because they had only released one other game before: Pipe Dreams 3D, two years prior to this game. Sick Puppies remained true to its name in the business due to the fact they were, well, a sick company. They disbanded only a year after the release of Ghost Master, though to this day the game still has a cult following, and for very good reasons. Ghost Master is an extremely original game, with unique, haunting and spiritual music (of which is perhaps my favorite aspect of this game), gameplay and level design. You play the role of a Ghost Master, which is basically just a name for you as you scroll around in this RTS 3D world and try to best command the spirits in your arsenal to accomplish certain objectives - mostly involving the casting of 'spells' (powers) to scare mortals until they run away from the level, earning you victory when all mortals are gone - or else left insane, which I might add is hard to do, but really funny to see. The abilities of your ghosts depend on the individual and type, and you can unlock more ghosts by playing levels and finding 'restless spirits' which you can talk to, and they give you a quest-like objective which you must find a way to complete before you finish their unfinished business, or else free them. The diversity and imagination of the ghosts themselves is really interesting as many are inspired by many spiritual cultures and myths, or even pop-culture as some are obvious parodies of famous horror movies. Some ghosts are elementals, others are Gremlins, which are the wild spirits of animals, and others are poltregiests, the tortured spirits of humans who were once mortals. Each ghost has a unique mini-profile with an amusing backstory, and a semi-unique set of powers you can purchas as training with the points you earn for completing levels. This currency is called Gold Plasm. Every ghost has a specific kind of fetter (a place or a type of thing) they can bind themselves to at your command when playing a level, based on their type or perhaps how they died. This also can relate to how a restless spirit might be trapped in a level, waiting for you to free them and unlock them. One of my more favorite spirits was an air elemental named Whisperwind, a fairy-like being who was trapped in a dream-catcher which you have to destroy. The game itself is quite tacky with its graphics, but at the same time the art style and atmosphere sends a very good at making you feel immersed in the creepiness of it all. It's easy to imagine how scared the mortals must be of you, walking around in all those locations you haunt because of how weirdly mystical everything seems, though you will sometimes still chuckle at the plastic hair of mortals and french-fry fingers of some of your ghosts with all their silly low quality models. The gameplay, as mentioned before, is extremely unique, as I've never seen a single game to this day that really has the same kind of mechanics you see in this classic gem. However, the game is also quite buggy sometimes, and I can't promis you you wont ever flip your table in rage due to mortals not doing what you want them to. This is the most frusterating part of the game, because manipulating the mortals into doing something or triggering something is usually the only way to unlock new ghosts as you use them to do something to set other spirits free. An example of frustration would be this one ghost of a murdered sales woman, whom would be unlocked after you help her with her unfinished business by lurring a woman to her makeup tray which was resting on a table near her hidden corpse. For some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason, the woman would actually use this product despite all the dust and the DEAD BODY, but the real trick is getting the female mortal to notice it. It takes several different lurring spells, and for what ever reason, this is the one ghost I have the most trouble saving because it's completely random. I've literally tried for hours sometimes to get her and the mortals keep glitching out and avoiding her room too soon, but then other times I get her unlocked WITH OUT EVEN DOING ANYTHING! That's right, sometimes, when there's a blue moon out in real life, and the stars align perfectly for you, your objectives for a few certain things in the game may be accomplished COMPLETELY ON THEIR OWN with no prompt from you. The game is stupid like this sometimes. Mortals will also teleport sometimes. When starting a level, first you select your ghosts. You use their powers to manipulate the environment and the mortals to complete various objectives, but it always ends with you scaring them all off. You assign your spirits a room or area based on their fetters - a gremlin for example will stay at any electronic you bind him to. In doing this, you strategize by looking at the path-finding patterns of the mortals to see how to lay traps. Some fetters however are semi-mobile, as in, a mortal may pick your object up and carry your spirit somewhere else. To stop this, just make your ghost scare that person. Almost every level, even without the ghosts, is a giant refference to a famous horror story or novel. You will play a parody of The Amityville Horror, Sleepy Hollow and Blair Witch for example. The game is a strange mix of humor and horror involving tacky and almost slap-stick themes while at the same time having a disturbingly chilling environment at times. This is perhaps one of the game's strongest qualties - the combination of a spooky atmosphere, fun gameplay and a light air of occasional black comedy that keeps the player on their toes as they enjoy the ride - up until at some point they trip and fall over due to one of the game's occasionally irritatingly hard levels. This game isn't perfect, and sometimes you *will* get mad at it. In the end, I think it's still a great classic and a shame that no sequels are being made. Not officially anyway. Though some indi developers are trying somewhat to get something going (you can find them easily by googling Ghost Master 2), there's no telling if they'll ever really finish, as very little is shown so far. Right now, Ghost Master is availabe to everyone here at the stock price of 5 USD, which in my opinion is a great price. It's definetly not a fancy game. It doesn't have amazing graphics (despite its interesting theme and art style), it's kind of glitchy sometimes, and hardly anyone knows about it and the developing company is literally dead now. If you're still unsure about this game, then wait for halloween. In all the time I've been on Steam, I've seen Ghost Master go on sale for 1.50 USD or so every single time, as one of the first things to go on sale. That's practically making this game free, and once its in your hands, it's easy to get addicted to. It has decent replayability, and I've finished it like 5 times already in all the time I've had this game. I actually grew up with this, but I lost the disc and recently saw the game for sale here. It was so cheap, I couldn't resist just getting it again. PS: Look for the popular All Ghosts Mod which brings very welcome rebalancing to the game's level select. Also, this game works for me on Windows 10, but some may have to use work-arounds.

Okay... there's one very good point I will give this game, and that that it's absolutely gorgeous and imaginative. A true piece of art. If you're looking for an abstract painting (you'll recognise its inspiration, such as MC Esher), but that you can interact with a little, than you've found something you'll like. Otherwise I have many grippes with this game. After less than an hour it was too annoying and I couldn't keep playing. First off, the interaction system is wayyy too clunky. I much prefer the good ol' verb-based system : push, pull, take, talk, etc. Here you have to actually pull stuff by making very specific motion with your mouse. And because of this, it took me the longest time to get out of the cage at the beginning. After clicking furiously all around the screen, after having poked and pulled at the paperclip to no effect I was about to give up already. Then I just went crazy on it, moving my mouse all around, and it finally fell. My only thought was : ARE YOUR SERIOUS? So yeah, this isn't nearly as intuitive nor as charming as Monkey Island, unfortunatly. The few characters there are only speak with speech bubbles and gibberish. This would be fine if their message was interesting, but they are only boring. Yes, the characters are pretty much untinteresting at best, shallow and blank at worst. Even the main character is weird and uncharacterised. He/she never speaks, you don't really know anything about him/her except that his/her parents moved in a new house and she is pulled into this miniature dimension. It would of added a lot to have given him/her an actual voice, so he/she could give his/her thoughts about the strange world he/she got into. The puzzles themselves seem very contrived and strange, which follows the style of the world. I guess I'm just not smart enough, but I honestly couldn't solve most of them. The problem being, I didn't even know what the problems were most of the time. One room I solved out of pure luck, distracting an evil teapot with a fly I randomly captured in a bottle. Half the time I just looked, scratching my head, trying to understand what I was looking at. If the character could at least of given me a hint or something to identify what I needed to do it would of helped. Unfortunatly, after seeing all the strange rooms and not making any progress, I decided to stop playing. Now you might decipher the cryptic solutions to these rooms, connected by a kind of MC Escher maze, but I wasn't enjoying it so I couldn't be bothered. The last straw was a room where a firework kept firing in an endless loop of ear-destroying pain, while I got posed by a piece-swapping puzzle to this noise. NO THANKS. I'M OUT. So yeah. Very pretty game, but mechanically too frustrating. If you're the type, like me, to enjoy artsy visuals, than I recommend this. Otherwise, if you want a well put together point n' click game, look elsewhere. Unless its on sale for very cheap. If you want a number, I'll give it a 6.5, 5 points for excellent visuals plus 1.5 for playability. It just couldn't pull me in (pun intented).

My overall rating for Cursed Sight: 88/100 Another visual novel from the creator Invertmouse, this time set in medieval fantasy of two kingdoms, who are struggling for control over the world and the key to solve this is a cursed sight of one priestess named Miyon. Lets see in detail, what went good and what should be better. GAMEPLAY + Nice timing of chapters + Animations + Multiple endings - Some cruel moments Chapters were timed perfectly, story was a bit cliché, but originally processed, what I count as a great plus for this title, due in time, when everything was discovered, original presentation is a key how to achieve a players attention. Also animations were fine, I am glad, that also multiple endings were positive feature, not just self-purpose. But the moment with rabbit was very cruel and disturbing. I know, this was the purpose, but I think it might be avoided. Just personal opinion. :-D CHARACTERS + Gai + Miyon + Sasa + Queen Hydrianne o King Lok - West Tarians Gai was funny, but also I liked his saracsm, as a kid who was torn from his world and sent to slavery. Miyon was a typical spoiled brat, but when you went under her mask, you saw, what was the true reason behind her behaviours. I liked Sasa from the very start, she was as catalysator of other relationships and a mentor who would everyone desire to have. Positive character was also Queen Hydrianne, I think that is how a leader should behave. King lok was neutral, I understand his pose, yet, the potential was not fully achieved. But West Tarians had their potentials a bit wasted, especially Gai's sister's companion, who was changing his appearance and poses too quickly and a bit cheaply. VISUALS + Shoujo style I liked, that this style was chosen, it fitted perfectly for the set-up and story. Nothing to complain here about. SOUNDTRACK + Fitting the stiuation + Atmospheric Efe Tozan did a great work composing those songs, I liked them and some of them I listen to even today. Songs were changing accordingly to the situation and atmosphere. Thumbs up here. SUMMARY Cursed sight has a rich story and no superheroes, what allows players to join them and enjoy, what authors presented to us. Even players out of this genre might find this novel interesting, as story is not disturbing, drawings are decent and atmosphere brilliant. Recommended, also with extras.

This is a complex and deep strategy game that I recommend for those that feel games like EU4 or CKII or HoI3 are too simple or too high-level. This is not quick wargame, and people that expect such a game will be disappointed. It is turn-based, and because both the players turns are executed simultaneously, an additional layer of complexity is added. It gets better if you turn the realism options on, because common sense then helps to understand what happens in the game. There are so many factors to consider that 'gaming the system' is difficult, and that's a good thing. The AI is challenging, for me at least. The dualplayer is Play By Email. It can take hours to issue the orders for 1 turn if you're a control-freak, and while a game-server of some sorts to coordinate games might be easier, emailing is easy enough. I've played their Civil War game (AACW) and Rise of Prussia for many hours and I'm enjoying myself in TEAW. Once you get over the learning curve, you'll find one of the better strategy games out there.

*MILD SPOILERS HERE* So... At first, I decided to delete my review, because it was 'too sentimental'. After I have put some tought into the matter, I came to a conclusion: If a game can somehow manipulate my emotions this hard, I don't give a damn about being sentimental. In my review I mentioned the moment, when the game got me hooked, and this is the scene, when you visit Chloe's house in the first episode. The little details, the sountrack and the gorgeus art direction did it's job. Nostalgy overload at it's finest. The wine stains on the carpet, the drawings on the wall, and the photos on the desk. If you, dear gamer a nostalgic person this setting is enough to bring tears to your eyes. I personaly had to leave my childhood house behind, and each time I visit it, I get the same bittersweet feeling, that time consumes all things. The great thing about this game, that it's full of moments like this. When you just sit on a treestump in the junkyard, or on a bench in the campus, and listen to Max's inner monologue, or discover your fellow students habits and life stories. The characters are some nice piece of writing. They start off like a typical teenage/youngadult stereotype, then as you submerge deeper into the story, you discover that they are human beings each with their own problems and emotions. I also love the 'I can touch everything' mechanic, you can get a lot of background story about places, and characters (wich can be game changing when it's coming to decisions). Ofc I have some problems with the game not just the pink love cloud.The lip sync, the sometimes sloppy animation, and weird dialogues are there, but they are not major flaws imo. Two things however, bugged me a bit. The first thing is the pacing of the last two episode. As things get more and more intense you still have the opportunity to talk with people, to sit down on a becnh or something to think, but the thing is, that you don't really give a ♥♥♥♥ about what are they gonna say, because you will rewind anyway, or just on a 'hurry' because of a ♥♥♥♥ing tornado is on it's way, and the tempo of the narrative requires you to move forward, and fast. Those dialogues (if you chose to sit through them) damage the flow a bit. *MAJOR SPOILER HERE* The second flaw that I can't get around is the ending, when you chose to save Chloe over the town. In contrast to the other ending (that you could see coming since the second episode), this was poorly written and executed. We could not see the results of the tornado, or the possible emotional breakdown of Chloe about her mothers mostly certain death, or Max's feelings about all her friends gone. I could keep up the writing about the possible things that could change that ending, but I don't think its worth to write a few thousand plus characters about the subject. In the end, it was the journey I fell in love, not the ending (however it's heartwrenching to think about we won't see these two again) and I don't give a rats ♥♥♥ about being sentimental anymore. I think you guys can see, that I strongly recommend this game, for the time being, this is one of the favorite games of my life.

Wolfenstein: TNO is a meathead shooter straight out of the 90s with absolutely no new ideas. I feel that everything you need to know about the game comes down to the selection of weapons it gives you. You have: - Pistols (with a silencer) - Assault rifles - Shotguns - Sniper rifles - A laser - Knives And that's it. You couldn't have a more bog standard set of armaments in an FPS if you tried. There's no grenade launcher, there's no jetpack, there's no light saber, there's no psychic telekinesis... just a standard set of weapons to use against a standard set of enemies. You can't even do something as radical as hold a shotgun in one hand and an assault rifle in the other. It's not aggressively bad, in spite of its stupid habit of taking away all your guns at arbitrary moments in the game, but there's just nothing here that I haven't seen before. Even the battle against the giant spider mech consists of tired 'shoot him in the eye and then hit the weakpoint' gameplay. Maybe that's enough for some people. Maybe all you want to do is point your gun at someone speaking German and fire. I get it. But I think that in a post-Bioshock world, our shooters should have higher standards than that. As for its story, I've seen it being lauded in a lot of different quarters. It's not terrible I guess, but I think that if you want to attempt to create serious alternate history fiction revolving around the Nazi regime then you probably should leave out the robot dogs. Just sayin'

This is a difficult review. I don't usually finish games, so generally to get to the end they must have something that grabs me. I remember playing the first few Hitman games and enjoying them enough, so seeing an improved new version on Steam I bought it on an Eidos sale. I finished the story mode for Hitman:Absolution and one of the core reasons was that there was something that drew me back. However overall it's not enough for me to recommend the game, or to want to play it again. Essentially I just ended up grinding it out. Pros: 1. Graphics and audio. Reasoonably well done. A little too much bloom, and the cutscenes are jarringly sub-par compared to the in-game graphics but nonetheless it looks the Hitman part. For the record, I have a medium rig. 2. Some of the Gameplay. I think when it works, this was the games strongest point. When playing in crowds or having lots of easily accessible hiding spots Hitman was quite enjoyable. Not unlike watching a guilty pleasure B-grade action movie. Cons: - When it doesn't work though. OMG then it's obvious; 1. Cutscene story inconsistency - what's the point of being a super-assassin (the story says you are), and playing like one (making sure not to make stupid mistakes), when the protaganist just throws it out the door at every cutscene? It was like a slap in the face whenever he kept making rookie mistakes and then you, have to get him out of the predicament. 2. Recon - Ugh. So I said that it had areas that worked. But overall, it was just bad. Instead of being able to survey the location, choose the best option(s) available and to prepare (with costumes, weapons etc) you were simply just dumped at the beginning of each location in full assassin uniform glory. 3. Disguises - So you can grab a disguise, that's great! Problem is that the second you do this, any NPC who have the same uniform are onto you. So you spend more time hiding from them. (also, can't he afford a wig or beard?). Which leads me to; 4. NPCs - The game makes you spend all of your time hiding out of the line of sight of any NPC. They just have a preset walking path (you can see that from your flames of hell vision) and all you end up doing is trying to walk between these paths. What's the point of disguises or stealth then? In addition any NPC that catches you, immediately notifies everyone else. How can that be? Wouldn't some NPC (like janitors) be slower to do that? Wouldn't they need to actually take the time to call someone (not just a generic soundbyte while you're strangling them). 5. Dumping bodies - So, you can hide bodies in lots of containers and boxes around the locations - but what ever happened to just being able to hide them in dark areas that NPC don't walk through? If you don't hide them in a box, then they're always found. In addition, if I'm an assassin and I make an NPC bleed, can't I mop up the blood instead of leaving evidence? 6. Control - The amount of times I pressed the wrong button or my character did the wrong thing was way too numerous. Hold Y for this, but press Y for that, Hold A for this, but press A for that. Why make it so convoluted? And when it's such a fine line in getting the timing right. This got really frustrating fast. 7. Agent 47's voice - OK not such a big one, but still I didn't like it. I never really liked his voice originally but now it really doesn't seem to match with what he looks like. No hate at the actor, more just the older articulate voice was mismatched with the bald angry so and so. Especially when I'm used to seeing Michael Chiklis, Jason Statham, and Bruce Willis where their voices actually match their looks. So the whole game just feels like you're constantly waiting for an NPC to pull the trigger on you. What kind of stealth game is that? There should be an element of getting caught but not to that extent (and maybe only in more difficult levels). If I was a real assassin wouldn't I be good at this by now? My disguise solid enough not to draw any attention because I'm great at not standing out? I'm really hoping that the next iteration will play more out like a proper recon game. Something like GTA V heists as the right way to pull a job. So you get to check the place out first and determine entry points. You then get to get (steal?) the devices and uniforms you need, and finally you then have to pull the job.
